•Definition: They are clonal diseases arising in hematopoietic myeloid stem or progenitor cells, including both chronic and acute neoplasms.

Pathogenesis

➢Genomic instability with multiple steps of genetic mutations of either proto- oncogenes or tumor suppressor genes leading to: 1-Impaired control of the cell cycle leading to its rapid uncontrolled proliferation with expansion of the growth over the expense of normal growth of other cells. 2-Speed through or even skip from cell cycle checkpoints passing the DNA mutations to the daughter cells. 3-Defects in terminal differentiation. 4- Inhibition of apoptosis.

➢Epigenetic alteration: 1-Transcription alteration result from alteration of the methylation state of the promotor causing either silencing or over-expression of the gene. 2-Post-transcriptional alteration that may alter translation of the gene through alteration of the methylation states of the promotors controlling the microRNase that regulate gene expression causing either silencing or over-expression of the gene.

Classes

–Myeloid precursor lesion (Clonal hematopoiesis)

–Myeloproliferative neoplasms.

–Mastocytosis.

–Myelodysplastic neoplasms.

–Myelodysplastic/ Myeloproliferative neoplasms.

–Acute myeloid leukemia

–Myeloid malignancies, secondary.

–Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and defining gene rearrangement.

–Acute leukemia of mixed or ambiguous lineage. 3

Original page 4

Clonal Hematopoiesis

4

Original page 5

•Clonal Hematopoiesis: Clonal outgrowth of hematopoietic cells from affected stem or progenitor cells regardless of cause or disease state

•Age-related clonal hematopoiesis: Clonal Hematopoiesis detected in the blood or bone marrow associated with aging without a diagnosed hematologic disorder or cytopenia. No specific gene alteration. It is a synonym for clonal hematopoiesis

•Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP): Clonal hematopoiesis detected in the blood or bone marrow with somatic mutations of myeloid malignancy present at a variant allele fraction of ⩾2% without a diagnosed hematologic disorder or unexplained cytopenia.

○Epidemiology: It is rare in individuals under 40 years old, but affects 10-40% of individuals after 65 years. Risk factors:

–Aging is the dominant risk factor

–Smoking

–Male sex

–Exposure to cytotoxic therapies

–Aplastic anemia.

–Several germline variants.

–Hispanic ancestry associates with decreased risk

○Pathogenesis:

–The mutations are most often base substitutions, small insertions/deletions, or chromosomal abnormality.

–The most frequently reported mutations occur in the key epigenetic modifiers DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1, PPM1D, TP53, ASXL1, SF3B1, SRSF2, and U2AF1.

–Possible causes in the absence of a known mutation, are unknown mutations. 5

Original page 6

○Essential criteria:

–Detection of one or more somatic mutations with variant allele fraction ≥ 2% (≥ 4% for X-linked gene mutations in males) in DNA from blood or bone marrow cells involving genes listed in the WHO table.

–Absence of unexplained cytopenias.

–Absence of diagnostic criteria for defined myeloid neoplasms. N.B.: Diagnosis can be made by abnormalities in FISH or karyotyping as monosomy Y N.B.: Abnormal red blood cell indices, does not exclude the diagnosis.

○Prognosis: Predominantly benign natural history.

–Progression to malignancy occur in 0.5-1%/year. Increased risk of progression is associated with:

○Large clone or of multiple gene mutations.

○Mutations in TP53, U2AF1, SRSF2, IDH2, IDH1, SF3B1 and ASXL1.

○Concomitant presence of mosaic clonal alterations

–Increased risk of all-cause mortality, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and autoimmune disease.

•Clonal cytopenias of undetermined significance (CCUS): Clonal hematopoiesis with one or more persistent cytopenias unexplained by hematologic or non-hematologic conditions that do not meet diagnostic criteria for any myeloid neoplasms. N.B.: Idiopathic cytopenias of unknown significance: Sustained unexplained cytopenia without evidence of blood cancer-associated driver mutations.

○Epidemiology:

–Anemia 4.2%, thrombocytopenia 1.6% and neutropenia 4.8 %. Anemia and thrombocytopenia prevalence increase with age but not neutropenia.

–30% of people with one or more cytopenias will have a mutation or a chromosomal abnormality. 6

Original page 7

Risk factors: As clonal hematopoiesis and can occur sporadically or after exposure to cytotoxic treatment.

○Pathogenesis: As clonal hematopoiesis

○Essential criteria:

–Detection of one or more somatic mutations with variant allele fraction ≥ 2% (≥ 4% for X-linked gene mutations in males) in DNA from blood or bone marrow cells involving genes listed in WHO Table or clonal chromosomal abnormalities in myeloid cells.

–One or more unexplained cytopenias that persist for more than 4 months.

–Absence of diagnostic criteria for defined myeloid neoplasms on bone marrow examination

○Prognosis: Risk factors of progression to myeloid neoplasm:

–Size of the clonal population

–The number of somatic alterations

–The presence of specific gene mutations such as those in TP53, PPM1D, JAK2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, IDH2, and IDH1.

–The number and depth of cytopenias particularly in patients with a prior history of exposure to cytotoxic therapy. N.B.: Isolated mutation in DNMT3A has a low risk of progression to MDS or AML. 7

•Definition: They are clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders characterized by the proliferation of one or more terminal differentiated myeloid cell lines(ie. granulocytic, erythroid, and megakaryocytic).

•Epidemiology:

–Annual incidence is 0.44- 5.87 per 100,000.

–The incidence is peaking in the fifth to seventh decades of life, but some subtypes are also reported in children.

•General characters:

–Hypercellularity of the bone marrow, with effective hematopoietic maturation and increased numbers of granulocytes, red blood cells, and/or platelets in the peripheral blood.

–Extramedullary hematopoiesis leading to hepatomegaly and splenomegaly.

–No dysplasia

–Hypercatabolism.

–Complication: 1-Acute leukemia. 2-Bone marrow failure. 3-Bone marrow fibrosis. 4-Ineffective hematopoiesis.

–Signs of progression: 1-Genetic evolution. 2-Increasing organomegaly. 3-Increasing or decreasing blood count. 4-Myelofibrosis. 5-Myelodysplasia. 6-Increasing blasts in peripheral blood or bone marrow. 9

Original page 10

–Subgroups:

○Chronic myeloid leukemia

○Chronic neutrophilic leukemia

○Chronic eosinophilic leukemia

○Polycythemia vera

○Primary myelofibrosis

○Essential thrombocythaemia

○Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia

○Myeloproliferative neoplasm, non-otherwise specified 10

Original page 12

•Definition: It is a myeloproliferative neoplasm caused by clonal autonomous proliferation of hematopoietic pluripotent bone marrow stem cells resulting in an overproduction of predominantly mature granulocytes and their precursors and characterized by positive BCR-ABL1.

Cell of origin

–Itarises from an abnormal pluripotent bone marrow stem cell.

–Disease progression may originate in more committed precursors as granulocyte- macrophage progenitor.

Incidence

–The annual incidence is less than 0.1 in children and more than 2.5 cases per 100,000 population.

–Sex: There is a slight male predominance.

–No Significant ethnic or geographical variations, but an earlier age of onset are reported in lower socioeconomic.

–The prevalence has increased due to the success of tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy in reducing mortality rates.

•Predisposing factors: There is slight or no inherited predisposition and predisposing factors are largely unknown but there is a high incidence of acute radiation exposure.

•Pathogenesis: Clonal hematopoietic disorder as a result of: 1-Philadelphia chromosome:

○It results from t(9; 22)(q34;q11) which leads to juxtaposition of breakpoint cluster region (BCR) on chromosome 22 and Abelson murine leukemia(ABL1) oncogene on chromosome 9 yielding the aberrant BCR-ABL1 fusion gene on 12

Original page 13

chromosome 22 “der chromosome 22” with an increased tyrosine kinase activity leading to constitutive activation of proteins in several signal transduction pathways and uncontrolled proliferation of cells irresponsive to the inhibitory mechanisms. Affected signal transduction pathways include:

➢JAK/STAT pathway which is involved in cell growth and survival.

➢Pl3K/AKT pathway which is involved in cell growth and survival, and inhibition of apoptosis.

➢RAS/MEK pathway which is involved in activation of transcription factors, including NF-KB.

○Sites of break points in the BCR gene: 1-The major breakpoint cluster region (M-bcr) spanning exons 12-16 yielding a protein product of 210 kD leading to CML. The most common breakpoints (98% of CML cases) are exon 13 or 14, spliced to ABL1 exon 2. 2-The minor breakpoint cluster region (m-bcr) (between exons 1 and 2) yielding a protein product of 190 kD leading to ALL. Small amount of 190 kD protein product can be found in more than 90% of CML cases due to alternative splicing of the BCR gene and is the protein product in 1 % of cases of CML which are associated with marked monocytosis. 3-The third breakpoint cluster region (-bcr) spanning exons 17-20 yielding a protein product of 230 kD leading to CML with a prominent neutrophilic maturation and/or conspicuous thrombocytosis.

○Philadelphia chromosome may be simple or complex involving chromosomes 9, 22 and other chromosomes. 13

Original page 14

2-Progression is usually associated with clonal evolution:

–70-80% of cases of transformed phases demonstrate additional cytogenetic changes including 3q26.2 rearrangement, monosomy 7, trisomy 8, isochromosome 17q, trisomy 19, trisomy 21 an additional Philadilphia chromosome and complex karyotypes.

❖The presence of any of these abnormalities at the time of initial diagnosis may be associated with increased risk of transformation. 14

Original page 15

❖The presence of any of these abnormalities is associated with an increased risk of death at low blast levels (1-15%), but has no effect at high blast level (20-30%).

–There may be mutation in TP53, RB1, MYC, CDKN2A (also known as p16INK4a), NRAS, KRAS, RUNX1 (also known as AML1), TET2, CBL, ASXL1, IDH1 and IDH2 genes, but their exact role in the transformation is unknown.

Phases

1.Chronic phase. 2.Blastic phase. N.B.: The term ‘accelerated phase’ is less useful with the use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and is now called 'high-risk chronic phase'.

Clinical picture

1-Clinical picture of the chronic phase: This is the presentation of most patients:

–50% of cases are asymptomatic and discovered accidently.

–Onset is insidious.

–Clinical picture of bone marrow failure: Weakness, recurrent infection and bleeding.

–Hypermetabolism: Night fever, night sweating, weight loss and gout.

–Palpable splenomegaly in 50% of cases

–Most untreated cases progress from advanced phase within 3–5 years after diagnosis. 2-Clinical picture of transformed stages: This is the presentation 5% patients:

–Declining performance status.

–Constitutional signs as fever and weight loss.

–Symptoms related to severe anemia, thrombocytopenia and increased WBC count.

–Splenic enlargement. 15

Original page 16

Complications

1-Acute leukemia:

–AML.

–ALL.

–Biphenotypic leukemia 2-Myelofibrosis. 3-Bone marrow failure.

Laboratory Diagnosis of the chronic phase

➢Evidence of clonality: 1-In-vitro culture yields granulocytic, monocytic, erythroid and megakaryocytic lineages with a positive Philadelphia chromosome. 2-All malignant cells in females carry the same G6PD isoenzyme. 1-Complete blood count:

○WBCs: 99

–Leukocytosis of 12-1000 X 10/L with a median of 80 X 10/L and higher 9 counts in children “Median count is 250 X 10/L”.

–Marked absolute neutrophilia

–Monocytes: Rarely exceeds 3% but this always give absolute monocytosis. Cases of BCR-ABL1 protein product of 190 kD are associated with marked monocytosis.

–Basophilia.

–Eosinophilia.

○RBCs: a-Normocytic normochromic anemia due to the decreased production, and due to the splenomegaly which causes pooling of red cells in the spleen and hypervolemia. b-Macrocytic anemia due to the secondary folate deficiency. 16

Original page 17

○Platelets: 9

–Normal count or thrombocytosis up to 1000 X 10/L or more.

–Thrombocytopenia in transformed phases. It is rare in chronic phases and may be caused by hypersplenism. 2-Blood film:

–Neutrophils in various stages of maturation with predominance of myelocytes and segmented neutrophils.

–No significant dysplasia but psudo Pelger-Heut cells are common.

–Blast count is less than 2%.

–Hypersegmented neutrophils due to folate deficiency.

–Hybrid cells with mixed eosinophilic and basophilic granules.

–Normoblastemia.

3-Neutrophil alkaline phosphatase (NAP) score: Decreased or absent. 4-Biochemical tests:

–Serum uric acid: increased

–Serum calcium: increased

–Serum LDH: increased.

–Serum vitamin B12 and transcobalamin I (TCI): increased

–Serum potassium: Psudohyperkalemia due to the extracellular leakage with normal potassium in citrared plasma. 5-Genetic studies:

–Cytogenetics: Positive Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)(q34;q11). 17

Original page 18

–Molecular genetics (FISH, reverse transcriptase PCR and southern blot): BCR-ABL fusion gene for cryptic translocations.

–New chromosomal abnormality: in blastic crisis

N.B.: Philadilphia positive acute leukemia: 1-Blastic crisis of CML. 2-AML unrelated to CML. 3-Philadelphia positive ALL. 6-Bone marrow:

18

Original page 19

A-Chronic phase:

–Hypercellular bone marrow with prominent granulocytic hyperplasia and relative increase in myelocytes.

–A layer of immature granulocytes (5–10 cells in thickness) is common around the bone trabeculae, in contrast to the normal thickness of 2– 3 cells

–No significant dysplasia.

–Blasts are less than 5% of ANC in chronic phase and increased blast count is a sign of acceleration.

–M/E ratio: increased.

–Erythroid precursors are relatively suppressed

–Megakaryocytes may be normal or slightly suppressed with dwarf megakaryocytes which are smaller than normal with hypolobulated nuclei. It may be moderately or markedly inceased in 40-50% of cases.

–Increased basophils, eosinophils and hybrid cells and their precursors.

–Pseudo-Gucher cells are common. 19

Original page 20

–Reticulin: Moderate to marked increase in 30-40% of cases at diagnosis which is correlated megakaryocytes and spleen size. Fibrosis at the time of diagnosis is associated with a bad prognosis but it has no prognostic value in patients treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

B-Blastic phase:

–Blasts are 20 % or more.

–Lymphoblasts of any level.

–Large foci or clusters of blasts in bone marrow biopsy.

20

Original page 21

7-Immunophenotyping: The main role of immunophenotyping is the analysis of the blasts in the blastic phase:

–Myeloid blasts: a-They have strong, weak, or no MPO activity.

b-They express one or more antigens associated with granulocytic, monocytic, megakaryocytic, and/or erythroid differentiation, such as CD33, CD13, CD14, CD11b, CD11c, CD11 7, CD15, CD41, CD61, and glycophorin A and C, and may express one or more lymphoid antigens (Expression of CD7 is a bad prognostic sign).

–Most lymphoblasts are B lymphoblasts expressing TdT and B lymphocyte markers as CD19, CD10, CD79a, PAX5, and CD20, but a minority of lymphoblasts are T lymphoblasts expressing T lymphocyte markers as CD3, CD2, CD5, CD4, CD8, and CD7. Lymphoblasts may express one or more myeloid markers.

–Bilineage cases or sequential lymphoblastic and myeloblastic blastic phases may occur.

–The frequency of basophil blasts or megakaryoblasts is rare but may occur more frequently with tyrosine kinase inhibitors. 21

Original page 22

WHO criteria

○Chronic phase: Essential criteria:

–Peripheral blood leukocytosis

–Detection of Philadilphia chromosome and/or BCR::ABL1 by cytogenetic and/or appropriate molecular genetic techniques Desirable criteria: Bone marrow aspiration to confirm disease phase, with bone marrow biopsy if:

–Findings in the peripheral blood are atypical

–Cellular aspirate cannot be obtained.

○The WHO criteria of the blastic phase: One or more of the following:

–Blasts in peripheral blood and/or bone marrow are 20 % or more.

–Extramedullary blast proliferation.

–Lymphoblasts in the peripheral blood or bone marrow (even < 10%).

•Differential diagnosis: 1-Polycythemia vera: differentiated by application of the WHO diagnostic criteria of each. 2-Essential thrombocythemia: differentiated by application of the WHO diagnostic criteria of each. 3-Reacetive leukocytosis ‘leukomoid reation”: Leukomoid reaction shows toxic granulation and vacuolation in granulocytes, increased NAP score and negative Philadelphia chromosome. 4-Leukoerythroblastic reaction due to bone marrow infiltration: Bone marrow examination shows infiltration sheets and philadilphia chromosome is negative. 5-Philadelphia positive acute leukemia: Blasts are 20% or more in peripheral blood and/or bone marrow with no history of CML. 22

Original page 23

Treatment

a-First generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor (Imatinib): competes with ATP for binding to BCR-ABL 1 kinase domain inhibiting the phosphorylation of tyrosine residue on its substrate. Resistance: i-Emergence of leukemic subclone with point mutation that inhibits binding of the drug to the kinase domain. It doesn’t occur early in the chronic phase. ii-Overexpression of β-glycoprotein which accelerates the exit of the drug from cells. b-Second and third generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor (Nilotinib, Dosatinib, Bosutinib and Ponatinib): Theyovercome resistance in most but not all kinase domain mutations.

–The molecular response is achieved faster and more frequently with these generations.

–The progression free survival rate is only marginally improved than in the first generation.

–Overall survival is the same as that of the first generation. c- STAMP inhibitors (asciminib): Specifically Target the ABL Myristoyl Pocket.

23

Original page 24

Prognosis

➢The most important good prognostic indicator is the good response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors at the hematological, cytogenetic, and molecular level.

➢Without treatment, most cases progress from chronic phase to blastic phase within 3-5 years after diagnosis.

➢Overall, the complete cytogenetic response rate to imatinib is 70–90%, with 5- year progression-free and overall survival rates of 80–95%.

➢Stable deep molecular response: Four-log reduction in tumor load sustained for at least a year

➢Blastic phase has a very poor outcome, even with tyrosine kinase inhibitor

➢Bad prognostic signs:

–High ELTS score:

–10–19% blasts in the peripheral blood and/or bone marrow

–≥20% basophils in the peripheral blood

–Additional chromosomal abnormalities in Philadelphia chromosome– positive cells, including 3q26.2 rearrangements, monosomy 7, isochromosome 17q and complex karyotype

–Clusters of small megakaryocytes (including true micromegakaryocytes similar to those seen in myelodysplastic syndromes), associated with significant reticulin and/or collagen fibrosis, which is best assessed in biopsy sections. 24

Original page 25

–Emerging on treatment of:

❖Failure to achieve a complete hematological response to the first tyrosine kinase inhibitor

❖Any hematological, cytogenetic, or molecular indications of resistance to two sequential tyrosine kinase inhibitor

❖Development of new additional chromosomal abnormalities

❖Occurrence of compound mutations in the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene during tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy

❖Signs of complete remission:

25

Original page 26

Original page 27

•Definition: It is a BCR::ABL1 negative myeloproliferative neoplasm, characterized by sustained peripheral blood neutrophilia, bone marrow hypercellularity due to neutrophil proliferation, and hepatosplenomegaly.

•Epidemiology:

–The true incidence is unknown.

–Age: It affects older adults with a median age of 66 years, but has also been reported rarely in adolescents and young adults.

–Sex: Male to female ratio is 1.6:1.

•Etiology and pathogenesis:

–The actual cause is unknown.

–Some cases have followed cytotoxic chemotherapy.

–Familial factors has been reported.

–Rare cases of multiple myeloma or monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance are associated with chronic neutrophilic leukemia which should be differentiated from the leukemoid reaction resulting from synthesis of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor by neoplastic plasma cells.

•Clinical picture:

–Splenomegaly which may be symptomatic.

–Hepatomegaly.

–Pruising, purpura, mucocutaneous bleeding or gastrointestinal bleeding.

–Gout. 27

Original page 28

•Laboratory diagnosis: 1-Chronic myeloid leukemia BCR-ABL1, reactive neutrophilia, other myeloproliferative neoplasms and myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms must be excluded. 2-Complete blood count: Persistent absolute neutrophilia.

3-Blood film:

–Segmented neutrophils and band forms are more than 80% of total leukocytic count.

–Immature granulocytes (promyelocytes, myelocytes and metamyelocytes) are less than 5% but occasionally they may reach 10% of total leukocytic count but could be up to 10%.

–Myeloblasts are less than 1%.

–No dysplasia.

–Neutrophils show toxic granulation and Dohle bodies, but they may also appear normal. Toxic granulation and Dohle bodies are more common with leukemoid reactions associated with plasma cell neoplasms.

28

Original page 29

4-Bone marrow:

–Hypercellular bone marrow with a high M/E ratio (may be > 20:1) and neutrophilic proliferation mainly the myelocytes and mature neutrophils. Myeloblasts and promyelocytes are not increased at the time of diagnosis.

–Erythroid and megakaryocytic proliferation may also occur.

–Megakaryocytes may be normal or there may be increased smaller forms.

–Reticulin fibrosis is uncommon. 5-Splenic biopsy: The red pulp is infiltrated by neutrophils. 6-Hepatic biopsy: Sinusoids and portal areas are infiltrated by neutrophils. 7-NAP score: It is usually high, but may be normal or low. So, it has no diagnostic significance in differentiating it from neutrophilic leukomid reaction or chronic myeloid leukemia BCR-ABL1.

8-Biochemical tests:

–Serum uric acid is high.

–Serum vitamin B12 is high.

9-Genetic tests:

–Normal cytogenetic studies in 90% of cases. 29

Original page 30

–There may be abnormal karyotyping which may be present at diagnosis or appear during the course of the disease mainly in the form of gains of chromosomes 8, 9, and 21; del(7q) and del(20q). Other less frequent abnormalities include del(11q); del(12p); nullisomy 17, a complex karyotype and several non-recurrent translocations.

–Clonal cytogenetic abnormalities may appear during the course of the disease. Cases with gene fusion/rearrangement that is defining for other diagnoses are specifically excluded.

–The overall mutational profile of CNL is quite similar to chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia, MDS/MPN-N, and MDS/MPN-NOS, with the exception of CSF3R mutations which are more common in CNL. A median of four mutations of known significance are observed.

–Mutations associated with clonal hematopoiesis are common.

–Nearly all cases exhibit mutation in ASXL1, TET2, and/or DNMT3A. Other gene mutation are reported.

–Unidentified fusion gene in cases with t(15; 19)(q13;p13.3) may be implicated as evident by the complete cytogenetic remission with imatinib.

–Philadelphia chromosome or BCR-ABL fusion gene: Negative.

–JAK2 mutation: rarely positive and may be homozygous.

•WHO diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria: The diagnosis requires exclusion of reactive neutrophilia and other myeloproliferative and myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms. 9

○Peripheral blood white blood cell count ≥ 25 × 10 / L

▪Segmented neutrophils plus banded neutrophils constitute ≥ 80% of the white blood cells 30

Original page 31

▪Neutrophil precursors (promyelocytes, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes) constitute < 10% of the white blood cells

▪Myeloblasts rarely observed

▪Monocytes constitute < 10% of peripheral blood leukocytes; absolute monocytosis not meeting criteria for CMML

○Bone marrow:

▪No dysgranulopoiesis.

▪Hypercellular bone marrow

▪Neutrophil granulocytes increased in percentage and number

▪Neutrophil maturation appears normal

▪Myeloblasts constitute < 5% of the nucleated cells

○Not meeting WHO criteria for BCR::ABL1–positive chronic myeloid leukemia, polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, or primary myelofibrosis.

○No evidence of disease-defining gene rearrangements such as PDGFRA, PDGFRB, or FGFR1, and no PCM1::JAK2 fusion

○Presence of:

▪CSF3R p.T618I or another activating CSF3R mutation OR

▪Persistent neutrophilia (≥ 3 months), splenomegaly, and no identifiable cause of reactive neutrophilia including absence of a plasma cell neoplasm OR

▪If a plasma cell neoplasm is present, demonstration of clonality of myeloid cells by cytogenetic or molecular studies. 31

Original page 32

•Prognosis:

–It is slowly progressive with variable survival, ranging from 6 months to more than 20 years.

–Neutrophilia is usually progressive.

–Anemia and thrombocytopenia may occur and are associated with worse prognosis.

–Transformation to acute myeloid leukemia may occur following cytotoxic therapy or spontaneously and may be marked by appearance of dysplastic features.

–Coexisting ASXL1 mutation is associated with a worse prognosis. 32

Original page 33

33

Polycythemia

Original page 34

•Definition: A disease state in which there’s increased hemoglobin, hematocrit and red cell count above the normal limits.

•Causes: I-Polycythemia vera. II-Others: 1-Primary: Familial and congenital polycythemia: Autosomal dominant mutation of erythropoietin receptor leading to hypersensitivity to erythropoietin.It is characterized by:

–Low erythropoietin level.

–No splenomegaly.

–Normal White blood cell and platelet count.

–Normal oxygen dissociation curve. 2-Secondary to high erythropoietin level:

A-Compensatory increased erythropoietin secondary to hypoxia:

–Neonates.

–High altitude.

–Cardiovascular disease especially congenital cyanotic heart disease.

–Chronic obstructive airway disease.

–Cigarette smoking.

–Hemoglobinopathies with high oxygen2affinity and methhemoglobinemia.

–Red cell metabolic defect with low levels of 2,3 di-phospho-glycerate.

sections.t: B-Inappropriate high levels of erythropoietin with no hypoxia:
sections.html:
–Inherited Chuvash polycythemia: Autosomal recessive mutation of von Hippel Lindau gene leading to a decrease in the degradation of hypoxia inducible factor increasing the erythropoietin production leading to polycythemia. 34

Original page 35

–Renal diseases as hydronephrosis, polycystic kidney, hyper nephroma or renal hypoxia.

–Hepatoma.

–Cereberal hemangioma.

–Uterine leiomyoma.

–Excess androgen as in Cushing syndrome, Conn’s syndrome and pheochromocytoma. 3-Idiopathic: increased hemoglobin, hematocrit and red cell mass with no other features. 4-Relative (↓ plasma volume – Normal RCM – Normal EPO):

–Dehydration as in vomiting, diarrhea and diuretics.

–Plasma loss as in burns.

–Stress polycythemia in Gaisbock syndrome which consists of obesity, hypertension and smoking.

–Excessive alcohol. 35

Original page 36

Erythropoietin:

•Origin:

–Fetus and neonates: Liver and kidney.

–Adults: 90% of erythropoietin arises from renal peritubular interstitial cells and 10% from the liver.

•Gene: Chromosome 7.

•Structure:

–Molecular weight: 34 kD (it can cross the placenta).

–Amino acids: 166 amino acids.

–Carbohydrates comprise about35%.

•Stimulants: 1-Hypoxia which may cause either: a-Appropriate increase of erythropoietin level:

–Anemia: sustained stimulation.

–Hypoxia increases it by 10000 fold with rapid rise and gradual return to normal even with sustained hypoxia. b-Inappropriate increase of erythropoietin level due to hypoxia of the renal tissue.

36

Original page 37

2-O2 dissociation curve:

–Shift to right increases the oxygen release to tissue decreasing the erythropoietin level.

–Shift to left decreases the oxygen release to tissue increasing the erythropoietin level.

•Deficiency of erythropoietin: 1-Renal failure and nephrectomy. 2-Endocrinal disorders as in hypopituitarism, hypothyroidism, hypocorticalism and hypogonadism. 3-Chronic disorders. 4-Polycythemia vera. c-Low hemoglobin affinity to oxygen. d-Protein caloric malnutrition.

•Action: It acts as a specific erythroid growth factor: 1-Late differentiation of erythroid progenitors into pronormoblasts. 2-Maturation of normoblasts. 3-Hemoglobin synthesis. 4-Premature release of reticulocytes. 5-Decreased apoptosis of erythroid progenitors. 6-Megakaryopoiesis through interaction with IL3, granulocyte- monocyte colony stimulating factor, IL1 and thrombopoiesis stimulating factors.

•Erythropoietin receptor:

➢Structure: 507 amino acids with a single transmembrane domain.

➢Gene: on chromosome 19.

➢Site: All committed erythroid progenitor cells: 37

Original page 38

–Colony formed unit- granulocyte erythroid- monocyte-macrophage (CFU-GEMM) and Burst forming unit-erythroid (BFU): Low number.

–Colony forming unit-erythroid (CFU-E) and proerythroblast: The highest number of receptors.

–Late normoblast: Low number.

–Reticulocyte: Absent.

•Erythropoietin signaling: Erythropoietin binds erythropoietin receptor leading to receptor dimerization and phosphorylation which in-turn phosphorylates and activates of Janus kinase (JAK) leading to phosphorylation of of signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) that dissociates from the receptor, dimerizes and moves to the nucleus causing activation of erythropoietin gene transcription.

➢JAK structure: 7 defined regions of homology called Janus homology domains (JH1-7).

–JH1 is the kinase domain important for the enzymatic activity of the JAK and contains tyrosine necessary for JAK activation. 38

Original page 39

–JH2 is a "pseudokinase domain": has an autoinhibitory function that normally suppresses the kinase activity of JAK1

JAK2 mutations are present in the following myeloid neoplasms:

1-Polycythemia vera. 2-Essential thrombocythemia. 3-Primary myelofibrosis. 4- Atypical chronic myeloid leukemia. 5-Chronic myelo-monocytic leukemia. 6-Chronic eosinophilic leukemia. 7-Refractory anemia with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis.. 8-40 % of cases of (5q-) syndrome. 39

Original page 40

•Definition: It is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by erythrocytosis frequently accompanied by leukocytosis, and/or thrombocytosis, and an associated increased hemorrhagic and thrombotic risk.

•Etiology and pathogenesis:

–The underlying cause is unknown in most cases.

–Virtually all patients carry: 1-The gain of function mutation in JAK2 called V617F mutation which means replacement of valine at the position 617 of amino acids by phenyle-analine leading to loss of the inhibitory function of JAK2 resulting in a continuous activation of JAK-STAT signaling pathway and autonomous proliferation of erythroid, granulocytic and megakaryocytic progenitors. 2-JAK 2 exon 12 mutation which has a similar effect.

–Increased RBCs production leads to hyperviscosity.

–Thrombosis may be due to:

–Hyperviscosity.

–Thrombocytosis.

–Origin:

▪Flushing.

▪Tachycardia. 126

Myelodysplastic Neoplasms

Original page 130

130

Original page 131

•Definition: It is clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders characterized by peripheral blood cytopenia, ineffective hematopoiesis, dysplasia of one or more myeloid lineage, and increased risk of leukemic transformation.

○Cytopenia in at least one hematopoietic lineage is required for a diagnosis of MDS:

–Hb < 13 g/dL in males and < 12 g/dL in females. 9

–Absolute neutrophil count < 1.8 x 10 /L. 9

–Platelets < 150 x 10 /L.

○The threshold for dysplasia is set as 10% for all lineages.

○The myeloid lineages affected by cytopenias are not necessarily those that manifest dysplasia.

•Cell of origin: Hematopoietic stem cells.

Epidemiology

–Age: The median age is 77 years. The incidence is very low below age 40.

–Sex: It has a male predominance except in the 5q- syndrome.

Etiology and predisposing factors

1-Primary or de novo MDS: It occurs without a known history of chemotherapy or radiation exposure and may be associated with:

–Cigarette smoking.

–Benzene.

–Agricultural chemicals or solvents.

–Family history of hematopoietic neoplasms.

–Inherited bone marrow failure syndromes as Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome and Diamond-Blackfan anemia.

–Acquired aplastic anemia 131

Original page 132

2-Secondary: It occurs secondary to exposure to alkalating agents, ionizing radiation or chemotherapy.

Pathogenesis

1-Stem cell disorder with multistep mutations as evident by: a-Trilineage dysplasia. b-Cytogenetic abnormalities are found in all dysplastic cells. 2-Immunological: This theory is evident by the fact that hypoplastic MDS share aplastic anemia in many points as: a-Macrocytosis. b-Various levels of dyserythropoiesis. c-Clonal T cell expansion. d-Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria related acquired mutation of PIGA gene. e-Response to anti-thymoglobulin. f-Evolution of aplastic anemia into MDS. 3-Apoptosis (ineffective hematopoiesis): as evident by:

–The peripheral blood cytopenia despite of the hypercellular bone marrow.

–The high levels of tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), first apoptosis signal (FAS) ligand and TNF related apoptosis inducing ligand (TRAIL).

–The low capacity of pluripotent stem cells to form colonies in bone marrow culture.

–Lower levels of granulocyte-monocyte colony stimulating factor (GM-CSF), granulocyte colony stimulating factor (G-CSF), IL6 and IL3.

–Low responsiveness of colony forming unit granulocyte-monocyte (CFU- GM) to GM-CSF and G-CSF. 4-Agiogenesis: Due to the autocrine production of agiogenic molecules as vascular endothelial growth factor with over expression of its receptors. 132

Original page 133

Clinical picture

–It may be asymptomatic and discovered accidently.

–Clinical picture of bone marrow failure: Weakness, repeated infection and bleeding. Most patients are presented by symptoms of anemia with one third of patients are transfusion dependent, whereas neutropenia and/or thrombocytopenia are less common.

–Organomegaly is infrequent.

–Careful medical history should be taken to exclude cases of cytopenia and/or dysplasia that may result from growth factor therapy, certain drugs, infections, metabolic deficiencies and immune disorders.

Complications

–Acute transformation: The incidence varies across the subtypes, and is much more with increased blast counts.

–Bone marrow failure.

Laboratory diagnosis

1-Complete blood count:

–Cytopenia in at least one hematopoietic lineage is required for a diagnosis of MDS:

➢Hb < 13 g/dL in males and < 12 g/dL in females. 9

➢Absolute neutrophil count < 1.8 x 10 /L. 9

➢Platelets < 150 x 10 /L.

–Thrombocytosis is allowed in MDS with isolated (5q-) syndrome.

–The threshold for dysplasia is set as 10% for all lineages.

–Cytopenias may occur in different lineages from those affected by dysplasia.

–To determine blast percentage:

➢Bone marrow: a 500-cell differential count of all nucleated cells is recommended

➢Peripheral blood: a 200-leukocyte differential count is recommended. 133

Original page 134

–Diagnostic evaluation should always include adequate bone marrow and peripheral blood smears examiation, coupled with one or more of the following: chromosome analysis, mutation analysis, and immunophenotyping. A-RBCs:

–Anemia in 85% of cases.

–Myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts (MDS-RS) is characterized by microcytosis, hypochromia and dimorphic population.

–Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria clone may emerge causing hemolysis with microcytic hypochromic anemia or normocytic normochromic anemia. B-White cells:

–Leukopenia with absolute neutropenia in 50% of cases.

–Eosinophils and basophils are variable. C-Platelets: Thrombocytopenia in 25 – 50% of cases. Platelet count may be normal and there may be mild thrombocytosis in (5q-) syndrome. 2-Blood film: High-quality slide preparations are required and specimens must be fresh:

–RBCs: Normoblastemia, Macrocytosis, anisopoikilocytosis, ovalocytes, ovalomacrocytes, elleptocytes, acanthocytes, stomatocytes, tear drops, fragmented red cells, basophilic stippling, Howel Jolly bodies and Pappenheimer bodies.

–Neutrophils: hypogranulation, Dohle bodies, pseudo Chidiak Higashi cells, hyposegmentation (acquired pelger Huet), non-segmentation hypersegmentation, coarse chromatin clumping ring nuclei, bizarre shaped nuclei or apoptotic nuclei. 134

Original page 135

–Paramyeloid cells: mononuclear cells with morphology intermediate between monocytes and myelocytes.

–Blasts: Variable number of blasts of less than 20% with or without Auer rods. To determine blast percentage 200 leukocytes are counted.

–Platelets: There may be giant and hypogranular platelets. 3-Reticulocytic count: Reticulocytopenia and low reticulocyte production index.

4-Bone marrow:

–Biopsy is of more diagnostic and prognostic importance and aspiration may fail due to hypercellularity or fibrosis.

–High-quality slide preparations are required and specimens must be fresh.

–Significant dysplasia means that at least 10% of erythroid, granulocytic or megakaryocytic cells are dysplasti A-Cellularity: Bone marrow is hypercellular in most cases and normocellular or hypocellular in 10% of cases. Hypocellularity may be assoaciated with a favourable prognosis. 135

Original page 136

B-The bone marrow histotopography: The biopsy shows alteration of the normal histotopography:

–Erythroid precursors and megakaryocytes are present in the paratrabecular areas, which are normally predominantly occupied by granulopoietic cells.

–Abnormal localization of immature precursors: Clusters or aggregates of blasts located away from bone trabeculae and vascular structures. C-Dyserythropoiesis:

–Erythroid hyperplasia or hypoplasia.

–Paratrabecular location of erythroblasts instead of the normal central position.

–Megaloblastic erythropoiesis with giant erythroblasts.

–Nuclear dysplasia: Nuclear budding, intranuclear bridging, karyorrhexis and multinuclearity.

–Cytoplasmic dysplasia: vacuolization and intercytoplasmic bridging.

136

–Cytochemistry:

▪Iron stain: Increased siderotic granules, increased sideroblasts and ring sideroblasts.

▪Periodic acid shiff (PAS): Aberrant positivity which may be diffuse or granular.

–Granulocytic hyperplasia.

–Agranularity, hypogranularity, pseudo Chidiac Higashi anomaly, Dohle bodies or Auer rods. 137

–Decreased staining with myeloperoxidase and Sudan Black B.

–Periodic acid shiff (PAS): Positive.

○Associated with Excess blasts.

○Aggressive course independent of blast count.

○Not associated with splenomegaly, leukoerythroblastosis or intra- sinusoidal hematopoiesis. 7)Inflammatory infiltration: by plasma cells and lymphoid aggregates. 5-Immunophenotyping: It doesn’t a major role in the diagnosis and is not routinely performed. It shows:

–Low side scatter.

–Decreased intensity of normal antigens. 139

–Aberrant expression of some markers as CD7 which has a bad prognosis. Aberrant findings in at least three tested features and at least two cell compartments is highly associated with an MDS or MDS/MPN.

○Immunohistochemical analysis with CD34 is especially useful for assessing blast percentage in cases of fibrosis or hypocellular marrow, in which blast percentages are often underestimated in the smear preparations. CD34 may be positive in megakaryocytes in some cases of MDS, but it may also stain megakaryocytes in megaloblastic anemia.

6-Genetic tests: See after 7-Bone marrow culture: Decreased capacity of hematopoietic stem cells to form colonies. 8-NAP score: Variable. 9-Granulocytes function tests: Decreased chemotaxis adhesion and phagocytosis. 10-Platelet function tests: Prolongation of bleeding time and defective platelet aggregation. 11-Hemoglobin electrophoresis: Increased Hb F or presence of Hb H. 12-High expression of i antigen and low expression of I antigen. 13-Low pyruvate kinase activity. 14-HAM’s test: Rarely Positive. 15-Autoantibodies may be positive. 16-Serum protein electrophoresis: Paraproteins may be present.

–Copper deficiency.

–Aplastic anemia.

–Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia.

–Hereditary autosomal dominant Pelger-Huet anomaly resulting from mutations in the LBR gene that encodes for lamin B receptor. 141

–Various thalassemias.

–Sideroblastic anemia.

–Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

–Liver or other solid organ transplantation.

–Primary myelofibrosis.

–Chronic myeloid leukemia.

–AML: M2-M4-M6.

–Large granular lymphocytic leukemia.

–Iatrogenic:

○Administration of growth factors as granulocyte colony stimulating factor (G- CSF).

○Chemotherapy.

○Antibiotic as cotrimoxazole.

○Immunosuppressants tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil.

–Acute alcohol intoxication

–Chronic infection

–Parvovirus B19 infection

–HIV infection. 142

Original page 147

•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with cytopenia and dysplasia characterized by chromosome 5q deletion occurring in isolation or with one other cytogenetic abnormality (other than monosomy 7 or 7q deletion). \

•Synonym: Myelodysplastic syndrome with low blasts and isolated del(5q).

•Epidemiology: 2.5% of all MDS cases. More frequently in women, with a median age of 67 years.

•Etiology: Unknown but history of benzene exposure or previous radio/chemotherapy has been reported.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Ring sideroblasts or SF3B1 mutation do not exclude the diagnosis of MDS with isolated 5q deletion

–CBC and blood film:

○Anemia in most patients which is often macrocytic.

○Thrombocytosis in one third of cases. Thrombocytopenia is uncommon and reflects advanced disease.

○Blasts is < 2% in the peripheral blood.

–Bone marrow:

○Normo/hypercellular

○Megakaryocytes are increased with normal/decreased size, and non- lobated/hypolobated nuclei.

○Erythroid hypoplasia with nor prominent erythroid or granulocytic lineages dysplasia.

○Significant monocytic proliferation.

○No fibrosis.

○Blasts is < 5% in the bone marrow.

○Ring sideroblasts may be present 147

Original page 148

–Immunohistochemistry: Prognostic assessment of p53 expression. Strong p53 expression in ≥ 1% of bone marrow cells is associated with higher risk of transformation to AML and shorter overall survival.

–Genetic tests:

○Interstitial deletion of chromosome 5with variable deletion of bands q31-q33.

○There may be a single additional clonal chromosomal abnormality except monosomy 7 or 7q deletion.

○SF3B1 mutation in 20% of the cases.

○JAK2 V617F or MPL W515L mutations in minority of cases.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○Anemia, with or without other cytopenias and/or thrombocytosis;

○Dysplasia involving megakaryocytes, with or without dysplasia involving other lineages;

○Blast < 5% in the bone marrow and < 2% in the peripheral blood;

○Detection of 5q deletion, isolated or with one other cytogenetic aberration other than monosomy 7 or 7q deletion;

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria of AML, MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation, MDS with increased blasts, or MDS/MPN.

•Prognosis:

–Good prognosis and most patients are stratified as low- or intermediate-1-risk.

–The immunomodulatory drug lenalidomide suppresses the abnormal clone and ransfusion independence is achieved in two thirds of patients

–Bad prognostic factors include: Male gender, older age, transfusion need, low absolute neutrophil count, low platelet count and mutation in TP53, RUNX1, TET2 and SF3B1 genes 148

•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with cytopenia and dysplasia characterized by SF3B1 mutation and ring sideroblasts.

•Synonym: MDS with low blasts and ring sideroblasts.

Epidemiology

–17% of all MDS cases

–Median age is 70-75 years.

–Slight male preponderance.

•Etiology: Unknown.

•Pathogenesis: Heterozygous mutations in SF3B1 gene of hematopoietic stem cells, which is critical for RNA splicing leading to mitochondrial apoptosis, and deregulated iron metabolisms resulting in ineffective erythropoiesis with ring sideroblasts and systemic iron overload.

Clinical picture

–Symptoms related to cytopenias.

–Symptoms related to iron overload.

Laboratory diagnosis

–Peripheral blood: Macro/normocytic anemia with dimorphic pattern with no Blasts.

–Bone marrow aspirate:

○Erythroid predominance with increased proerythroblasts and dyserythropoiesis in the form of megaloblastoid features, binucleation and/or nuclear segmentation and increased numbers of ring sideroblasts

○Hemosiderin-loaded macrophages are often abundant 149

Original page 150

○Dyplasia may be unilineage in erythroid lineage only or multilineage affecting granulocytic or megakaryocytic lineages or both

○Blasts < 5% of the nucleated bone marrow cells.

–Bone marrow biopsy:

○Hypercellular arrow with erythroid predominance.

○Dysmegakaryopoiesis is infrequent.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Lower expression of CD71 on erythropoietic precursors

○CD34- positive myeloid precursors are not increased (<5%)

○Erythroid cells can be highlighted using glycophorin A or CD71

○Dyserythropoiesis and increased proerythroblasts can be highlighted with E- cadherin and CD117.

–Genetic tests:

○Heterozygous SF3B1 mutations at high variant allelic frequency (≥ 5%), is required for diagnosis.

○Certain co-mutations have been correlated with adverse prognosis as TP53, RUNX1, EZH2, FLT3, BCOR, BCORL1, NRAS, RUNX1, SRSF2 or STAG2 mutations

Differential diagnosis

–Acute myeloid leukemia

–MDS with increased blasts

–MDS with low blasts and 5q deletion may show ring sideroblasts and/or SF3B1 mutation but these cases are diagnosed as MDS with low blasts and 5q deletion.

–Myelodysplastic/ myeloproliferative neoplasm may be presented by thrombocytosis with detection of SF3B1 mutation concurrently with JAK2 p.V617F, CALR, or MPL mutations 150

Original page 151

–Non-neoplastic causes of ring sideroblasts, including alcohol, toxins (e.g. lead and benzene), drugs (e.g. isoniazid), copper deficiency (which may be induced by zinc administration), and congenital sideroblastic anemia must be excluded. Congenital sideroblastic anemia occurs in younger age and with microcytic (rather than macrocytic) anemia.

Diagnostic criteria

–Essential criteria:

○Cytopenia involving one or more lineages, without thrombocytosis

○Erythroid lineage dysplasia;

○Blasts < 5% in the bone marrow and < 2% in the peripheral blood

○Detection of SF3B1 mutation. If SF3B1 mutation analysis is not available, demonstration of ring sideroblasts comprising ≥15% of erythroid precursors

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria of AML, MDS with low blasts and 5q deletion, MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation, MDS with increased blasts, or any MDS/MPN type.

Prognosis

–It has the best outcome among MDS types. Most patients are stratified into lower risk groups

–Bad prognostics include transfusion-dependence, complex karyotype, monosomy 5 or 5q deletion, monosomy 7 or 7q deletion, chromosome 3 abnormalities and mutations in TP53, RUNX1 and EZH2 genes. 151

sections.t: Myelodysplastic neoplasm with biallelic TP53 inactivation
sections.html:
Original page 152

•Definition: It is defined as a myeloid neoplasm with cytopenia, dysplasia and less than 20% blasts or 30% erythroblasts, characterized by two or more TP53 mutations or one TP53 mutation and concurrent evidence of TP53 copy loss or copy neutral loss of heterozygosity.

•Etiology: Expansion of age related TP53-mutated clone spontaneously, following DNA-damaging agents, or with inherited predisposition.

Pathogenesis

–Biallelic TP53 alterations are associated, with genomic instability, dysregulation of cell cycle, and altered response to oxidative stress.

–Inactivation of the second TP53 allele in a patient with monoallelic alteration can occur after years or even decades, leading to rapid progression and expansion of a genetically unstable clone that often also acquires complex karyotypic changes.

•Clinical picture: Symptoms are related to cytopenias.

Laboratory diagnosis

–BM: Higher blast count, fibrosis and dysplasia

–Immunohistochemistry: Detection of p53 protein accumulation, blast count and estimation of erythroblasts number (E-staining).

–Genetic tests:

○Biallelic TP53 alterations: Sequencing with FISH.

○Chromosome abnormalities in > 90% of patients. 152

Original page 153

Diagnostic criteria

–Essential criteria:

○Myeloid neoplasm fulfilling diagnostic criteria of MDS.

○Detection of one or more TP53 mutations.

○In the presence of one TP53 mutation, evidence of TP53 copy loss or copy neutral LOH.

•Prognosis: Patients have increased blast counts, higher risk of leukemic transformation and higher risk of death. 153

Myelodysplastic neoplasms, morphologically defined

Original page 154

1-Myelodysplastic neoplasms with low blasts (MDS-LB) 2-Myelodysplastic neoplasms, hypoplastic (MDS-h) 3-Myelodysplastic neoplasms with increased blasts (MDS-IB) 4-Myelodysplastic neoplasms with fibrosis (MDS-f) 154

Original page 155

•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with cytopenia and dysplasia but without defining genetic abnormalities, defined by having < 5% bone marrow blasts and < 2% peripheral blood blasts.

Subtypes

–MDS with low blasts and single lineage dysplasia (MDS-LB-SLD)

–MDS with low blasts and multilineage dysplasia (MDS-LB-MLD)

•Etiology: Expansion of age-related clonal hematopoiesis and genetic alterations.

•Pathogenesis: Imbalance of the cell cycle leads to ineffective hematopoiesis of at least one hematopoietic lineage.

Laboratory findings

–CBC: Cytopenia in at least one hematopoietic lineage is required for a diagnosis:

○Anemia (>70% of cases), with macrocytosis and anisopoikilocytosis.

○Thrombocytopenia and neutropenia are less common

○Dysgranulopoiesis: Pseudo-Pelger-Huët anomaly or hypersegmentation, hypogranularity, pseudo-Chédiak-Higashi granules and small size. Blasts are rare present and if present they are < 2%. N.B.: Finding of rare blasts in peripheral blood on two separate occasions may qualify for MDS with excess blasts.

–Bone marrow:

○Hypercellular

○Dyserythropoiesis: Nuclear alterations, including budding, internuclear bridging, karyorrhexis and multinuclearity, megaloblastoid changes, cytoplasmic vacuolation giving a positive PAS reaction. There may also be diffuse cytoplasmic PAS positivity. Ring sideroblasts are < 15%.

○Granulocytes may be relatively increased with dysgranulopoiesis in the form of Pseudo-Pelger-Huët anomaly or hypersegmentation, hypogranularity, pseudo-Chédiak-Higashi granules and small size. Blasts are < 5%. 155

Original page 156

○Dysegakaryopoiesis in the form of variable sizes with non-lobated nuclei or multiple widely separated nuclei.

○Fibrosis may be present.

–Immunophenotyping: Abnormal antigen expression particularly on neutrophils and monocytes. Blast count can be made using CD34 staining.

–Genetic tests:

○Normal karyotype in most patients

○Mutations: Involving TET2, SRSF2, ASXL1, DNMT3A, U2AF1, RUNX1, ASXL1 and SRSF2 genes.

Differential diagnosis

–Secondary causes of dysplasia.

–Other types of MDS.

Diagnostic criteria

–Essential criteria:

○Cytopenia involving one or more lineages.

○Dysplastic changes in one or more lineages, involving at least 10% of cells.

○< 5% bone marrow blasts and < 2% peripheral blood blasts

○Exclusion of folate and vitamin B12 deficiency.

○No fulfilling diagnostic criteria of MDS with defining genetic alterations or hypoplastic MDS.

–Desirable criteria:

○Hypercellular bone marrow for age.

○Detection of clonal cytogenetic and/or molecular abnormality.

•Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the type and degree of cytopenia with most patients have stable disease for years before progression to MDS with increased blasts or transformation to AML. 156

Original page 157

•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with cytopenia and dysplasia, characterized by significantly decreased age-adjusted bone marrow cellularity as determined on a trephine biopsy.

Epidemiology

–10-15% of all MDS.

–Patients are usually younger than other MDS types but older aplastic anemia.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis: Clonal hematopoiesis. Hypoplasia is caused by immune attack on hematopoiesis mediated by CD8+ T-cells overproducing IFNγ and/or TNFα.

Laboratory diagnosis

–CBC: Profound cytopenias with granulocyte dysplasia and expansion of large granular lymphocytes

–Bone marrow:

○Cellularity < 30% of normal cellularity in patients < 70 years and < 20% in patients > 70 years. Hypocellularity is usually diffuse but may be patchy.

○Dysplasia in one or more hematopoietic lineages. Megakaryocytes may be scattered or form loose clusters with dysplasia. The presence of micromegakaryocytes is rare.

○Blast counts are variable which may be in clusters.

○Reticulin fibrosis is rare

○Ring sideroblasts >5%

○Expansion of large granular lymphocytes

–Immunophenotyping:

○CD34 or CD117 staining are helpful to recognise microclusters of blasts on the core biopsy.

○CD61 and/or CD42b may be helpful to highlight megakaryocytes. 157

Original page 158

–Genetic tests:

○Chromosomal abnormalities in 25-40% with more low- and intermediate- risk as +8 and 20q-deletion.

○Partial or total monosomy 7 are associated with increased risk of AML transformation.

○Lower prevalence of somatic mutations with lower variant allelic frequencies compared to other MDS types including mutation in TP53, EZH1, IDH1and IDH2 genes or co-mutation patterns involving TET2, DNMT3A and ASXL1 genes.

Differential diagnosis

–PNH: PIGA mutations

–Aplastic anemia: Marked decrease in megakaryocytes and hemoglobin F- containing erythroblasts. It may be associated only with dyserythropoiesis without dysplasia in myeloid or megakaryocytic lineages. Germline mutations of GATA2, DDX41, Fanconi anemia or telomerase complex genes may be present.

Diagnostic criteria

–Essential criteria:

○Cytopenia involving one or more lineages; Hypocellular bone marrow (assessed on a trephine core biopsy, adjusted for age of the patient) not explained by drug/toxin exposure or pertinent nutritional deficiency;

○Dysplasia involving myeloid and/or megakaryocytic lineages;

○< 5% blasts in bone marrow and < 2% blasts in peripheral blood;

○Not meeting criteria for MDS with defining genetic abnormalities or MDS with increased blasts.

–Desirable criterion: Detection of clonal cytogenetic and/or molecular abnormality.

•Prognosis: Good response to immunosuppressive therapy with prognosis better than other MDS types and poorer than aplastic anemia 158

Original page 159

•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with cytopenia and dysplasia but without defining genetic abnormalities, defined by having 5-19% bone marrow blasts and/or 2-19% peripheral blood blasts.

Synonym

–MDS with excess blasts-1

–MDS-with excess blasts-2

–Refractory anemia with excess blasts-1

–Refractory anemia with excess blasts-2

Subtype

–MDS with increased blasts-1: -9% blasts in the bone marrow and/or 2-4% blasts in the peripheral blood, without significant reticulin fibrosis

–MDS with increased blasts-2: 10-19% blasts in the bone marrow and/or 5-19% blasts in the peripheral blood, without significant reticulin fibrosis; or, with presence of Auer rods.

–MDS with increased blasts and fibrosis (MDS-F): 5-19% blasts in the bone marrow and/or 2-19% blasts in the peripheral blood, with significant (defined as grade 2 or 3).

•Epidemiology: 28-39% of MDS cases.

•Etiology: Expansion of age-related clonal hematopoiesis and accumulation of genetic alterations.

•Pathogenesis: Somatic mutations in genes regulating the cell cycle leads to ineffective hematopoiesis of one or more lineages. 159

Original page 160

•Clinical picture: Most patients present with clinical features related to anemia, thrombocytopenia and/or neutropenia.

Laboratory diagnosis

–CBC and blood Smears: Progressive cytopenia with dysplasia:

○Deserythropoiesis: Anisopoikilocytosis and macrocytosis.

○Dysgranulopoiesis: Nuclear hyposegmentation or hypersegmentation, cytoplasmic hypogranularity, pseudo-Chédiak-Higashi granules and small size.

○Dysmegakaryopoiesis: Large or hypogranular platelets.

○Blasts are commonly present

–Bone marrow:

○Hypercellular but occasionally can be normocellular or hypocellular

○Alteration of the normal histotopography: Both erythroid precursors and megakaryocytes are dislocated towards paratrabecular areas, which are normally predominantly occupied by granulopoietic cells.

○Abnormal localization of immature precursors: Blasts form clusters (3–5 cells) or aggregates (> 5 cells), away from bone trabeculae and vascular structures

○Varying degrees of dysplasia:

➢Dysmegakaryiopoiesis: Nuclear hyposegmentation or hypersegmentation, cytoplasmic hypogranularity, multinucleated cells, and micromegakaryocytes with a tendency to cluster.

➢Dyserythropoiesis: Hyperplasia, with megaloblastic changes; abnormally lobated nuclei and internuclear bridging.

➢Dysgranulopoiesis: Megakaryocytes may be normal or increased Subtype: 160

Original page 161

➢MDS with increased blasts-1: -9% blasts in the bone marrow and/or 2-4% blasts in the peripheral blood, without significant reticulin fibrosis

➢MDS with increased blasts-2: 10-19% blasts in the bone marrow and/or 5- 19% blasts in the peripheral blood, without significant reticulin fibrosis; or, with presence of Auer rods.

➢MDS with increased blasts and fibrosis (MDS-F): 5-19% blasts in the bone marrow and/or 2-19% blasts in the peripheral blood, with significant (defined as grade 2 or 3).

–Immunophenotyping:

○Increased CD34 and/or CD117 positive cells which are usually positive for CD38, HLA-DR and the myeloid-associated antigens CD13 and CD33.

○Asynchronous expression of granulocytic maturation antigens: CD15, CD11b and/or CD65 can be seen in the blast population.

○Aberrant expression of CD7 or CD56 on blasts.

○Immunohistochemistry:

➢Confirmation of excess of blasts using CD34 and their arrangement into clusters (3-5 cells).

➢Identification of micromegakaryocytes and other small dysplastic megakaryocytes using CD61 and CD42b.

–Genetic tests:

○Clonal cytogenetic abnormalities in 50-70%: High prevalence of high-risk abnormalities as 7q deletion, -7, and complex karyotype.

○Mutations in 90%: Overrepresentation of higher risk mutations as ASXL1, RUNX1, EZH2, N-/KRAS and TP53.

○Sequential cytogenetic and molecular analyses between 3 months and once a year: Monitoring clonal evolution. 161

Original page 162

Diagnostic criteria

–Essential criteria:

○Cytopenia involving one or more lineages.

○Dysplastic changes in one or more lineages, involving at least 10% of cells.

○> 5% bone marrow blasts and ≥ 2% peripheral blood blasts

○No fulfilling diagnostic criteria of MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation or AML.

–Desirable criterion: Detection of clonal cytogenetic and/or molecular abnormality.

Prognosis

–Blasts:

○5-9% blasts in the bone marrow: 25% develop AML in 2.2 years.

○10-19% blasts in the bone marrow: develop AML in 0.93 years.

–Genetic abnormalioties predict survival and time to AML evolution.

–Fibrosis has a worse outcome.

–CD7 expression has a worse outcome.

–Comorbidities, have an impact on survival. 162

Myelodysplastic neoplasms of childhood

Original page 163

–Childhood myelodysplastic neoplasm with low blasts

–Childhood myelodysplastic neoplasm with increased blasts 163

sections.t: Childhood myelodysplastic neoplasm with low blasts
sections.html:
Original page 164

•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with cytopenia and dysplasia arising in children and adolescents (<18 years of age), defined by <5% bone marrow blasts and < 2% peripheral blood blasts.

•Synonym: Refractory cytopenia of childhood

Subtypes

–Myelodysplastic neoplasms of childhood with low blasts, hypocellular

–Myelodysplastic neoplasms of childhood with low blasts, not otherwise specified

•Epidemiology: > 60% of childhood MDS with similar frequency in males and females.

•Etiology: Unknown, but some cases have germline mutations associated with bone marrow failure syndrome or predisposition to myeloid neoplasia.

•Pathogenesis:

–Genetic predisposition and immune dysregulation disorders such as aplastic anemia leading to bone marrow insufficiency, chromosomal instability, and selective growth of hematopoietic clones with acclerated proliferation.

–Suppression of normal hematopoiesis leading to cytopenias

–Additional somatic genetic abnormalities causes progression to acute myeloid leukemia.

Clinical picture

–Clinical picture of cytopenias, including fatigue, infections, and bleeding tendency.

–Clinical picture of inherited bone marrow failure syndromes or genetic germline predisposition: Congenital malformations and family history. 164

Original page 165

Laboratory diagnosis

–Dysplasia in peripheral blood and bone marrow

–Bone marrow:

○Hypocellular in 80% of cases: 5-10% of age-matched cellularity, with morphologic overlap with severe aplastic anemia (SAA).

○Cases with hypercellular and normocellular BM show slight to moderate increase in erythropoiesis, with frequent multilineage dysplasia and abnormal localization of immature hematopoietic precursors

○Reticulin fibrosis is usually absent.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Asynchronous expression of maturation antigens and lineage antigens on blasts “ can occur in severe aplastic anemia”

○Aberrant expression of CD56 or CD7 “Absent in severe aplastic anemia”.

○There may be a small clone of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

–Genetic tests:

○Monosomy 7 is the most common cytogenetic abnormality which may be associated with somatic mutations as in SETBP1 gene or germline GATA2 deficiency and SAMD9 or SAMD9L disorders.

○Trisomy 8, complex karyotype and other chromosomal alterations with karyotype evolution suggestive of disease progression. 165

Original page 166

○Somatic mutations associated with other MDS subtypes as mutation involving spliceosome complex genes, TET2, DNMT3A or TP53 genes are absent.

○Abnormalities associated with bone marrow failure syndromes or germline predisposition syndromes.

•Differential diagnosis: Non-neoplastic causes of cytopenia, such as infections, nutritional deficiencies, metabolic diseases, bone marrow failure syndromes, and germline mutations:

–Bone marrow failure syndromes and severe aplastic anemia: “Table above”:

–Germline predisposition: Interpretation of morphological changes should be integrated with the germline mutation

Diagnostic criteria

–Essential criteria:

○Cytopenia involving one or more lineages.

○Dysplastic changes in one or more lineages, involving at least 10% of cells.

○< 5% bone marrow blasts and < 2% peripheral blood blasts

○Meeting at least one of the following criteria:

➢Detection of clonal cytogenetic and/or molecular abnormality.

➢Exclusion of other causes of cytopenia (non-neoplastic and some germline mutations).

➢If hypocellular bone marrow, meeting morphologic criteria of cMDS-LB, hypocellular

Prognosis

–Karyotyping is the best prognostic indicator of progression to advanced MDS/AML:

○Monosomy 7, 7q deletion, or complex karyotype progress to AML. 166

Original page 167

○Monosomy 7 in children less than 5 years of age with SAMD9L germline mutations may undergo spontaneous resolution.

○Normal karyotype or trisomy 8 have stable disease.

–Bone marrow morphology findings, as increasing blast percentage, dysgranulopoiesis, or dysmegakaryopoiesis are associated with disease progression.

sections.t: Childhood myelodysplastic neoplasm with increased blasts
sections.html:
•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with cytopenia and dysplasia arising in children and adolescents (<18 years of age), defined by 5-19% bone marrow blasts and/or 2-19%% peripheral blood blasts.

•Clinical picture: Clinical picture of cytopenias, including fatigue, infections, and bleeding tendency.

•Epidemiology: It represents 10-25% of childhood MDS, with males are affected more than females.

•Etiology: Mostly unknown, but some cases have preceding severe aplastic anemia, bone marrow failure syndrome, germline mutations predisposing to myeloid neoplasm. N.B.: Cases arising following exposure to cytotoxic therapy are classified as Myeloid neoplasms post cytotoxic therapy. 167

Original page 168

•Pathogenesis: Similar to childhood myelodysplastic neoplasm with low blasts with more acquired cytogenetic abnormalities and RASopathies.

•Laboratory diagnosis: Similar to childhood myelodysplastic neoplasm with low blasts, except with increased numbers of blasts.

–Acquired cytogenetic abnormalities are more common, with an increased frequency of 7q deletion, and s complex karyotypes.

–RAS pathway mutations are common and often involve PTPN11.

–Trisomy 21 is an exclusion criteria

Diagnostic criteria

–Essential criteria:

○Cytopenia involving one or more lineages.

○Dysplastic changes in one or more lineages, involving at least 10% of cells.

○5-19% bone marrow blasts and/or 2-19%% peripheral blood blasts

○Exclusion of Down syndrome, juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, and AML with defining genetic abnormalities.

–Desirable criterion: Detection of clonal cytogenetic and/or molecular abnormality.

Prognosis

–The overall cure rate with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is 60%.

–Cytogenetics are the most important prognostics, with complex karyotype having the worst prognosis. 168

Myelodysplastic/Myeloproliferative Neoplasms

Original page 169

169

Original page 170

•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with overlapping pathologic and molecular features of myelodysplastic neoplasms and myeloproliferative neoplasms

•Characteristics:

–Hypercellularity of the bone marrow due to increased proliferation of one or more myeloid lineages.

–Increased numbers of circulating cells due to the effective proliferation.

–Morphological and/or functional dysplasia.

–There may be cytopenia in one or more of the other lineages due to an ineffective proliferation.

–Cases of well-defined MPNs which develop dysplasia and ineffective hematopoiesis are not placed in this category.

–Cases with BCR-ABL 1; with rearrangement of PDGFRA, PDGFRB, or FGFR1; or with PCM1-JAK2 are not placed in this category.

•2022 WHO classification: 1-Chronic myelo-monocytic leukemia (CMML). 2-Myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm with neutrophilia 3-Myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm with SF3B1 mutation and thrombocytosis 4-Myelodysplastic/Myeloproliferative neoplasm Not-otherwise specified 170

Original page 171

171

Original page 172

(CMML)

•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative features characterized by sustained peripheral blood monocytosis and various combinations of somatic mutations involving epigenetic regulation, spliceosome, and signal transduction.

•Classification: A-CMML can be classified according to the percentage of blasts and promonocytes in the blood and bone marrow into:

–CMML-1: Blasts and promonocytes are <5 % in the peripheral blood OR <10% in the bone marrow with no Auer rods.

–CMML-2: Blasts and promonocytes are 5-19% in the peripheral blood OR 10- 19% in the bone marrow OR Auer rods are present. B-CMML can be classified according to the total leukocytic count into:

–Myelodysplastic chronic myelomonocytic leukemia: The total leukocytic 9 count is less than 13 x 10/L.

–Myeloproliferative chronic myelomonocytic leukemia: The total 9 leukocytic count is 13 x 10/L or more.

•Epidemiology:

–The median age at diagnosis is 71-76 years.

–Male to female ratio is 1.6:1- 2.6:1.

•Etiology:

–Stochastic acquisition of age-related clonal hematopoiesis

–Some cases arise in patients with familial germline predisposition.. 172

Original page 173

•Pathogenesis:

–Accumulation of somatic mutations that affect:

○DNA methylation (e.g., TET2)

○Histone modifications (e.g., ASXL1)

○Splicing (e.g., SRSF2, U2AF1)

○Signaling (e.g., NRAS, KRAS, CBL or JAK2).

○Transcription factors and nucleosome assembly (e.g., SETBP1, RUNX1)

–Hypersensitivity to granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor

–Abnormal levels of cytokines and chemokines secreted by malignant cells

–Deficient secretion of IL-10 contributes to myelomonocytic expansion

•Clinical picture:

–Hepatosplenomegaly is more frequent in patients with leukocytosis.

–Constitutional symptoms as weight loss, fever, and night sweats are higher with the proliferative type.

–Symptoms of bone marrow failure as fatigue, infection, and bleeding are more common with the dysplastic type.

–Lymphadenopathy is uncommon and may indicate acute transformation.

•Laboratory diagnosis: 1-Complete blood picture and blood film:

–Total leukocytic count is variable and life-threatening hyperleukocytosis may be present. CMML can be classified according to the total leukocytic count into: 9 a)Myelodysplastic CMML: TLC < 13 x 10/L. 9 b)Myeloproliferative CMML: TLC > 13 x 10/L or more. 9

–Persistent absolute monocytosis (>0.5X10/L) and relative monocytosis 99 (>10%). It is usually 2-5 x 10/L, but can be more than 80 x 10/L. 173

Original page 174

–Monocytes are mature with some of them are immature but have denser chromatin, more nuclear convolutions and folds, and more abundant greyish cytoplasm than monoblasts and promonocytes. Blasts and promonocytes are < 20%.

–Neutrophilia is more common but there may be neutropenia.

–Neutrophil precursors; promyelocytes and myelocytes are usually < 10%.

–Dysgranulopoiesis (hyposegmentation or abnormal segmentation or abnormal cytoplasmic granulation) is less prominent myeloproliferative subtypes.

–Mild basophilia may be present.

–Eosinophils are usually normal or slightly increased except in CMML with 9 eosinophilia (> 1.5 x 10/L).

–Anemia in most patients, often normocytic but sometimes macrocytic and nucleated red blood cell precursors may be seen.

–Thrombocytopenia with large platelets is common but there may be thrombocytosis.

2-Bone marrow:

–Bone marrow is hypercellular but may be normocellular or rarely hypocellular.

–Granulocytic hyperplasia, Monocytic hyperplasia and left shift

–Blasts and promonocytes < 10% with abnormal localization of immature precursors. CMML is subdivided into CMML-1 with Blasts and promonocytes <5 % in the peripheral blood OR <10% in BM with no Auer rods and CMML-2 with Blasts and promonocytes 5-19% in the peripheral blood OR 10- 19% in BM OR Auer rods. 174

Original page 175

–Dysgranulopoiesis including hyposegmentation or abnormal segmentation or abnormal cytoplasmic granulation.

–Relative decrease in erythropoiesis with mild Dyserythropoiesis may be seen.

–Increased megakaryocytes without clustering with Micromegakaryocytes and/or megakaryocytic hyposegmentation.

–Nodules composed of mature clonal plasmacytoid dendritic cells with round nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and a rim of eosinophilic cytoplasm are present in 20% of cases.

–No pseudo-Gaucher cells.

–Mild reticulin fibrosis. Few cases have moderate or severe reticulin fibrosis especially the myeloproliferative subtypes with more absolute monocytosis, splenomegaly, and higher frequency of JAK2 p.V617F mutation.

3-Cytochemistry: Positive for fluoride sensitive alpha-naphthyl butyrate esterase, alpha-naphthyl acetate esterase and lysozyme.

175

Original page 176

4-Immunophenotyping:

–Positive for myelomonocytic antigens; CD33 and CD13 with increased proportion of classical (CD14+/CD16-) monocytes and decreased CD14 expression (monocyte immaturity).

–Monocytes may show aberrant antigen expression as CD56, CD2 and decreased expression of HLA-DR, CD13, CD11c, CD15, CD16, CD64 and CD36.

–Myeloid cells may show aberrant antigen expression and aberrant light-scatter

–Increased CD34+ cells with increased intensity of expression of CD13, CD34, CD117 and CD123, and decreased intensity of CD38 expression, aberrant expression of CD2, CD5, CD7, CD19, and CD56 and asynchronous expression of mature myelomonocytic markers such as CD15 and CD64.

–Aberrant antigen expression is associated with an early acute transformation.

–Immunohistochemistry is less sensitive than cytochemistry or flowcytometry with the most reliable marker is CD14. CD68R and CD163 can also be helpful.

–Mature plasmacytoid dendritic cells are positive for CD123, CD2AP, CD4, CD43, CD45RA, CD68/CD68R, CD303, BCL11A and granzyme B with rare expression of CD2, CD5, CD7, CD10, CD13, CD14, CD15, CD33 and CD56 and negative for TIA1 and perforin. The Ki-67 proliferation index is usually low.

176

Original page 177

5-Splenic biopsy: Splenic enlargement with infiltration of the red pulp by leukemic cells with a possible diffuse infiltration of plasmacytoid dendritic cells. 6-Lymph node biopsy: Diffuse infiltration by myeloid blasts with a possible diffuse infiltration of plasmacytoid dendritic cells. 7-Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia is common. 8-Genetic studies:

–No Philadelphia chromosome or BCR/ABL fusion gene.

–No rearrangement of PDGFRA, PDGFRB or FGFR1 or PCM1-JAK2 fusion gene.

–Clonal cytogenetic abnormalities in 23-34% of cases with the most common abnormalities are gain of chromosome 8, loss of chromosome 7 or del(7q). Other cytogenetic abnormalities include loss of Y chromosome and trisomy 12. Complex karyotype is not common

–Mutations that affect:

○DNA methylation (e.g., TET2)

○Histone modifications (e.g., ASXL1)

○Splicing (e.g., SRSF2, U2AF1)

○Signaling (e.g., NRAS, KRAS, CBL or JAK2).

○Transcription factors and nucleosome assembly (e.g., SETBP1, RUNX1)

•2022 WHO criteria for diagnosis:

177

Original page 178

N.B.: In the presence of known active autoimmune diseases and/or systemic inflammatory syndromes, increased classical monocytes (>94%) is not considered.

•Differential diagnosis:

•CML with the p190 BCR::ABL1: BCR::ABL1 is positive

•Post cytotoxic therapy CMML should be classified as myeloid neoplasms post cytotoxic therapy.

•AML with NPM1 mutation: Patients with NPM1 mutations

•Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase rearrangement: Patients who fulfill the diagnostic criteria

•Patients with systemic mastocytosis should be classified according to the criteria of systemic mastocytosis.

•Patients who are diagnosed with MPN at presentation and evolution to a CMML should be regarded as having disease progression and not be reclassified as CMML.

•Patients who present with MDS and subsequently meet the diagnostic criteria of CMML may be reclassified as CMML.

•Prognosis:

•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative features characterized by sustained peripheral blood neutrophilia and neutrophilic left-shift

•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative features characterized by SF3B1 mutation, ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis.

–The median age at the time of diagnosis is 68-75 years.

–There is a slight female prevalence.

–MDS with low blasts and SF3B1 mutation

–MDS with low blasts and isolated 5q deletion

–chronic myeloid leukemia and other MPN types

–AML with MECOM rearrangement

–Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase fusions

•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with dysplastic and proliferative features that does not meet the criteria for other defined MDS/MPN entities.

•Epidemiology:

–The second most common overlap syndrome.

–Males are > 60% of cases

–There may be thrombocytosis of more than 450X10/L or leukocytosis of more than 9 13X10/L.

–Serum LDH is increased

–TP53 mutations

–SF3B1 mutation should prompt careful exclusion of MDS/MPN-SF3B1-T

–Rearrangements of PDGFRA, PDGFRB, JAK2 or FGFR1;
