Acute Myeloid Leukemia

Original page 192

192

Original page 193

(AML)

•Definition: It a heterogeneous aggressive malignant disorder of hematopoietic cells, in which malignant transformation occurs in the hemopoietic stem cell or early progenitors resulting in clonal expansion of myeloid blasts in the bone marrow, peripheral blood, or other tissues with arrest of differentiation leading to accumulation of blasts and suppression of hematopoiesis.

•Epidemiology:

–Adults: It is the most common acute leukemia accounting for 80% of leukemia in adults with a median age at diagnosis of 65 years. It is slightly more common in males.

–Children: It accounts only for 10-15% of leukemia.

–Neonates: It is the predominant form of leukemia.

–Acute promyelocytic leukemia: Does not change greatly in incidence with age.

•Predisposing factors: I-Environmental factors: 1-Radiation. 2-Benzene. 3-Alkylating agents, topoisomerase II inhibitors, and other cytotoxic drugs. 4-Tobacco smoke. II-Acquired diseases: 1-Clonal myeloid diseases: Clonal progression can occur spontaneously, or may be enhanced by radiation or chemotherapy:

–Chronic myelogenous leukemia.

–Primary myelofibrosis. 193

Original page 194

–Essential thrombocythemia.

–Polycythemia vera.

–Clonal cytopenias.

–Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. 2-Other hematopoietic disorders:

–Aplastic anemia.

–Eosinophilic fasciitis. 3-Other disorders:

–Human immunodeficiency virus infection.

–Thyroid disorders.

–Polyendocrine disorders. III-Inherited or Congenital Conditions: 1-Sibling with AML. 2-Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia. 3-Ataxia-pancytopenia. 4-Bloom syndrome. 5-Kostmann syndrome. 6-Congenital agranulocytosis. 7-Chronic thrombocytopenia with chromosome 21q 22.12 microdeletion. 8-Diamond-Blackfan syndrome. 9-Down syndrome. 10-Dubowitz syndrome. 11-Dyskeratosis congenital. 12-Familial (pure, nonsyndromic) AML. 13-Familial platelet disorder. 14-Fanconi anemia. 15-Naxos syndrome. 194

Original page 195

16-Neurofibromatosis. 17-Noonan syndrome. 18-Poland syndrome. 19-Rothmund-Thomson syndrome. 20-Seckel syndrome. 21-Shwachman syndrome. 22-Werner syndrome (progeria). 23-Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome. 24-WT syndrome.

•Pathogenesis: Clonal evolution (Cooperative mutations):

–Carcinogenesis induces somatic mutations in either a hematopoietic multipotential cell or, occasionally, a more differentiated, lineage-restricted progenitor cell leading to an imbalance between oncogenes and anti- oncogenes yielding a small clonal progeny stable in size.

–Additional mutations lead to a new sub-clone that expands more aggressively.

–Continuous clonal evolution with further sub-clones leads to acute leukemia.

195

Original page 196

•Clinical picture 1-Clinical picture of bone marrow failure:

○Anemia: Pallor, weakness, dizziness, dyspnea, loss of concentration and blurring of vision. Symptoms can be disproportionate to the severity of anemia.

○Infection: Recurrent fever, arthralgia, headache and malaise. Infection becomes more prominent after chemotherapy.

○Thrombocytopenia: bleeding tendency.

○Acute promyelocytic leukemia and monocytic variants: Severe hemorrhage, primary fibrinolysis and DIC like picture (bleeding with multi- organ failure). 2-Clinical picture of organ infiltration:

○Moderate splenomegaly and hepatomegaly: 1/3 of cases.

○Monocytic variants are associated with lymphadenopathy, gum infiltration, skin lesions, hepatosplenomegaly, proptosis and renal failure

○Eye involvement is very unusual, but retinal, choroidal, iridial, and optic nerve infiltration can occur.

○Otitis externa and interna, inner ear hemorrhage, and mastoid tumors with seventh nerve involvement may be presenting signs.

○Gastrointestinal infiltration may occur but functional disturbances are unusual.

○Respiratory tract infiltration may occur with laryngeal obstruction, alveolar septal infiltration, or pleural seeding.

○Cardiac involvement is frequent but rarely causes symptoms.

○Urogenital system can be affected but functional abnormalities are rare.

○Osteoarticular pain and necrosis may occur. 196

Original page 197

○Central and periphreral nervous system infiltration is very uncommon with increased intracranial tension leading to headache, vomiting and blurring of vision.

○Myeloid sarcoma is an extramedullary mass composed of myeloblasts or monoblasts. It may be found in virtually any location, including the skin; orbit; paranasal sinuses; bone; chest wall; breast; heart; gastrointestinal, respiratory, or genitourinary tract; central or peripheral nervous system; or lymph nodes and spleen. 3-Clinical picture of hyper-leukocytosis:

○5% of cases develop signs or symptoms of hyper-leukocytosis usually 9 greater than 100 x 10/L.

○CNS, lungs, and penis are the most sensitive to the hyper-leukocytosis with dzziness, stupor, diabetes insipidus, dyspnea, and priapism.

○Chemotherapy in hyper-leukocytic patients may lead to a pulmonary leukostatic syndrome.

○Larger-vessel occlusion is rare.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

➢Evidence of Clonality: a)Acquired cytogenetic abnormalities in all cells of the clone. b)Clonal X chromosome inactivation patterns in all neoplastic cells as evidenced by the presence of the same G6PD isoenzyme or by X-linked restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) which shows hypomethylation of the active X-chromosome. c)Clonal immunophenotyping.

1-Complete blood count and blood film:

a-Variable numbers of blast cells: 197

Original page 198

–Myeloblasts: Larger with 2-4 nucleoli and basophilic agranular cytoplasm and may be Auer rods in small percent of blasts in about 15% of cases.

–Monoblasts: The largest with 3 – 5 nucleoli and basophilic cytoplasm.

–Megakaryoblasts: They resemble small lymphocytes with cytoplasmic blebs.

b-RBCs:

○Normocytic normochromic anemia in 80% of cases. Causes of anemia include:

–Decreased red cells production is the main cause.

–Decreased red cell life span.

–Red cell autoantibodies are extremely rare.

○Normoblasts may be present.

○Red cell morphology is mildly abnormal, with marked anisocytosis and occasional poikilocytes. c-Platelets: Thrombocytopenia in 90% of cases with more than 50% of patients 9 have a platelet count less than 50 x 10/L and may be giant platelets and poorly 198

Original page 199

granulated platelets. Thrombocytopenia may be caused by decreased production and/or decreased survival. d-White blood cells: 9

–The total leukocyte count is less than 5 x 10/L in about 50% of cases. 9

–The absolute neutrophil count is less than 1 x 10/L in more than 50% of cases.

–Patients with hyperleukocytosis may have a normal absolute neutrophil count with few mature neutrophils.

–Hypersegmented, hyposegmented, and hypogranular neutrophils may occur. e-Pancytopenia in M3 and M7. 2-Reticulocytic count: It is usually between 0.5-2%.

3-Bone marrow:

A-Bone marrow aspiration:

–Hypercellular bone marrow with replacement of normal series by blasts. Auer rods can be found in the marrow blasts in one sixth of cases. The 20% blast requirement are eliminated for AML types with defining genetic abnormalities (with the exception of AML with BCR::ABL1 fusion and AML with CEBPA mutationwhich require at least 20% blasts for diagnosis)

–There may be basophilia or eosinophilia in some cases.

–Normal erythropoiesis, megakaryocytopoiesis, and granulopoiesis are decreased or absent.

–There may be dysplasia in 30-50% of cases in the form of very small or large erythroblasts with nuclear fragmentation or binucleation or delayed nuclear condensation; small or monolobed megakaryocytes; or hypogranulated, bilobed, or monolobed neutrophils. 199

Original page 200

B-Bone marrow trephine biopsy:

–Biopsy is indicated only in:

•Dry tap.

•Differentiation of packed bone marrow (with rapid clotting) of acute leukemia from aplastic anemia.

•Follow up of treatment.

–Hypercellular bone marrow.

–There may be residual islands of erythroblasts or megakaryocytes.

–Reticulin fibrosis is common but usually is slight to moderate except in cases of megakaryoblastic leukemia, in which intense fibrosis is common.

–Increased vascularization which may be caused by increased levels of vascular endothelial growth factor, basic fibroblast growth factor, angiogenin, and angiopoietin-1.

4-Cytochemistry:

Reaction Positive Myeloperoxidase AML except M0-M5-M7 Sudan black B AML except M0-M5-M7 Specific esterase AML except M0-M5-M7 200

Original page 201

Non-specific esterase M4-M5 Acid phosphatase T ALL Periodic acid shiff M6

5-Immunophenotyping:

–Markers of immaturity: CD34, CD117 (C-kit) and HLA DR (except M3).

–Myeloid markers: CD33, CD13 and MPO.

–Markers of maturation: CD15 and CD65.

–Monocytic markers: CD11b, CD14, CD64 and lysozymes.

–Erythroid markers: Glycophorin A and CD71, CD36.

–Megakaryocytic markers: CD41, CD42 and CD61.

–Negative lymphocytic markers as CD19 “may be aberrantly positive” and CD3.

6-Genetic tests:

–60% of cases have abnormal karyotyping.

–The most common cytogenetic abnormalities are trisomy 8, monosomy 7, monosomy 21, trisomy 21, and loss of an X or Y chromosome.

–Therapy related AML is commonly associated with, loss of part or all of chromosome 5.

–Translocations (8;21) and (15;17) and inversion 16 have a more favorable prognosis.

–Deletion of all or part of chromosomes 5 and 7 or the complex changes have an unfavorable prognosis.

–Other findings as normal karyotype, trisomy 8 and abnormalities of 11q23 have an intermediate prognosis.

–85% of cases with normal karyotyping have mutations in at least one of five genes; NPM1, FLT3, CEPBA, MLL, and NRAS. 201

Original page 202

–Mutations in NPM1 or CEPBA are associated with more favorable prognosis.

–Mutations in FLT3 and wild type expression of NPM1 and CEPBA without FLT3 mutation have poor prognosis.

–Down-regulation of the microRNA-181 family has a poor outcome.

7-Bone marrow culture:

–85% of cases have no colony-forming cells, but 60% of cases have cells capable of forming small clusters (4–40 cells).

–15% of cases have colony-forming cells, but often in reduced numbers and with abnormal maturation patterns.

–Restoration of colony-forming cells in the marrow of treated patients often precedes morphologic evidence of remission.

8-Electron microscopy is useful in:

○M0: positive myeloperoxidase at ultrastructural level.

○M7: positive platelet peroxidase at ultrastructural level.

○Acute basophilic leukemia.

9-Biochemical parameters:

–Serum LDH: Mild to moderate increase. It is higher in myelomonocytic and monocytic AML than in other phenotypes.

–Serum uric acid: Mild to moderate increase and may be markedly elevated after chemotherapy if no hypouricemic agent is added to the treatment. It is higher in myelomonocytic and monocytic AML than in other phenotypes.

–Hyperclacemia can occur due to secretion of parathormone like protein from leukemic cells and severe lactic acidosis.

–Hypophosphatemia can occur due to phosphate uptake by leukemic cells. 202

Original page 203

–Abnormalities of sodium is uncommon and usually mild. Severe hyponatremia due to inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion or severe hypernatremia due to diabetes insipidus may occur.

–Abnormalities of potassium is uncommon and usually mild. Hypokalemia is more frequent due to the proximal renal tubular dysfunction and can be severe and worsened by the treatment. Pseudo-hyperkalemia may occur in hyper- leukocytosis as a result of in vitro leakage from white cells.

–Pseudo-hypoglycemia pseudo-hypoxia can occur from the effects of high blast cell counts in blood.

–Increased liver enzymes due to hepatic infiltration may occur.

–Renal dysfunction due to renal infiltration may occur.

–Ectopic adrenocorticotropic hormone secretion may occur.

10-Coagulopathy:

–Abnormal concentrations of coagulation factors or their inhibitors may be present with normal or near normal prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times.

–Elevations of platelet factor 4 and thromboxane B2.

–Decreases in α2-antiplasmin, protein C, and antithrombin III which may be associated with venous thrombosis.

–Acute promyelocytic and monoblastic leukemia are associated with DIC. 11-Urine: microscopic hematuria and uric acid crystals.

N.B.: Hypoplastic acute leukemia:

–2% of cases which have pancytopenia and absent blood blast cells. 203

Original page 204

–These cases are associated with absence of hepatic, splenic, or lymph nodal enlargement and hypocellular bone marrow with evident blasts.

N.B.: Oligoblastic (Subacute, Smoldering) acute leukemia:

–10% of cases which are manifested by anemia, thrombocytopenia and low, normal, or increased leukocyte count with a small proportion of blast cells in the peripheral blood and marrow (3–20%).

–These cases have a high morbidity and mortality from infection and hemorrhage and can evolve into overt polyblastic AML.

–Dysplasia is more frequent and more striking.

•Differential diagnosis:

–Lymphocytosis: Blasts may be misdiagnosed as lymphocytes and can be differentiated by immunophenotyping.

–Bone pain in osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis: must be differentiated by CBC and bone scan.

–Bone marrow infiltration: Leukemia, lymphoma, neuroblastoima and metastatic carcinoma must be differentiated by immunophenotyping

–M0: must be differentiated from L2, M1, M5a, M6b and M7 by immunophenotyping and cytochemistry.

–M3 variant must be differentiated from M5b (convoluted nucleus) by immunophenotyping and cytochemistry.

–M4 must be differentiated from M2, M5 and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) by immunophenotyping and cytochemistry.

–Acute promyelocytic leukemia must be differentiated from cases of pseudoleukemia in which there is a recovery from drug-induced or Pseudomonas aeruginosa–induced agranulocytosis and is characterized by a striking cohort of promyelocytes in the marrow. In pseudoleukemia, the 204

Original page 205

platelet count may be normal; the degree of leukopenia often is more 9 profound (<1.0 x 10/L) than usually seen in AML; promyelocytes contain a prominent Golgi zone with no Auer rods. Differentiation is made by immunophenotyping and genetic tests.

–Hypoplastic acute leukemia must be differentiated from aplastic anemia by careful examination for blasts and dysplasia. Differentiation is made by immunophenotyping and genetic tests.

–Leukemoid reactions can be distinguished from AML by the absence of leukemic blast cells in the blood or marrow.

–Nonleukemic pancytopenias can be distinguished from AML by the absence of leukemic blast cells in the blood or marrow.

–Nonleukemic thrombocytopenia can be distinguished from AML by the absence of leukemic blast cells in the blood or marrow.

Treatment

1-Chemotherapy:

A-Induction treatment: Simultaneous use of multiple agents or a planned sequence of therapy called timed sequential treatment.

–Remission: It is the elimination of the leukemic cell population in marrow as judged by microscopy and flowcytometry and the restitution of normal or virtually normal white cell, hemoglobin, and platelet concentrations in the blood. B-Post-induction treatment: Cytotoxic chemotherapy, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, or low-dose maintenance chemotherapy, depending upon patient performance status and risk factors. C-If relapse occurs; different chemotherapy regimens, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, or other investigational regimens are indicated. 205

Original page 206

2-Bone marrow transplantation: in patients less than 40 years in the first or second remission or early in relapse.

–Allogenic: Totally matched sibling.

–Autologous: If no matching sibling. 3-Transfusion therapy: For improvement of cytopenias and hypofibrinogenemia. 4-Hyperleukocytosis: leukapharesis or exchange transfusion, hydration and alkalinization, cytoreductive therapy and inhaled nitric oxide to improve the hypoxia. 5-Meningeal infiltration: Intrathecal chemotherapy. 6-Myeloid Sarcoma:Intensive AML induction therapy with surgical resection and local irradiation. 7-Prophylactic antibacterial, antifungal, and/or antiviral: This is a matter of controversy. 8-Growth factors: This is a matter of controversy. 9-Hyperuricemia: allopurinole. 10-Hyperphosphatemia: Allominium hydroxide.

Response to treatment

–Complete remission (CR):

○Bone marrow blasts <5%.

○Absence of circulating blasts and blasts with Auer rods.

○Absence of extramedullary disease. 9

○Absolute neutrophil count >1.0 x 10/L. 9

○Platelet count >100 x 10/L.

–Complete remission without minimal residual disease (CRmdr-): Complete remission negativity for a genetic marker by PCR or flowcytometry. 206

Original page 207

–Complete remession with incomplete hematological recovery(CRi):

○Bone marrow blasts <5%.

○Absence of circulating blasts and blasts with Auer rods.

○Absence of extramedullary disease. 9

○Absolute neutrophil count < 1.0 x 10/L. 9

○Platelet count < 100 x 10/L.

–Morphologic leukemia free state (MLFS):

○Bone marrow blasts <5%.

○Absence of blasts with Auer rods.

○Absence of extramedullary disease.

○No hematologic recovery required.

–Partial remission (PR): All hematologic criteria of CR; decrease of bone marrow blast percentage to 5% to 25%; and decrease of pretreatment bone marrow blast percentage by at least 50%Bone marrow blasts 5 – 25 %.

–Primary refractoriness: No CR or CRi after 2 courses of intensive induction treatment; excluding patients with death in aplasia or death due to indeterminate cause.

–Hematological relapse: Bone marrow blasts ≥5%; or reappearance of blasts in the blood; or development of extramedullary disease.

–Molecular relapse: Reoccurrence of minimal residual disease as assessed by PCR or flowcytometry.

•Prognostic factors: 1-General health and co-morbidities. 207

Original page 208

2-Performance status. 3-Age: Increasing age is a bad prognostic factor. 4-Cytogenetic prognostic factors:

Good Intermediate Bad

–t(8;21) -+8 --5

–inv(16) -+21 --7

–t(15;17) -+22 -de(5q)

–Normal cytogenetic with NPMI -del(7q) -Abnormal 3q or CEBPA mutations without -del(9q) -Complex cytogenetics FLTI3-ITD mutation -Abnormal 11q23 -Normal cytogenetics with

–t(8;21), inv(16) and t(15;17) FLTI3-ITD mutation with kit mutation

sections.html:
Original page 209

•The French–American–British classification system represents the first attempt to distinguish between different types of AML.

•It is established in 1970s.

•It defines eight subtypes (M0 through M7) based on the morphological and cyto- chemical characteristics of the leukemic cells.

➢M0 = undifferentiated myeloblastic leukemia:

•Blast cells > 30% of bone marrow All nucleated cells (ANC).

•Morphology: Small to moderate sized blasts with no granules or Auer rods.

•Associated dysplasia with no multi-lineage dysplasia.

•Cytochemistry:

–Negative Sudan black B (SBB), myeloperoxidase (MPO) and specific esterase.

–Negative for non-specific esterase and acid phosphatase.

209

Original page 210

➢M1 Acute myeloblastic leukemia without maturation:

•Blast cells > 30% of bone marrow ANC and > 90% of bone marrow non- erythroid cells (NEC).

•Bone marrow maturing graualocytic component < 10% of NEC.

•Bone marrow maturing monocytic component < 10% of NEC.

•Cytochemistry:

–Positive for MPO, SBB and specific esterase.

–Negative for non-specific esterase and acid phosphatase.

210

Original page 211

➢M2 Acute myeloblastic leukemia with maturation:

•Blast > 30% of ANC and 30-89% of NEC.

•Bone marrow maturing granulocytic component is > 10% of NEC.

•Bone marrow maturing monocytic component is < 20% of NEC.

•Granulocytic maturation is along the neutrophil lineage, but may be along the eosinophil or basophils lineages (M2 Eos or M2 Baso).

•Auer rods are more than in M1.

•Cytochemistry:

–Positive for MPO, SBB and specific esterase.

–Negative for non-specific esterase and acid phosphatase.

211

Original page 212

➢M3 Acute promyelocytic leukaemia:

•The predominant cell is Promylecyte.

•Blasts < 30% bone marrow ANC.

•Abnormal promnyelocyte: Cytoplasm is tightly packed with dense red or purpule granules which may be so dense that the nuclear outline is obscured. Auer rods are present in 50% of cases and in some cases there are giant granules or multiple Auer rods which are often in sheafs or faggots. Minority of cells are agranular.

•Pancytopenia.

•Coagulopathy mainly in the form of DIC.

•Cytochemistry: Strongly positive for MPO, SBB and specific esterase.

•M3 variant: Leukocytosis and bilobed kidney shaped, multilobed or convoluted nuclei with either sparce fine granules or agranular cytoplasm.

212

Original page 213

➢M4 Acute myelomonocytic leukemia:

•Blast > 30% of bone marrow ANC.

•Bone marrow maturing granulocytic component >20%.

•Significant monocytic component as evidenced by two of the following:

–Bone marrow monocytic component > 20% of NEC. 9

–Peripheral blood monocytes > 5 x 10 / L.

–Positive for non-specific estrase or high urinary or serum lysozyme.

•Granulocytic differentiation may be in the direction of eosinophils (M4 eso).

•Cytochemistry: Positive dual esterase, MPO, SBB and acid phosphatase.

213

Original page 214

➢M5 Acute monocytic / monoblastic leukemia:

•Blast > 30% of ANC.

•Bone marrow monocytic component > 80% of NEC.

–M5a (acute monoblastic leukemia): Monoblast > 80 % of bone marrow monocytic component.

–M5b (acute monocytic leukemia): Monoblas < 80 % of bone marrow monocytic component.

•Cytochemistry:

–Positive for non-specific esterase and acid phosphatase.

–Negative for MPO, SBB and specific esterase. 214

Original page 215

➢M6 Acute erythroleukemia:

•Erythroid cells show megaloblastic changes and nuclear lobulation, karyorrhexis, binuclearity and cytoplasmic vacuolation.

•Granulocytic and megakaryocytic lineages usually show dysplastic changes.

•Old WHO Classification:

–M6a (acute erythro-myeloid leukemia): Erythroblasts > 50% of bone marrow ANC and myeloblasts > 20% of NES.

–M6b (acute erythroid leukemia): Erythroblasts > 80% of bone marrow ANC.

•Cytochemistry: Positive for periodic acid shiff (PAS) and: 215

Original page 216

–M6a: Positive for MPO, SBB and specific esterase.

–M6b: Negative for MPO, SBB and specific esterase.

➢M7 Acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia:

•Blast > 30% of bone marrow ANC.

•Cytochemistry: Negative for MPO, SBB and specific esterase and positive for platelet peroxidase.

•Blasts are demonstrated to be megakaryoblasts by immunophenotyping.

216

Original page 217

Original page 218

✓Changes from the 2016 WHO classification:

–The separation of AML with defining genetic abnormalities from AML defined by differentiation and elimination of the previously confusing use of the term AML not otherwise specified, under which types based on differentiation were listed.

–Elimination of the 20% blast requirement for AML types with defining genetic abnormalities (with the exception of AML with BCR::ABL1 fusion and AML with CEBPA mutation which require at least 20% blasts for diagnosis). This requiress estimation of variant allele frequency or fusion transcript quantitation.

–Introduction of the subtype; AML with other defined genetic alterations.

–Three AML subtypes with characteristic rearrangements involving KMT2A, MECOM, and NUP98 are recognized. They may be cryptic on conventional 218

Original page 219

karyotyping. AML with KMT2A rearrangement replaces “AML with t(9;11)(p22;q23); KMT2A-MLLT3” to include more than 80 KMT2A fusion partners

–Prognostic factors of PML::RARA, AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1, and AML with CBF::MYH11, have expanded from KIT mutations, which are still relevant, to include additional cytogenetic features and MRD status post induction.

–The definition of AML with CEBPA mutation has changed to include biallelic (biCEBPA) as well as single mutations located in the basic leucine zipper (bZIP) region of the gene (smbZIP-CEBPA).

–AML with myelodysplasia-related changes, is now called AML, myelodysplasia- related with removal of morphology alone as a diagnostic premise to make a diagnosis, update of defining cytogenetic criteria; and introduction of a mutation- based definition based on a set of 8 genes – SRSF2, SF3B1, U2AF1, ZRSR2, ASXL1, EZH2, BCOR, STAG2.

–Pure erythroid leukemia, is now called acute erythroid leukemia. 219

➢Acute myeloid leukemia with other defined genetic alteration 220

Original page 221

•Definition: It is an acute leukemia associated with formation of the PML::RARA (Promyelocyte leukemia gene - Retinoic acid receptor alpha gene) fusion gene which results in predominance abnormal promyelocytes.

•Synonyms:

–Acute promyelocytic leukemia, t(15;17) (q22;q11-12).

–Acute promyelocytic leukemia.

•Subtypes: APL with a variant RARA translocation.

•Corresponding FAB category: M3 and M3 variant.

•Epidemiology:

–It accounts for 5-8% of AML cases in middle-aged adults.

–It has a lower relative frequency in elderly patients.

•Etiology and pathogenesis:

–Etiology is unknown.

–The PML geneon 15q24.1has both growth suppressor and pro-apoptotic activity.

–The RARA gene on 17q21.2 is a transcription factor that mediates the effect of retinoic acid, which is necessary for normal myeloid maturation.

–Acute promyelocytic leukemia is caused by translocation (15;17)(q24.1;q21.2) leading to formation of the gain-of-function PML::RARA fusion gene that impairs the normal growth suppressor and proapoptotic activity of PML and represses the target genes of retinoic acid preventing the differentiation of myeloid cells resulting in constitutive proliferation and inhibition of terminal differentiation.

•Clinical features:

–Both hypergranular and microgranular variants are frequently associated with disseminated intravascular coagulopathy and increased fibrinolysis which is associated with significant early death rates. 221

Original page 222

•Laboratory findings:

–Peripheral blood and bone marrow :

•Bone marrow is hypercoagulable with rapid clotting and is usually hypercellular but aspirate smears may be aparticulate.

•The hypergranular APL is associated with:

▪Pancytopenia.

▪Only occasional obvious leukemic promyelocytes may be observed in the peripheral blood.

▪These abnormal promyelocytes are characterized by:

○Irregular and greatly variable nuclear size and shape.

○Nuclei are often kidney-shaped or bilobed.

○The cytoplasm is filled by bright pink, red, or purple densely packed or even coalescent large granules. These granules may be so large and/or numerous that they totally obscure the nuclear-cytoplasmic margin.

○Auer rods are usually larger than those in other types of AML.

○Characteristic cells containing bundles of Auer rods “faggots” randomly distributed within the cytoplasm are present in most cases.

○In some cells, the cytoplasm is filled with fine dust-like granules.

▪Myeloblasts with single Auer rods may also be observed.

•The microgranular APL is associated with:

▪A very high leukocytic count with a short doubling time.

▪The abnormal microgranular promyelocytes are present in large numbers in the peripheral blood.

▪The abnormal microgranular promyelocytes are characterized by:

○An apparent paucity or absence of granules which may cause confusion with acute monocytic leukemia. The hypogranular appearance of the cytoplasm is due to the submicroscopic size of the azurophilic granules.

○Bilobed nuclei. 222

Original page 223

▪A small number of abnormal promyelocytes with clearly visible granules and/or bundles of Auer rods can be identified in many cases.

▪Abnormal promyelocytes with deeply basophilic cytoplasm may be present mainly in the relapse phase after treatment with tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid).

•Bone marrow mature granulocytes, erythroid series and megakaryocytic series are markedly decreased in number without dysplasia.

•Bone marrow biopsy sections show an increased vascularity with uncommon collagen. Treatment induces maturation, increases cellularity and induces bone marrow necrosis and collagen fibrosis.

–Cytochemistry:

○The MPO reaction is always strongly positive in all the leukemic promyelocytes, with the reaction product covering the entire cytoplasm and often the nucleus.

○The non-specific esterase reaction is weakly positive in rare cases.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Promyelocytes characteristically have high side scatter and forward scatter. Microgranular blasts are frequently located in the blast gate on CD45 vs. side- scatter plots.

○Markers of immaturity: Promyelocytes mostly show expression of KIT (CD117), although this is sometimes weak, low or negative expression of HLA-DR and CD34. CD34 is frequently positive in some cells in the microgranular variant.

○Leukocyte integrins: Promyelocytes show negative expression of CD11a, CD11b, and CD18. CD11c may be expressed in some cells. Expression of CD11 b and CD11 c can be up-regulated after tretinoin treatment.

○Myeloid markers: Promyelocytes show homogeneous bright expression of CD33 and heterogeneous expression of CD13.

○Markers of maturation: Promyelocytes show negative or weak CD15, CD65, CD66b, and CD66c and positive CD64 expression. 223

Original page 224

○Monocytic markers: Promyelocytes are negative for CD14 and lysozymes.

○Erythroid markers: Promyelocytes are negative for glycophorin A and CD71.

○Megakaryocytic markers: Promyelocytes are negative for CD41, CD42 and CD61.

○Lymphocytic markers: Promyelocytes are negative for CD19 and CD3. Rare cases may have weak cytoplasmic CD3 or TdT expression.

○Aberrant markers: CD2 is frequently positive in some cells in the microgranular variant and is associated with FLT3-ITD. CD56 is expressed in approximately 10% of cases and is associated with bad prognosis.

○Immunocytochemistry: Antibodies against the PML gene product show a characteristic nuclear multigranular pattern with nucleolar exclusion, in contrast to the speckled, relatively large nuclear bodies seen in normal promyelocytes or the blasts in other types of AML.

–Genetic tests:

○Translocation (15;17)(q24.1;q21.2) which is confirmed by detection of PML::RARA fusion gene. Depending on the PML breakpoint location on chromosome 15, three PML::RARA transcript isoforms can be detected:

✓Long transcript located in intron 6 (bcr1).

✓Variant transcript located in exon 6 (bcr2)

✓Short transcript located in intron 3 (bcr3).

✓Atypical isoforms of PML::RARA transcripts involving intron 4, exon 6, and exon 7 can also be detected in sporadic cases.

○Rare cases lack the classic t(15;17)(q24.1;q21.2) on routine cytogenetic studies with complex variant translocations involving chromosomes 15 and 17, with an additional chromosome or with cryptic or masked t(15;17)(q24.1 ;q21.2)leading to the expression of the PML::RARA transcript and giving the same morphological patterns. 224

Original page 225

○Secondary cytogenetic abnormalities are present in about 40% of cases, Deletion 7q and trisomy 8 are the most frequent alterations.

○Mutations involving FLT3, including FLT3 internal tandem duplication (FLT3-ITD) “the most common and are associated with a higher white blood cell count and microgranular morphology” and FLT3 p.D835 mutation, occur in 40% of cases. Other mutations include WT1 (14%), NRAS (7- 10%), USP9X (9%), ARID1A (4%), EED (4%) and KRAS (3-4%) mutations.

○Variant RARA translocations: A subset of cases, often with morphological features resembling those of APL, show variant translocations involving RARA and should be diagnosed as APL with a variant RARA translocation which may be resistant to tretinoin. The variant fusion partners include:

•ZBTB16 at 11q23.2: Some of these cases show some morphological differences, with a predominance of cells with regular nuclei, many granules and usually with an absence of Auer rods, an increased number of pelger-Huet neutrophils and a strong MPO activity.

•NUMA1 at 11q13.

•NPM1 at 5q35.

•STAT5B at 17q21.

•PRKAR1A at 17q24

•FIP1L1 at 4q12

•BCOR at Xp11

•OBFC2A at 2q32

•TBLR1 at 3q26

•GTF2I at 7q11

•IRF2BP2 at 1q42

•FNDC3B at 3q26. 225

Original page 226

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○Myeloid neoplasm with increased peripheral blood and/or bone marrow atypical promyelocytes showing characteristic abnormal hypergranular promyelocytes or microgranular blasts (may be < 20%).

○Detection of PML::RARA.

○No history of exposure to cytotoxic therapy.

–Desirable criterion: Detection of t(15;17)(q24;q21).

•Prognosis:

–Good response (> 90%) to a combination of all-transe retinoic acid (ATRA) and arsenic trioxide which act as differentiating agents with anthracycline added for high-risk patients.

–Risk categories: 9

○High-risk subsets: A WBC ≥10 x 10 /L at diagnosis 9

○intermediate-risk subsets: A WBC < 10 x 10 /L at diagnosis with platelet count 9 ≤40 x 10 /L 9

○Low -risk subsets: A WBC < 10 x 10 /L at diagnosis with platelet count < 40 9 x 10 /L 226

sections.t: Acute Myeloid Leukemia with RUNX1::RUNXT1 fusion
sections.html:
Original page 227

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia characterized by fusion of the RUNX family transcription factor 1 (RUNX1) and RUNX1 partner transcriptional co- repressor 1 (RUNX1T1) genes.

•Synonyms: Acute myeloid leukemia with t(8;21)(q22;q22.1).

•Corresponding FAB category: 90% of cases correspond to M2 Eos or M2 Baso while 10% of cases correspond to M1.

•Epidemiology:

–It occurs in 1-5% of AML cases.

•Etiology and pathogenesis:

–The core-binding factor (CBF) is a hematopoietic transcription factor. Its alpha subunit is coded by the RUNX1 gene and the beta subunit is coded by the CBFB gene.

–The RUNX1 is a master transcriptional regulator of adult hematopoiesis and RUNX1T1 is a transcriptional co-repressor

–The RUNX1::RUNX1T1 fusion gene product binds the CBFβinstead of its alpha subunit resulting in:

○Inhibition of the expression of the tumor suppressor; p14ARF (CDKN2A) which is normally activated by RUNX1 “The normal RUNX1 transcripts are inhibited”.

○Inhibition of the expression of the tumor suppressor; neurofibromin (NF1).

○Inhibition of the expression of the microRNA -223, leading to blocking of the differentiation.

○Activation of the microRNA-24 which normally blocks differentiation. 227

Original page 228

○Activation of the anti-apoptotic gene BCL-2 leading to inhibition of apoptosis.

–This translocation alone is insufficient to induce leukemia but can induce leukemia in cooperation with other mutations.

•Clinical picture:

–Presentation of bone marrow failure including fatigue, bleeding, and infection.

–Organomegaly may be present.

–Myeloid sarcoma.

•Laboratory findings: 1-Peripheral blood and bone marrow:

–Bone marrow trephine biopsy or clot preparation usually show extensive replacement by immature cells.

–In 90% of cases, bone marrow smears show increased blasts and myeloid precursors at various stages of maturation while 10% of cases have features of AML without maturation.

–Blasts are large with abundant basophilic cytoplasm, numerous azurophilic granules and peri-nuclear hoof and Auer rods.

–Blasts may show pseudo- Chediak- Higashi granules suggesting abnormal fusion.

–Increased eosinophil precursors are common (M2 Eos) without the cytological or cytochemical abnormalities characteristic of AML with inv(16)(p13.1q22) or t(16;16)(p13.1 ;q22).

–Bone marrow maturing granulocytic component is usually more than 10% of NEC.

–Bone marrow monocytic component is usually minimal or absent (usually less than 20% of NEC). 228

Original page 229

–Basophils and/or mast cells may increase (M2 Baso) and there may be an associated systemic mastocytosis which is masked by the acute leukemia.

–Promyelocytes, myelocytes, and mature neutrophils show variable dysplasia with pseudo- Pelger-Huet nuclei and/or cytoplasmic staining abnormalities, including homogeneous pink cytoplasm in neutrophils.

–Dysplasia of erythroid or megakaryocytic series are uncommon.

2-Cytochemistry:

–Blasts are positive for MPO, SBB and specific esterase.

–Blasts may show a Golgi zone signal with non-specific esterase which is not an evidence of monocytic differentiation.

3-Immunophenotyping:

–Markers of immaturity: A subpopulation of blast cells showing high-intensity expression of CD34 and HLADR.

–Myeloid markers: A subpopulation of blast cells showing high-intensity expression of MPO and CD13 and relatively weak expression of CD33.

–Markers of maturation: A subpopulation of cells is positive for CD15 and/or CD65.

–Maturation asynchrony may be present in populations of blasts as the coexpression of CD34 and CD15.

–Monocytic markers: Blasts are negative for CD11b, CD14, CD64 and lysozymes.

–Erythroid markers: Blasts are negative for glycophorin A and CD71, CD36.

–Megakaryocytic markers: Blasts are negative for CD41, CD42 and CD61.

–Lymphoid markers: Blasts are negative for CD10, CD22 and CD3. 229

Original page 230

–Aberrant markers: Positive expression of CD19 “weak” and PAX5 by blasts is common and they may express cytoplasmic CD79a, TdT “weak” and/or CD56 “which has a bad prognosis and strong association with KIT mutations”.

4-Genetic tests:

–Translocation (8;21)(q22;q22) and RUNX1::RUNXT1fusion.

–At least one mutation can be identified in 85-90% of AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1cases, but more mutations may be present in some cases.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria :

○Myeloid neoplasm with increased peripheral blood and/or bone marrow blasts (may be < 20%)

○Detection of RUNX1::RUNX1T1.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria for myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy.

–Desirable criterion: Detection of t(8;21)(q22;q22.1).

•Prognosis:

–It is associated with a high rate of complete remission and long-term disease-free survival when treated with intensive consolidation therapy.

–Adverse prognostics include KIT mutations in adults, presence of two or more associated mutations, CD56 expression and failure to achieve complete remission after consolidation therapy.

–Good prognostics include hyperdiploidy and/or presence of del(9q) 230

sections.t: Acute Myeloid Leukemia with CBFB::MYH11 Fusion
sections.html:
Original page 231

•Definition: Acute myeloid leukemia characterized by fusion of the core-binding factor subunit beta (CBFB) and the myosin heavy chain 11 (MYH11) genes.

•Synonyms:

–Acute myeloid leukemia with t(16;16)(p13.1;q22)

–Acute myeloid leukemia with inv(16)(p13.1q22)

•Corresponding FAB category: M4 Eos.

•Normal counterpart: The hematopoietic progenitor cell with thepotential to differentiate along granulocyticand monocytic lineages.

•Epidemiology:

–It is found in 5- 8% of younger patients with AML.

–The frequency is lower in older adults.

•Etiology and pathogenesis:

–MYH11 codes for a smooth muscle myosin heavy chain and acts as a transcriptional repressor.

–CBFB codes for the beta subunit of the core-binding factor (CBF) a hematopoietic transcription factor.

–The product of CBFB::MYH11 fusion gene binds RUNX1”the alpha subunit of core-binding factor” instead of its beta subunitsuppressing the function of the core binding factor heterodimer either through sequestration of the RUNX1 or through converting it into a transcriptional repressor by the action of MYH11 gene.

–The CCAAT/enhancer binding protein (C/EBPa), a myeloid transcription factor required for granulocytic differentiation is down-regulated.

–This results in failure to develop definitive hematopoiesis and impairment of neutrophilic differentiation. 231

Original page 232

–The CBFB::MYH11 fusion genes are present in potential leukemic precursor cells but additional mutagenic ‘hits’ are necessary for transformation.

•Clinical picture:

–Myeloid sarcoma may be present at the initial diagnosis or at relapse and may represent the only evidence of relapse.

–The main presentation is that of bone marrow failure including fatigue, bleeding, and infection.

•Laboratory findings: 1-Peripheral blood and bone marrow:

–Bone marrow is hypercellular with myeloid predominance and increased immature cells.

–Morphological features of acute myelomonocytic leukemia.

–The white blood cell count at diagnosis is significantly higher than in cases with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 fusion.

–Blasts are at the 20% threshold or occasionally lower.

–Auer rods may be observed in myeloblasts. 9

–Absolute monocytic count is usually more than 5 x 10/L.

–Maturing granulocytic component is usually more than 20% of NEC.

–Monocytic component are usually more than 20% of NEC.

–Peripheral blood eosinophilia may be present, but abnormal circulating eosinophils are usually rare.

–Variable number of eosinophils are present in the bone marrow with all stages of maturation, without significant maturation arrest.

–The most striking abnormality is the immature eosinophilic granules, mainly of the late promyelocyte and myelocyte stages and absent in thelater stages of 232

Original page 233

maturation. These granules are often larger than normal, purple-violet in colour, and may be dense that they obscure the cell morphology.

–The mature eosinophils occasionally show nuclear hyposegmentation.

–Rare cases are associated with no increase in eosinophils or monocytes in the bone marrow.

–Neutrophils are usually few and sparse in the bone marrow.

2-Cytochemistry:

–Myeloblasts are positivefor specific esterase, MPO and SBB.

–Monoblasts and promonocytes are positivefor non-specific esterase although it may be weaker than expected or even absent in some cases.

–Eosinophils are aberrantly positive for the specific esterase with faint positivity. 3-Immunophenotyping: Most of cases are characterized by a complex immunophenotype with the presence of multiple blast populations (CD45 dim) with a more mature monocytic component (CD45-bright and CD34 negative):

–Markers of immaturity: Blasts show strong positive expression of CD34 and CD117.

–Myeloid markers: A subpopulation of blasts is positive for CD33, CD13 and MPO.

–Markers of maturation: A subpopulation of cells is positive for CD15 and CD65.

–Maturation asynchrony is often seen.

–Monocytic markers: A subpopulation of blasts is positive for CD14, CD4, CD11b, CD11c, CD64 CD36, and lysozyme. 233

Original page 234

–Erythroid markers: Blasts are negative for glycophorin A and CD71.

–Megakaryocytic markers: Blasts are negative for CD41, CD42 and CD61.

–Lymphocytic markers: Blasts are negative for CD19 and CD3.

–Aberrant markers: Blasts are positive for CD2.

4-Genetic abnormalities:

–Inversion (16) or t(16;16) (p13.1;q22) and CBFB::MYH11 fusion gene.

–Occasionally, the patient has a normal karyotyping because inversion (16)(p13.1 q22) is a subtle rearrangement.

–Other chromosomal abnormalities are present in about 45% of cases as Trisomy 22, trisomy 21, trisomy 8 and del(7q).

–Secondary gene mutations are present in more than 90% of cases as KIT mutation, mutations of NRAS, KRAS, ASXL2, ASXL1, FLT3, NF1, TET2 or EZH2.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○Myeloid neoplasm with increased peripheral blood and/or bone marrow blasts (may be <20%).

○Detection of CBFB::MYH11.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria for myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy.

–Desirable criterion: Detection of inv(16)(p13.1q22.1) or t(16;16)(p13.1;q22.1)

•Prognosis:

–It is associated with a high rate of complete remission and favorable overall survival when treated.

–The impact of additional chromosome abnormalities on outcome is still unclear.

–Bad prognostics include KIT mutations, multiple kinase mutations (e.g. KIT, RAS, FLT3) and lack of molecular remission post induction therapy. 234

sections.t: Acute myeloid leukemia with DEK-NUP214 Fusion
sections.html:
Original page 235

•Definition: Acute myeloid leukemia characterized by fusion of the protooncogene (DEK) and nucleoporin 214 (NUP214).

•Epidemiology:

–It accounts for 0.6-1.7% of AML cases in children and 1% of AML cases in adults.

–The median age is 10-13 years in childhood and 35-51 in adults.

•Synonym: Acute myeloid leukemia with t(6;9)(p22.3;q34.1).

•Pathogenesis: The DEK::NUP214 fusion gene results in formation of the oncogeneic nucleoporin fusion protein which acts as an aberrant transcription factor disrupting the localization of proteins essential for nucleocytoplasmic transport.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Peripheral blood:

○Anemia and thrombocytopenia.

○There may be pancytopenia.

○Basophils are usually at least 20% of the total leukocytic count.

–Bone marrow:

○Hypercellular bone marrow

○Increased blasts with maturation or with myelomonocytic differentiation.

○Auer rods are infrequent

○Basophils may be increased in a minority of cases.

○Multilineage dysplasia.

–Immunophenotyping: 235

Original page 236

○Leukemic cells are usually positive for CD13, CD33, CD34, CD38, CD117, CD123, HLA-DR, and myeloperoxidase.

○CD7, CD9, CD15, CD64, and TdT are variably expressed.

○CD34 may be negative.

–Genetic tests:

○t(6;9)(p23;q34.1) and DEK::NUP214 fusion.

○Additional karyotypic abnormalities and occasionally a complex karyotype

○FLT3-ITD and RAS mutations are common.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○Myeloid neoplasm with increased peripheral blood and/or bone marrow blasts (may be <20%).

○Presence of DEK::NUP214 fusion

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria for myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy.

–Desirable criterion: Detection of t(6;9)(p22.3;q34.1)

•Prognosis:

–It has a poor prognosis.

–FLT3-ITD does not impact overall survival but has been associated with faster relapse kinetics.

–Allogeneic stem cell transplantation seems to improve survival. 236

sections.t: Acute myeloid leukemia with RBM15-MRTFA fusion
sections.html:
Original page 237

•Definition: It is acute myeloid leukemia associated with RBM15::MRTFA and characterized by megakaryocytic differentiation.

•Synonym:

–Acute myeloid leukemia with RBM15::MKL1

–Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia with RBM15::MRTFA

–Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia with RBM15::MKL1

•Epidemiology:

–It is an uncommon accounting for less 1% of all AML cases.

–It occurs most commonly in infants without trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) and young children aged 3 years or younger, with most cases occurring in the first 6 months of life.

–It has a female predominance.

–Some cases are congenital.

•Corresponding FAB category: M7.

•Pathogenesis: The RBM15::MRTFA fusion gene product may modulate chromatin organization, differentiation, and signaling pathways.

•Clinical picture:

–Marked hepatosplenomegaly

–Fatigue and bleeding.

–Infants often present with extramedullary disease and fibrotic abdominal organs such as liver with Budd-Chiari syndrome.

•Laboratory findings:

–Peripheral blood and bone marrow:

○Anemia.

○Thrombocytopenia.

○White blood cell count is moderately elevated. 237

Original page 238

○Bone marrow is normocellular to hypercellular, with reticulin and collagen fibrosis.

○Due to the often dense fibrosis, the pattern of bone marrow infiltration may mimic that of a metastatic tumour.

○The presence of fibrosis may cause difficulties in establishing the blast percentage in the bone marrow based on the aspirate; correlation with bone marrow biopsy findings may be crucial.

○Megakaryoblasts may be present admixed with more morphologically undifferentiated blast cells with a high N:C ratio, resembling lymphoblasts.

○The megakaryoblasts are usually medium-sized to large with a round, slightly irregular or indented nuclei, fine reticular chromatin and 1- 3 nucleoli. The cytoplasm is basophilic, often agranular, and may show distinct blebs or pseudopod formation.

○Micromegakaryocytes are common.

○Dysplasia of granulocytic and erythroid lineages are not usually present.

–Cytochemistry:

○Megakaryoblasts are negative for Sudan Black B and MPO.

○Megakaryoblasts are positive for platelet peroxidase.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Megakaryocytic markers: Megakaryoblasts express one or more of the megakaryocytic markers: CD41, CD61, and CD42b. Cytoplasmic expression of CD41 or CD61 is more specific and sensitive than is surface staining.

○Myeloid markers: Blasts are negative for MPO but CD13 and CD33 may be positive.

○Markers of immaturity: CD34, and HLA-DR are often negative

○CD45 is often negative.

○CD36 is characteristically positive but not specific.

○Lymphoid markers and TdT are not expressed. 238

Original page 239

–Genetic tests:

○t(1 ;22)(p13.3;q13.1) or molecular genetic evidence of RBM1::MRTFA fusion. In most cases, it is the sole karyotypic abnormality.

•Diagnostic criteria

–Essential criteria:

○Detection of RBM15::MRTFA fusion by fluorescence in situ hybridization and/or RT-PCR or similar molecular technique.

○Myeloid neoplasm with increased peripheral blood and/or bone marrow blasts (may be <20%).

–Desirable criteria:

○Detection of t(1;22)(p13.3;q13.1) by karyotype analysis.

○Demonstration of megakaryocytic differentiation.

•Prognosis: Intermediate to poor. 239
