Original page 240

•Definition: It is a de novo acute myeloid leukemia associated with BCR::ABL1 fusion at initial diagnosis with no evidence of established chronic myeloid leukemia.

•Synonym: Acute Myeloid Leukemia with t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2).

•Epidemiology:

–Itaccounts for less than 0.5% of all AML cases and less than 0.5% of all BCR- ABL1 positive acute and chronic leukemias.

–It occurs primarily in adults.

–It has a male predominance.

•Pathogenesis: BCR::ABL1 with the 210 transcript.

•Clinical picture: Splenomegaly is less frequent than in blast transformation of CML.

•Laboratory findings:

–Peripheral blood:

○Blast predominance.

○Leukocytosis

○Basophilia is less frequent than in blastic phase of CML.

○Variable anemia and thrombocytopenia.

–Bone marrow:

○It can encompass AML with minimal differentiation, without maturation, or with monocytic differentiation.

○Myeloblasts are characterized by features ranging from those of minimal differentiation to those of granulocytic maturation.

○Bone marrow cellularity (80%) is less than that of blast transformation of CML (95- 100%).

○Dwarf megakaryocytes are less than that of blast transformation of CML.

○The non-blast cell M:E ratio is relatively normal compared with the more elevated ratio in blast transformation of CML. 240

Original page 241

–Immunophenotyping:

○Myeloid markers: Blasts are positive for CD13 and CD33.

○Markers of immaturity: Blasts are positive for CD117, CD34 and HLA-DR.

○Aberrant markers: Blasts are positive for CD19, CD7, and TdT.

–Genetic tests:

○t(9;22) (q34.1 ;q1 1.2) or molecular genetic evidence of BCR::ABL 1 fusion. Most cases demonstrate the p210 protein product and very few cases demonstrate the p190 protein product.

•Diagnostic criteria:

– Essential criteria:

○Myeloid neoplasm with >20% blasts expressing a myeloid immunophenotype in the bone marrow and/or peripheral blood.

○Detection of BCR::ABL1 at initial diagnosis.

○Lack of features of CML prior to or at diagnosis or after therapy.

–Desirable criteria:

○Presence of t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2) on conventional karyotyping.

○Determination of the BCR::ABL1 transcript subtype and establishing a baseline level of BCR::ABL1 transcript for monitoring treatment response.

•Prognosis:

–It is an aggressive disease, with poor response to traditional AML therapy or tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy alone.

–It may respond to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy followed by allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation. 241

sections.t: Acute myeloid leukemia with KMT2A rearrangement
sections.html:
Original page 242

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia with fusion of the KMT2A locus on chromosome 11q23.3 with any of a number of partner genes.

•Synonym:

–Acute myeloid leukemia with KMT2A::MLLT3 or other exact fusion.

–Acute myeloid leukemia with t(9;11)(p21.3;q23.3) or other exact balanced translocation.

•Normal counterpart: Hematopoietic stem cells or granulocyte- macrophage progenitors.

•Epidemiology:

–It can occur at any age, but is more common in children, exceeding 50% in infant AML and 10% in adolescent AML and found in 2-3% in adult AML.

•Pathogenesis:

–The KMT2A (Lysine Methyltransferase 2A) gene encodes a histone methyltransferase that increases gene transcription by chromatin remodelling.

–KMT2A gene rearrangements result from deletions, duplications, inversions and translocations at the 11q23 locus.

–It may be associated with several gene mutations.

•Clinical picture: Extramedullary involvement manifesting as gingival hypertrophy or skin lesions is common.

•Laboratory findings:

–Complete blood picture: White blood cell count varies from leukopenia to up 9 to 200x10/L with children often present with hyperleukocytosis.

–Morphology:

○Most cases have monocytic, monoblastic, or myelomonocytic features. In children especially, KMT2A::MLLT3 and KMT2A::MLLT10 can present as acute megakaryoblastic leukemia. 242

Original page 243

○Monoblasts are large cells with abundant, moderate to intensively basophilic cytoplasm, pseudopods, azurophilic granules, vacuoles; round nuclei, lacy chromatin and one or more prominent nucleoli.

○Promonocytes are blast equivalent and have basophilic cytoplasm with granules and occasional large azurophilic granules, vacuoles; irregular and delicately convoluted nuclei.

–Cytochemistry:

○Monoblasts and promonocytes are usually strongly positive for non-specific esterase.

○Monoblasts and promonocytes are negative for MPO.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Markers of immaturity: Expression of CD34, CD117 is mostly negative in monocytic cases. HLA-DR is positive.

○Myeloid markers: Strong expression of CD33, CD13 may be positive.

○Markers of maturity: CD15 is positive.

○Monocytic markers: Positive expression of CD11b, CD11c, CD64, CD36, and CD36, variable expression of lysozyme, strong expression of CD4 and weak expression of CD14.

○Expression of the chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 (NG2) is very common.

○Erythroid markers: Negative for glycophorin A and CD71.

○Megakaryocytic markers: Negative for CD41, CD42 and CD61.

○Lymphocytic markers: Negative for CD19 and CD3.

○Aberrant markers: Weak expression of CD56. Expression of CD7 is rare.

•Genetic tests: KMT2A rearrangemet either by karyotyping or by molecular techniques in cryptic cases. Some rearrangements such as KMT2A::USP2 may be cryptic by FISH. 243

Original page 244

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○Myeloid neoplasm with increased peripheral blood and/or bone marrow blasts (may be < 20%), or presence of a myeloid sarcoma.

○Blasts express myeloid immunophenotype, not fulfilling immunophenotypic criteria for mixedphenotype acute leukemia. –

○Presence of a KMT2A rearrangement.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria for myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy.

–Desirable criterion: - Identification of the KMT2A fusion partner

•Prognosis:

–In adults, the prognostic impact depends on the fusion partner; KMT2A::MLLT3 fusion have an intermediate risk of relapse, whereas other KMT2A rearrangements are associated with a poor prognosis.

–In children, the prognosis depends on the treatment protocol. 244

Original page 245

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia characterized by rearrangements involving the MDS1 and EVI1 complex locus (MECOM).

•Epidemiology:

–All age groups are affected but most commonly in adults.

–No sex predilection.

•Pathogenesis: EVI1 is an oncogenic transcription factor. Its expression in neoplastic myeloid cells disrupts myeloid differentiation, cell cycle regulation, and cell signaling pathways.

•Clinical picture: Hepatosplenomegaly in some patients.

•Laboratory findings:

–Peripheral blood:

○Most patients present with cytopenias, but some may have leukocytosis or thrombocytosis.

○Increased peripheral blood blasts are usually present, but approximately one- third of patients present with a low blast counts.

○Giant and hypogranular platelets are common

○Bare megakaryocyte nuclei may be present.

○Hypogranular neutrophils with a pseudo Pelger- Huet anomaly.

○Red blood cell changes are usually mild, without teardrop cells.

–Bone marrow:

○It corresponds to M2, M4 or M7.

○Bone marrow cellularity is variable 245

Original page 246

○Multilineage dysplasia of non-blast bone marrow elements with dysplastic megakaryocytes being the most common with many small non-lobated or bilobed forms, but other dysplastic megakaryocytic forms may also occur.

○Erythroid and granulocytic dysplasia is also common.

○Marrow eosinophils, basophils, and/or mast cells may be increased.

○Fibrosis is variable.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Markers of immaturity: Blasts are positive for CD34, CD1147 and HLA-DR. CD34 expression is stronger with inv(3) than with t(3;3).

○Myeloid markers: Blasts are positive for CD33 and CD13.

○Basophil markers: Basophils are positive for CD38.

○Megakaryocytic markers: Some cases are positive for CD41 and CD61.

○Lymphocytic markers: Negative for CD19 and CD3

○Erythroid markers: Negative for glycophorin A and CD71.

○Aberrant markers: Blasts are positive for CD7.

–Genetic tests:

○MECOM rearrangement either by karyotyping or by FISH. Quantitative RT- PCR can be performed to detect increased EVI1 expression.

○The most frequent rearrangement is GATA2::MECOM results from either inv(3)(q21.3q26.2) or t(3;3)(q21.3;q26.2), but more than 30 partner genes have been described

○Additional chromosomal abnormalities are common including monosomy 7 or del(7q), del(5q), and complex karyotype.

○Virtually all cases are associated with gene mutations. 246

Original page 247

N.B.: Patients with chronic myeloid leukemia may acquire MECOM rearrangement, and such a finding is defined as blast phase regardless of the number of blasts. Although rare, cases with concurrent BCR::ABL1 and MECOM rearrangement at presentation are best regarded as having blast phase CML

•Diagnostic criteria:

– Essential criteria

○Myeloid neoplasm with increased peripheral blood and/or bone marrow blasts (may be < 20%).

○Detection of MECOM rearrangement.

○No history of myeloproliferative neoplasm.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria for myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy.

–Desirable criterion: Detection of inv(3)(q21.3q26.2), t(3;3)(q21;q26), t(3;21)(q26.2;q22) or t(3;12)(q26.2;p13).

•Prognosis:

–It is an aggressive disease with short survival.

–Poor prognostic factors include:

○Complex karyotyping.

○Monosomy 7.

○Two or more additional mutations 247

sections.t: Acute myeloid leukemia with NUP98 rearrangement
sections.html:
Original page 248

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia characterized by chromosomal translocations involving NUP98 on chromosome 11p15.4 and various partner genes.

•Epidemiology: 2-4.8% of childhood AML and 2.3% of adult AML.

•Pathogenesis:

–The NUP98 gene encodes a component of the nuclear pore complex.

–This rearrangement involves more than 40 partners categorized into HOX and non-HOX genes.

–Fusion influences NUP98-associated functions and the transcriptional and epigenetic regulatory activities of the partner genes.

•Laboratory findings:

–Peripheral blood: Anemia, thrombocytopenia and usually leukocytosis but NUP98::KDM5A tend to have lower white blood counts.

–Bone marrow:

○Most cases have a high blast count in the bone marrow with or without maturation, which tends to be myelomonocytic or monocytic. Some children have megakaryoblastic or erythroid differentiation.

○Dysplastic changes may be seen.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Immaturity markers: Blasts are positive for CD34, CD117 and HLA-DR

○Myeloid markers: Blasts are positive for CD13, CD33 and myeloperoxidase.

○Other markers: Blasts may be positive for CD123, CD11b, CD11c, CD14, CD36, CD7, CD15, and CD64.

○Megakaryocytic markers (CD41, CD42b and CD61) and erythroid markers (CD71, E-cadherin) usually correlate with morphologic features.

–Cytochemistry: The blasts are often positive for myeloperoxidase. 248

Original page 249

–Genetic tests:

○Rearrangements are often cryptic on conventional karyotyping and is determined by FISH, RT-PCR for NUP98::NSD1 and RNA sequencing

○Associated chromosomal abnormalities include trisomy 8 and chromosome 13 abnormalities

○Associated gene mutations include FLT3 ITD and/or WT1 mutations and other gene mutations.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○Myeloid neoplasm with increased peripheral blood and/or bone marrow blasts (may be < 20%).

○Detection of the NUP98 rearrangement and/or specific fusion products such as NUP98::NSD1.

–Desirable criterion: Identification of the NUP98 fusion partner at diagnosis is desirable to enable PCR-based disease monitoring.

•Prognosis:Poor especially with FLT3- ITD mutations. Allogeneic stem cell transplantation should be considered. 249

Original page 250

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia characterized by the presence of somatic mutations involving the nucleophosmin gene.

•Epidemiology:

–One-third of AML adult AML and 6-8% of pediatric AML

–The peak incidence is in middle age, with female predominance

–Most cases show normal karyotype.

•Etiology and pathogenesis:

–It develops from a background of clonal hematopoiesis in most cases.

–Wildtype resides predominantly in the nucleolus with domains allowing its cytoplasmic, nucleoplasmic and nucleolar localization. It is involved in several key cellular functions including ribosome biogenesis, maintenance of genomic stability, stress response and growth suppression and response to apoptotic stimuli. The protein may be exported to the cytoplasm to perform select functions.

–Mutations result in loss of the nucleolar localization signal and addition of a nuclear export signal leading to aberrant localization in the cytoplasm

–Leukemogenesis mechanisms include binding and exporting several nuclear proteins, including tumor suppressors and transcription factors, to the cytoplasm, likely inhibiting their normal functions.

•Laboratory findings:

–It is commonly presented as acute myelomonocytic and acute monocytic leukemia. More than 10% of blasts have cup-like nuclear morphology 250

Original page 251

–Peripheral blood and bone marrow:

○It is commonly presented as acute myelomonocytic and acute monocytic leukemia.

○Anemia.

○Thrombocytopenia.

○Higher white blood cell and platelet counts than other AML types.

○The bone marrow is usually markedly hypercellular.

○Multilineage dysplasia is present in 25% of cases which usually have a normal karyotype and CD34 negative blasts.

–Cytochemistry:

–Blasts are positive for MPO

–Monocytic component is positive for the non-specific esterase.

– Immunophenotyping: variable

○Markers of immaturity: CD117 is common. HLA-DR is often negative. CD34 is negative in most cases but CD34+ cases may occur and is associated with a bad prognosis.

○A very small fraction of cells with the immunophenotyping of leukemic stem cells (CD34+, CD38-, CD123+) is detectable in most cases.

○Subgroups:

➢One with an immature myeloid immunophenotypic profile.

➢Acute promyelocytic leukemia-like (CD34-/HLA-DR- /CD117+/myeloperoxidase+)

➢One subgroup with a monocytic (CD36+, CD64+, CD14+) immunophenotypic profile.

○Immunohistochemistry: Aberrant cytoplasmic expression of NPM1 in paraffin sections. 251

Original page 252

–Genetic tests:

○NPM1 mutation by molecular techniques

○Karyotyping is normal in most cases.

○Karyotyping abnormalities in 5-15% of cases: Gain of chromosomes 8 and 4 and del(9q).

○Secondary mutations are common involving FLT3, DNMT3A, IDH1, KRAS, NRAS, and cohesion-complex genes.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○Myeloid neoplasm with increased peripheral blood and/or bone marrow blasts (may be < 20%)

○Detection of NPM1 mutation

○No history of exposure to cytotoxic therapy.

–Desirable criterion:Detection of cytoplasmic NPM1 by immunohistochemistry.

•Prognosis:

–It shows a good response to induction therapy.

–Cases with a normal karyotyping and absence of FLT3-ITD mutation have a good prognosis. Patients with NRAS mutation or FLT3 TKD double-mutated AML have relatively good prognosis.

–Cases with FLT3-ITD mutation have an intermediate prognosis.

–Co-occurrence of NPM1, FLT3-ITD, and DNMT3A mutations is associated with a particularly poor outcome. Concurrent WT1 mutations is associated with poor outcome. Higher NPM1 mutant transcript levels following induction and consolidation therapy is associated with higher rate of relapse. 252

sections.t: Acute myeloid leukemia with CEBPA mutation
sections.html:
Original page 253

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia characterized by CEBPA mutation that should be biallelic (biCEBPA) or, if single, must be located in the basic leucine zipper (bZIP) region of the gene.

•Synonym: Acute myeloid leukemia with biallelic CEBPA mutation

•Epidemiology: It accounts for 5% of AML in children and 5-11% in adults.

•Clinical picture: Symptoms and signs of bone marrow failure and include fatigue, bruising or bleeding, and infection.

•Etiology and pathogenesis:

–Some cases with biallelic CEBPA mutation have a germline mutation.

–The gene CEBPA encodes for a protein that regulates myeloid differentiation and stem/progenitor cell function. The bZIP region is required for dimerization and DNA binding of this protein.

•Laboratory findings:

–Peripheral blood and bone marrow:

○Most cases correspond to M2 or M1.

○Dysplasia is common, especially dysgranulopoiesis and dysmegakaryopoiesis.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Markers of immaturity: Most of blasts express HLA-DR and CD34.

○Myeloid markers: Blasts express CD13, CD33, and CD15.

○Monocytic markers: Rare expression of CD14 or CD56.

○Aberrant markers: CD7 is often expressed. 253

Original page 254

•Genetic tests: Biallelic CEBPA mutation or, if single, must be located in the basic leucine zipper (bZIP) region of the gene by molecular methods.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○≥20% blasts with myeloid immunophenotype in bone marrow or blood

○Presence of biallelic mutations in CEBPA, or a single mutation located in the bZIP region.

○Absence of criteria allowing for classification into other AML with defining genetic abnormalities.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria for myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy.

•Prognosis: Cases with biallelic mutations have a favorable prognosis. 254

Original page 255

•Definition: It is a myeloid neoplasm with ≥20% blasts harbouring specific cytogenetic and molecular abnormalities associated with myelodysplastic syndrome, arising de novo or following a known history of myelodysplastic syndrome or myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm.

•Synonym:

–Acute myeloid leukemia post myelodysplastic syndrome

–Acute myeloid leukemia post myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm

•Epidemiology:

–It accounts for 24 to 35% of AML cases.

–Patients have a median age of around 70 years, with male predominance.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Peripheral blood and bone marrow:

○It is associated with severe pancytopenia.

○Blasts in the peripheral blood and/or bone marrow are at least 20%.

○Most cases have multilineage dysplasia. Dysplasia must be assessed on well- stained smears of peripheral blood and bone marrow:

❖Dysgranulopoiesis: Hypogranular cytoplasm, hyposegmented nuclei (pseudo-PelgerHuet anomaly) or bizarrely segmented nuclei.

❖Dyserythropoiesis: Megaloblastosis, karyorrhexis, nuclear irregularity, fragmentation or multinucleation, ring sideroblasts and cytoplasmic vacuoles.

❖Dysmegakaryopoiesis: Micromegakaryocytes and normal-sized or large megakaryocytes with non-lobated or multiple nuclei. 255

Original page 256

–Immunophenotyping:

○Markers of immaturity: Blasts are positive for CD34, CD117 and HLA-DR.

○Maturing myeloid cells, monocytes and erythroid cells may show abnormal patterns of antigen expression and abnormal light-scattering.

○Myeloid markers: Blasts often express panmyeloid markers as CD13 and MPO with an aberrant high or low expression.

–Genetic tests:

•Diagnostic criteria: The diagnosis of AML-MR requires that the following 3 criteria are met:

○≥ 20% blasts in blood or marrow

○Presence of at least one of the following:

➢History of MDS or MDS/MPN

➢One or more cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities listed above 

○Absence of the following:

➢History of exposure to cytotoxic therapy

➢History of myeloproliferative neoplasm

➢Criteria for AML with defining genetic abnormalities

➢Criteria for myeloid neoplasms associated with germline predisposition. 256

Original page 257

•Prognosis:

–It has a poor prognosis, with a lower rate of complete remission than in other AML subtypes.

–TP53 mutation has a worse prognosis

–Cases with prior MDS and relatively low blast counts (20-29%) are associated with less aggressive disease. 257

sections.t: Acute myeloid leukemia with other defined genetic alterations
toc: Acute myeloid leukemia, defined by differentiation
sections.html:
Original page 258

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia that includes emerging or provisional AML subtypes with distinct genetic features.

•Subtypes:

•Pathogenesis:

–CBFA2T3::GLIS2: Enhanced self-renewal in vitro.

–KAT6A::CREBBP: Deregulation of the HOXA cluster member genes and interference with hematopoietic differentiation.

–MNX1::ETV6: Ectopic expression of MNX1 may promote leukemogenesis.

–NPM1::MLF1: It influences the organization of the chromatin remodeling complexes in hematopoietic cells resulting in differential gene expression. 258

Original page 259

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○≥20% blasts with myeloid immunophenotype in bone marrow and/or blood.

○Detection of one or more cytogenetic or molecular aberrations listed in Table above.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria for AML with defining genetic abnormalities, AML myelodysplasia related, AML post cytotoxic therapy or mixed phenotype acute leukemia. 259

Acute myeloid leukemia, defined by differentiation

Original page 260

•Definition: It is acute myeloid leukemia which includes cases that do not fulfil the criteria for inclusion in AML with defining genetic abnormalities.

•This group includes: AML with minimal differentiation. AML without maturation. AML with maturation. Acute basophilic leukemia. Acute myelomonocytic leukemia. Acute monocytic leukemia. Acute erythroid leukemia.  Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia. 260

sections.t: Acute myeloid leukemia with minimal differentiation
sections.html:
Original page 261

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia with immunophenotypic but not morphologic or cytochemical evidence of myeloid differentiation that lacks defining genetic abnormalities.

•Epidemiology:

–It accounts for less than 5% of AML cases.

–It can occur at any age, with slight male predominance.

•Pathogenesis: Rearrangements of BCL11B on chromosome 14q32 are present in ~30% of AML with minimal differentiation. It associated frequently with cooperative mutations in FLT3 and mutations of epigenetic modulators.

•Laboratory findings:

–Bone marrow:

○The bone marrow is usually markedly hypercellular with sheets of poorly differentiated blasts.

○Blasts are medium-sized, with agranular variably basophilic cytoplasm and round or slightly indented nuclei with dispersed chromatin and one or two nucleoli. No Auer rods.

○Less frequently, the blasts are small, with more-condensed chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and scanty cytoplasm resembling that of lymphoblasts.

–Cytochemistry: Blasts are negative for MPO, Sudan Black B and specific esterase. 261

Original page 262

–Immunophenotyping:

○Markers of immaturity: Most cases express CD34, and HLA-DR.

○Myeloid-associated markers: Blast cells express at least two of them usually CD13, CD33 and CD117. MPO is negative.

○Markers of myeloid and monocytic maturation: Negative expression CD11b, CD15, CD14, CD64, CD36 and CD65.

○B-cell and T-cell cytoplasmic lymphoid markers: Negative expression of cCD3, cCD79a, and cCD22.

○Aberrant markers: Some cases express TdT and CD7.

–Genetic tests: 40% of cases have an abnormal karyotype and structural abnormalities.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○≥20% blasts in bone marrow and/or blood lacking morphological and cytochemical evidence of myeloid differentiation.

○Positive for ≥2 myeloid-associated markers (e.g. CD13, CD33, CD117).

○Criteria for AML types with defined genetic alterations are not met.

○Criteria for mixed-phenotype acute leukemia are not met.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria for myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy 262

Original page 263

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid differentiation and maturation arrest that lacks defining genetic abnormalities.

•Laboratory findings:

–Complete blood count and blood film :

○Anemia.

○Thrombocytopenia.

○Neutropenia, but there may be leukocytosis and markedly increased blasts with azurophilic granules and/ or Auer rods or blasts resembling lymphoblasts with lack azurophilic granules.

–Bone marrow :

○Biopsy sections are usually markedly hypercellular, but may be normocellular or hypocellular.

○Medium sized to large myeloblasts with pale blue grey cytoplasm, azurophilic granules and/ or Auer rods, round or slightly indented nuclei, and one to two distinct nucleoli. Blasts may resemble lymphoblasts with lack of azurophilic granules.

○Granulocytic maturation < 10% of cellular elements in the bone marrow

–Cytochemistry

○MPO and Sudan Black B are positive and is usually negative for specific esterase.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Markers of immaturity: CD34 and HLA-DR are positive. 263

Original page 264

○Myeloid-associated Markers: A population of blasts express MPO and two or more myeloid-associated markers as CD13, CD33, and CD117.

○Markers of granulocytic maturation: No expression of CD15 and CD65.

○Monocytic markers: No expression of CD14 and CD64. CD11 b is expressed in some cases.

○B-cell and T-cell cytoplasmic lymphoid markers: Blasts are negative for cCD3, cCD79a, and cCD22.

○Aberrant markers: CD7 and CD56 are positive in one third of cases.

–Genetic tests

○No specific defining abnormalities.

○One third of cases has abnormal karyotyping and gene mutations.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○≥20% blasts in bone marrow and/or blood with cytochemical evidence of myeloid differentiation and limited (<10%) morphologic features of granulocytic maturation.

○Positive for ≥2 myeloid-associated markers (e.g. myeloperoxidase, CD13, CD33, CD117).

○Criteria for AML types with defined genetic alterations are not met.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria for myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy 264

Original page 265

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia with morphologic features of granulocytic maturation that lacks defining genetic abnormalities.

•Laboratory findings:

–Complete blood count:

○Anemia.

○Thrombocytopenia,

○Neutropenia but there may be leukocytosis.

–Blood film:

○Myeloid blasts with and without azurophilic granulation. Auer rods are common.

–Bone marrow:

○Bone marrow biopsy sections usually show hypercellularity.

○Blasts with and without azurophilic granulation. Auer rods are common.

○Promyelocytes, myelocytes, and mature neutrophils constitute at least 10% of bone marrow cells.

○Variable degrees of mainly neutrophilic dysplasia

○Monocytic component is < 20% of bone marrow cells.

–Cytochemistry: Blasts are positive for myeloperoxidase and/or Sudan Black B. They are negative or show limited positivity for specific esterase.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Markers of immaturity: Some blasts express HLA-DR, CD34, and/ or CD117. 265

Original page 266

○Myeloid- associated markers: The blasts usually show intermediate to strong expression of myeloperoxidase and two or more myeloid-associated antigens, such as CD13, CD33, and CD117.

○Markers of granulocytic differentiation: Some cells expressCD11b, CD15 and CD65.

○Monocytic markers: CD14, CD36, and CD64 are absent.

○Lymphoid markers: Expression of lymphoid markers is rare.

○Aberrant markers: CD7 and CD56 are occasionally expressed.

–Genetic tests:

○No specific defining abnormalities.

○One thirds of cases have abnormal karyotyping or rare structural abnormalities.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○≥20% blasts in bone marrow and/or blood with cytochemical evidence of myeloid differentiation and morphologic features of granulocytic maturation in ≥10% of bone marrow marrow cells.

○Positive for ≥2 myeloid-associated markers (e.g. myeloperoxidase, CD13, CD33, CD117).

○Monocyte lineage cells constitute < 20% of bone marrow cells.

○Criteria for AML types with defined genetic alterations are not met.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria for myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy. 266

Original page 267

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia with basophilic differentiation that lacks defining genetic abnormalities.

•Epidemiology:

–It is a very rare disease accounting for less than 1% of AML cases.

•Pathogenesis:

–Recurrent translocation of t(X;6)(p11;q23) resulting in MYB::GATA1 fusion gene has been reported in male infants. The fusion product promotes basophilic differentiation by inducing expression of interleukin IL33 and nerve growth factor

–A case of acute basophilic leukemia with t(16;21)(p11;q22) resulting in FUS::ERG fusion has also been reported.

–Other genetic aberrations reported include U2AF1 mutation and monosomy 7.

–Sporadic cases with TET2, TP53, and NPM1 mutations have also been reported.

•Clinical Picture:

–Clinical picture of bone marrow failure.

–Cutaneous lesions.

–Organomegaly.

–Lytic lesions.

–Symptoms related to hyperhistaminemia.

•Laboratory findings:

–Peripheral blood and bone marrow:

○Blasts are medium-sized, with a high N:C ratio; an oval, round, or irregular nucleus characterized by dispersed chromatin, and 1-3 prominent nucleoli. 267

Original page 268

The cytoplasm is moderately basophilic with a variable number of coarse basophilic metachromatic granules and may be vacuolated of the cytoplasm.

○Immature forms can be seen.

○Mature basophils are usually sparse.

–Cytochemistry:

○Metachromatic staining with toluidine blue.

○Negative for specific esterase which distinguish these blasts from mast cells.

○Negative for Sudan Black B, MPO, and non-specific esterase.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Markers of immaturity: Blasts but may express CD34 with weak CD117 and negative HLA-DR.

○Myeloid markers: Blasts express two or more myeloid markers as MPO, CD117, CD13 and CD33.

○Basophilic markers: Blasts express CD123, CD203c, and CD11b.

○Monocytic markers: Blasts are negative for monocytic markers.

○Blasts usually express CD9.

○Lymphoid markers: Blasts are negative for lymphoid markers.

–Genetic tests:

○No defining genetic abnormalities.

○No consistent chromosomal abnormality, but a recurrent t(X;6)(p11 .2;q23.3) resulting in MYB:: GATA1 are common in male infants with acute basophilic leukemia. 268

Original page 269

•Differential diagnosis:

–Blast phase of a myeloproliferative neoplasm: Differentiation is made by clinical and cytogenetic pattern.

–Other AML subtypes with basophilia, as AML with DEK::NUP214, AML with BCR-ABL1 with prominent coarse granules: Differentiation is made by clinical, cytochemical, immunophenotyping and cytogenetic pattern.

–Mast cell leukemia: Immunophenotypic detection of abnormal mast cells expressing KIT, mast cell tryptase, and CD25 distinguishes mast cell leukemia from acute basophilic leukemia.

–Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○≥20% of blasts with increased immature and mature basophils.

○Blasts/basophils with metachromasia on toluidine blue staining and negative for myeloperoxidase, or SBB, and NSE.

○Blasts positive for ≥2 myeloid-associated markers (e.g. myeloperoxidase, CD13, CD33, CD117).

○Criteria for AML types with defined genetic alterations are not met.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria for myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy.

–Desirable criterion: Blasts positive for CD9 and/or CD203c, and negative for HLA- DR 269

Original page 270

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia with evidence of granulocytic and monocytic maturation that lacks defining genetic abnormalities.

•Epidemiology: It occurs in all age groups, but more common in adults.

•Laboratory findings:

–Complete blood count:

○Anemia.

○Thrombocytopenia.

○White blood cell count may be high.

–Blood film and bone marrow:

–Bone marrow is hypercellular

–Myeloblasts with azurophilic granules and/ or Auer rods or blasts resembling lymphoblasts with lack azurophilic granules.

○Monoblasts are large cells with abundant moderately to intensely basophilic cytoplasm showing pseudopod formation. Scattered fine azurophilic granules and vacuoles. Nuclei are round with delicate lacy chromatin and one or more large prominent nucleoli.

○Promonocytes have a more irregular and delicately convoluted nuclei. The cytoplasm is less basophilic and sometimes more obviously granulated, with occasional large azurophilic granules and vacuoles.

○Increase in monocytes which are often more evident and more mature than those in the bone marrow. 270

Original page 271

–Cytochemistry:

○MPO is positive.

○Monoblasts, promonocytes, and monocytes are positive for non-specific esterase, although reactivity can be weak or absent in some cases. If the cells meet the morphological criteria for monocytes, absence of non-specific esterase does not exclude this diagnosis.

○Double staining for non-specific and specific esterases may reveal dual- positive cells.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Markers of immaturity: a population of blasts expresses CD34 and/or CD117. Most cases are positive for HLA-DR.

○Myeloid markers: a population of blasts variably expresses the myeloid markers CD13, CD33, CD65, and CD15.

○Monocytic markers: a population of blats is positive for monocytic markers as CD14, CD64, CD11b, CD11c, CD4, CD36, CD68, CD163, and lysozyme. Coexpression of CD15, CD36, and strong CD64 is characteristic of monocytic differentiation.

○Lymphoid-associated markers are negative.

○Aberrant markers: CD7 and CD56.

–Genetic tests:

○No specific defining abnormalities.

○One thirds of cases have abnormal karyotyping or rare structural abnormalities. 271

Original page 272

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○≥20% blasts and blast equivalents (promonocytes) in bone marrow and/or blood.

○Positive for myeloid-associated markers (e.g. myeloperoxidase, CD13, CD33, CD117).

○Maturing granulocytes constitute ≥20% of bone marrow cells. –

○Monocyte lineage cells constitute ≥20% of bone marrow cells.

○Criteria for AML types with defined genetic alterations are not met.

○No fulfilment of diagnostic criteria for myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy. 272

Original page 273

•Definition: It is an acute myeloid leukemia with monocytic differentiation that lacks defining genetic abnormalities.

•Epidemiology: It can occur at any age but the monoblastic form is more in children.

•Laboratory findings:

–Peripheral blood and bone marrow:

○Monoblasts are large cells with abundant moderately to intensely basophilic cytoplasm which may show pseudopod formation. Scattered fine azurophilic granules and vacuoles may be present. Nuclei are round with delicate lacy chromatin and one or more large prominent nucleoli.

○Promonocytes have a more irregular and delicately convoluted nuclear configuration. The cytoplasm is usually less basophilic and sometimes more obviously granulated, with occasional large azurophilic granules and vacuoles. Auer rods are rare and present in myeloblasts.

○Mature monocytes.

○The bone marrow is usually hypercellular, with a predominant population of large, poorly differentiated blasts with abundant cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli.

–Cytochemistry:

○Monoblasts and promonocytes are strongly positive for the non-specific esterase but may be negative or very weakly positive in 10-20% of cases.

○Monoblasts are MPO-negative and promonocytes may show some scattered MPO positivity. 273

Original page 274

–Immunophenotyping:

○Markers of immaturity: CD34 and HLA-DR are positive.

○Myeloid markers: Common of CD13, CD33 (bright), CD117, CD15, and CD65. MPO can be expressed in acute monocytic leukemia and less often in monoblastic leukemia.

○Monocytic markers: Coexpression of two or more monocytic markers is characteristic of monocytic differentiation. There is expression of at least two monocytic markers as CD14, CD4 (dim), CD11b, CD11c, CD64 (bright), CD68, CD36 (bright), and lysozyme.

○Monocytes can be identified in tissue sections by immunohistochemistry with CD68R (PGM-1) and CD163.Lysozyme and CD68 KP-1 are also positive, but not specific for monocytic differentiation.

–Genetic tests:

–No specific defining abnormalities.

–Rare cases have abnormal karyotyping or rare structural abnormalities.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○≥20% blasts and blast equivalents (promonocytes) in bone marrow and/or blood.

○≥80% of the leukemic cells are monocytes and their precursors, including monoblasts and promonocytes.

○< 20% maturing granulocytic cells.

○Criteria for AML types with defining genetic abnormalities are not met.

○No fulfilment of diagnostic criteria for myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy 274

Original page 275

•Definition: It is a neoplastic proliferation of erythroid cells with features of maturation arrest (increased erythroblasts) and high prevalence of biallelic TP53 alterations.

•Synonyms: Pure erythroid leukemia.

•Epidemiology:

–It is extremely rare < 1% of cases of acute leukemia.

–Patients are elderly.

–It is more common in males.

•Pathogenesis: Aberrant expression of key transcriptional regulators, including SKI, ERG, and ETO2 with blockage of erythroid differentiation.

•Laboratory Findings:

–Bone marrow:

○Erythroblasts are usually at least 80% and proerythroblasts are at least 30% of all nucleated bone marrow cells.

○Medium-sized to large erythroblasts, usually with round nuclei, fine chromatin, and one or more nucleoli (proerythroblasts). The cytoplasm is deeply basophilic, agranular and frequently contains vacuoles.

○In bone marrow biopsy sections, the cells appear undifferentiated and are arranged in a sheet-like pattern with an intrasinusoidal growth pattern in some cases.

○Ring sideroblasts and dysmegakaryopoiesis are common.

–Cytochemistry:

○Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) usually show a block-like staining pattern.

○Ring sideroblasts. 275

Original page 276

–Immunophenotyping: Erythroblasts are positive for CD36, CD71, and CD117 (often subset), negative for CD34 and MPO:

○CD71 is positive but non-specific

○E-cadherin, which stains early erythroid forms, is positive in the vast majority of cases and is specific for erythroid differentiation.

○Other markers such as ferritinand α-hemoglobin-stabilizing protein may also be used to highlight pronomoblasts.

○CD235 (Glycophorin A) is positive in a subset of cells that often corresponds to the CD117-negative subset.

○CD45 expression is variable but often dimly positive.

○HLA-DR is negative or partially positive.

○Neoplastic erythroblasts may show aberrant CD13, increased CD4, or decreased CD38 expression.

○Although not increased in numbers, CD34-positive myeloblasts in AEL frequently show an aberrant immunophenotype.

–Genetic tests:

○Biallelic TP53 loss of function: It often shows mutation in one allele and deletion in another allele, or two or more TP53 mutations in cases without TP53 deletion.

○Complex karyotype, frequently with losses of 17/17p, 5/5q and 7/7q.

•Diagnostic criteria

–Essential criterion: Erythroid predominance, usually ≥80% of bone marrow elements, of which ≥30% are erythroblasts.

–Desirable criterion: Evidence of TP53 mutation.

•Prognosis: Extremely poor outcome with a median survival of 2-4 months. 276

Original page 277

•Definition: It is an acute leukemia characterized by ≥ 20% blasts with megakaryocytic differentiation.

•Epidemiology:

–It is an uncommon disease, accounting for less than 5% of AML cases.

–Incidence is higher in young children and rare in adults.

–There is an association with mediastinal germ cell tumors in young adult males.

•Pathogenesis: It has three clinical groups:

○Children with Down syndrome

○Children without Down syndrome: >75% of cases. I t is associated with chromosomal translocations that encodes a fusion oncogene as CBFA2T3::GLIS2 “sufficient for leukemogenesis”, RBM15::MRTFA, NUP98::KDM5A “co-occur with additional mutations”, and KMT2A “co- occur with additional mutations”. Cases without fusion proteins often have similarities to Down syndrome with amplification of the chromosome 21, which includes several genes involved in megakaryopoiesis (RUNX1, ERG and ETS2) with mutations in GATA1 and cohesin/CTCF.

○Adults: These cases are less well defined, with mutations usually in TP53, RB1, cohesin complex, splicing factors, ASXL1 and DNMT3A.

•Laboratory findings:

–Peripheral blood and bone marrow:

○Cytopenias especially thrombocytopenia, but some may have thrombocytosis.

○Circulating micromegakaryocytes, megakaryoblast fragments, dysplastic large platelets, and hypogranular neutrophils. 277

Original page 278

○Dysplastic features in the neutrophils, erythroid precursors, platelets, and megakaryocytes without fulfillment of the criteria of AML with myelodysplasia related changes.

○Megakaryoblasts are medium- sized to large blasts with a round, slightly irregular, or indented nucleus with fine reticular chromatin and 1-3 nucleoli. The cytoplasm is basophilic, agranular, and may show distinct blebs or pseudopod formation. Blasts may be small with a high N:C ratio, resembling lymphoblasts. Large and small blasts may be present in the same patient. Occasionally, blasts occur in small clusters.

○Bone marrow fibrosis with variable degrees.

○If bone marrow fibrosis is extensive with dry tap, blasts percentage is estimated from the bone marrow biopsy and biopsy imprints. The histopathology of the biopsy varies with some cases have poorly differentiated blasts and others have a mixture of poorly differentiated blasts and maturing dysplastic megakaryocytes.

–Cytochemistry

○Megakaryoblasts are negative for MPO, Sudan Black B and specific esterase.

○Blasts may be positive for periodic acid Schiff (PAS) reaction and acid phosphatase and show punctate or focal non-specific esterase reactivity.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Megakaryocytic markers: Megakaryoblasts express one or more of the platelet glycoproteins: CD41, CD61 and CD42b. Cytoplasmic expression of CD41 or CD61 is more specific and sensitive than surface expression due to possible adherence of platelets to blast cells.

○Myeloid markers: CD33 is commonly expressed, but CD13 and CD117 expression are less frequent. MPO is consistently negative.

○Panleukocyte marker; CD45: Weak to negative. 278

Original page 279

○Markers of immaturity: CD34 and HLADR may be positive.

○Lymphoid markers, granulocytic markers and monocytic markers are negative.

○Aberrant markers: CD7 and CD56 may be positive.

○Immunohistochemistry in cases with fibrosis: Positive expression of von Willebrand factor, CD61, and CD42b.

–Genetic profile: Cytogenetics and mutation profiling for CBFA2T3::GLIS2, RBM15::MRTFA, NUP98::KDM5A, and KMT2A rearrangements.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○≥20% blasts with megakaryocytic differentiation in bone marrow and/or peripheral blood.

○Blasts express at least one or more of the platelet glycoproteins: CD41, CD61, or CD42b

○Does not meet criteria for other defined AML types.

○No history of myeloproliferative neoplasm.

–Desirable criterion: Evaluation for possible Down syndrome

•Prognosis: It depends on the molecular drivers:

–Down syndrome-associated cases has an excellent prognosis with high rates of chronic remission and long-term overall survival

–Non- Down syndrome cases with fusion oncogene expression have a poor prognosis.

–Adult cases has an extremely poor prognosis. 279

toc: Acute Leukemias of Mixed or Ambiguous Lineage
sections.html:
Original page 280

•Definition: It is a tumor mass consisting of myeloid blasts, with or without maturation, occurring at an anatomical site other than the bone marrow with affection of the tissue architecture.

•Epidemiology: It is rare:

–It can occur at any age. The median age is 46 to 59 years

–The male: female ratio is 1.2 :1.

•Etiology:

–The same as that of acute myeloid leukemia and other myeloid neoplasms.

–The specific reasons for homing and clustering outside the hematopoietic system as an extramedullary mass are unknown. Adhesion molecules (e.g. integrin alpha 7), chemokine receptors/ligand interactions, extracellular matrix interactions, and perturbation of the RAS pathway may be involved.

•Pathogenesis: It shares cytogenetic and molecular abnormalities with other AML:

–t(8;21)/RUNX1-RUNX1T1 “often involves the orbital region in children”.

–inv(16)/CBFB-MYH11 “more common in the abdominal region”.

–Trisomy 4 and 8.

–Monosomy 7.

–deletions of 5q and 20q

–Somatic mutations in NPM1 “monocytic differentiation”.

–KMT2A rearrangement “monocytic differentiation”

–RAS pathway mutations.

–Mutations of the epigenetic pathway, signaling, transcription, and tumour suppressor genes.

•Localization:

–Almost any site in the body can be involved.

–The most frequently affected sites are the skin, lymph nodes, gastrointestinal tract, bone, head and neck, reproductive organs, brain, and lungs. 280

Original page 281

•Association with other malignancies:

–It is reported in 2-9% of patients with acute myeloid leukemia and 5-12% of patients who have undergone allogeneic stem cell transplantation.

–It most often occurs concurrently with or as a relapse of AML. Rarely, myeloid sarcoma can precede the onset of AML.

–Myeloid sarcoma may also present as the transformation of other myeloid neoplasms, including myelodysplastic neoplasm, myeloproliferative neoplasm, MDN/MPN or myeloid neoplasm secondary to prior cytotoxic therapy. De novo isolated myeloid sarcoma with morphologically normal-appearing bone marrow is rare.

•Laboratory findings:

–Morphology:

○Macroscpic appearance: Involved organs are commonly enlarged, have a fish- flesh cut surface. Neoplasms with granulocytic maturation may appear green because cells express myeloperoxidase.

○Microscopic appearance: Large cells with cytoplasmic granules in maturing neoplastic cells. Auer rods, or morphologic features of myelodysplasia in the background may be identified.

–Cytochemistry: MPO, specific esterase, and non-specific esterase differentiate granulocytic-lineage forms and monoblastic forms.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Immunohistochemistry: Tumors with a more immature myeloid profile express CD33, CD34, CD68/KP1, and CD117.

○Staining for TdT, MPO, and CD45 is varying.

○Promyelocytic cases lack CD34 and TdT but express MPO and CD15.

○Myelomonocytic tumors are homogeneously positive for CD68/KP1, with MPO and CD68/PGM1 confined to distinct subpopulations, which are CD34-negative.

○Monoblastic variant expresses CD68/PGM1 and CD163 but lacks MPO and CD34.

○CD14 and KLF4 are also useful markers. 281

Original page 282

○The rare erythroid cases show strong positivity for glycophorin A and C, hemoglobin and CD71.

○Megakaryoblastic myeloid sarcoma expresses CD61, LAT, and von Willebrand factor.

○CD99 is positive in more than 50% of cases.

○About 20% of cases show variable degrees of CD56 expression.

○Foci of plasmacytoid dendritic cell differentiation (CD123+, CD303+, CD56) are occasionally detected, more often in cases with inv(16).

○About 16% of cases stain for NPM1 at the nuclear and cytoplasmic level which indicates the presence of NPM1 mutations.

○Aberrant antigenic expressions as cytokeratins, B-cell or T-cell markers, or CD30 are observed.

○Cases that meet the criteria for mixed-phenotype acute leukemia are not classifie as myeloid sarcoma.

–Genetic tests: See pathogenesis.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○Effacement of tissue architecture by a mass composed of myeloid blasts, with or without maturing elements.

○Positive immunophenotyping for granulocytic and/or monocytic markers.

•Prognosis:

–It is similar to that of other AML patients.

–Patients who present with isolated myeloid sarcoma appear to have a better prognosis especially with disease involving the head/neck and skin. 282

sections.t: Acute Leukemias of Mixed or Ambiguous Lineage (ALAL)
sections.html:
Original page 284

•Definition: They are leukemias composed of at least 20% abnormal progenitors that do not show differentiation along a single lineage.

•Subtypes:

–Acute undifferentiated leukemia (AUL): Lacking clear lineage commitment

–Mixed phenotype acute leukemia (MPAL): Differentiation along more than one lineage which includes:

○Biphenotypic acute leukemia: Single population of blasts expressing antigens from two or more lineages

○Bilineage acute leukemia: Two populations of blasts each of a different lineages. N.B.: Immunophenotypic features in acute leukemia may change over time or under the influence of therapy with switch from one lineage to another, especially with KMT2A rearrangements, ZNF384 fusions, DUX4 rearrangement, and PAX5 p.P80R.

•Epidemiology: It is rare, accounting for less than 4% of all acute leukemia and occurs in both children and adults.

•Diagnosis and lineage assignment:

–Lineage assignment is best performed by flow cytometric immunophenotyping

–Immunohistochemistry may be used but discrimination of normal from leukemic populations may be difficult.

–Cytochemical stains for MPO may also be used to demonstrate myeloid lineage in conjunction with flow cytometric immunophenotyping. 284

Original page 285

N.B.:T lineage: CD3 with a level of expression exceeding 50% of that seen on normal mature T cells in the same sample should be seen on at least a portion of the leukemic cells. Immunohistochemistry for CD3: Polyclonal antibodies may react with the CD3 zeta-chain also present in normal NK cells. N.B.:B lineage: When T lineage is a consideration, the specificity of CD79a for B lineage is reduced due its frequent expression in T-LL/LBL, so should not be included in the assessment of B lineage. B lineage in the absence of CD19 expression is rare but can be established by expression of three B lineage antigens as above. N.B.:Myeloid lineage: If MPO is dim and variable, its specificity is improved by an increased light scatter or expression of other myeloid associated antigens such as CD117 or bright CD13/CD33 that differs from the remaining leukemic population having more lymphoid characteristics. If MPO is dim or negative, demonstration of monocytic differentiation by flowcytometry or diffuse positivity for non-specific esterase by cytochemistry, is considered sufficient. 285

Original page 286

•Classification:

–Acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage with defining genetic abnormalities:

○Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia with BCR::ABL1 fusion

○Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia with KMT2A rearrangement

○Acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage with other defined genetic alterations

–Acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage, immunophenotypically defined:

○Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia, B/myeloid

○Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia, T/myeloid

○Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia, rare types

○Acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage, NOS

○Acute undifferentiated leukemia 286

Original page 287

Acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage with defining genetic abnormalities

○Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia with BCR::ABL1 fusion

○Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia with KMT2A rearrangement

○Acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage with other defined genetic alterations 287

sections.t: Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia with BCR::ABL1 fusion
sections.html:
Original page 288

•Definition: It is a de novo acute leukemia that fulfils the criteria for MPAL with BCR::ABL1 at initial diagnosis, without evidence of chronic myeloid leukemia.

•Synonym: MPAL with t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2)

•Clinical picture: Symptoms of anemia and thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, and/or hepatomegaly.

•Epidemiology:

–< 0.5% of all cases of acute leukemia

–15-20% of all cases of MPAL “the most common cytogenetic abnormality”

–Most patients are adults with a male predominance.

•Etiology: Unknown.

•Pathogenesis: Constitutively active tyrosine kinase.

•Laboratory findings:

–Leukocytosis, anemia and thrombocytopenia

–Blasts resemble lymphoblasts or myeloblasts, or may be dimorphic.

–Immunophenotyping: Most cases are B/myeloid, and rarely T/myeloid, B/T, or B/T/myeloid

–Karyotyping: t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) which may be accompanied with additional chromosome abnormalities.

–Molecular methods: BCR::ABL1 fusion

•Differential diagnosis:

–B-ALL with BCR::ABL1 frequently expresses myeloid-associated antigens

–AML with BCR::ABL1 may express lymphoid antigens

–Post cytotoxic therapy cases

–MPAL acquiring BCR::ABL1 secondarily at a later time during disease course.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria: 288

Original page 289

○≥20% blasts in bone marrow and/or blood with an immunophenotype that meets the diagnostic criteria for MPAL

○BCR::ABL1 and/or t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) detected at initial diagnosis.

○No prior or subsequent evidence of chronic myeloid leukemia.

○No history of exposure to cytotoxic therapy.

–Desirable criterion: Determination of the BCR::ABL1 transcript subtype and establishment of a quantitative baseline for monitoring treatment response.

• Treatment: ALL-directed therapy with tyrosine kinase inhibitor 289

toc: Acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage, immunophenotypically defined
sections.html:
Original page 290

•Definition: It is an acute leukemia that fulfills the criteria of MPAL with KMT2A (11q23.3) fusion with any partner gene.

•Clinical picture: Clinical features of cytopenias.

•Epidemiology: Rare, more common in children and relatively more common in infancy.

•Etiology: Unknown.

•Pathogenesis: KMT2A gene rearrangements result in a chimeric protein with a KMT2A-encoded amino terminus and a carboxy-terminus encoded by the partner gene. The most common partners are AFF1(AF4) at 4q21, MLLT3(AF9) at 9p22 and MLLT1 (ENL) at 19p13.

•Laboratory findings:

–Peripheral blood and bone marrow: Dimorphic blast population, including monoblasts, promonocytes and lymphoblasts. Some cases may show only one, or an undifferentiated blast morphology.

–Immunophenotyping: B/Myeloid immunophenotype and rarely B/T

–Genetic tests: KMT2A rearrangements using conventional karyotyping, FISH or RNA sequencing.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○- ≥20% blasts in bone marrow and/or blood with an immunophenotype that meets the diagnostic criteria for MPAL

○Presence of a KMT2A rearrangement.

○No history of exposure to cytotoxic therapy.

–Desirable criterion: Identification of the KMT2A fusion partner.

•Prognosis: Some reports describe it as a high-risk disease with poor survival even in younger patients. 290

Original page 291

Acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage with other defined genetic alterations

•Definition: They include acute leukemias with mixed-lineage or ambiguous immunophenotypes withnewly recognized defined genetic alterations.

•Subtypes:

–Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia with ZNF384 rearrangement

–Acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage with BCL11B rearrangement

•Epidemiology:

–MPAL with ZNF384 rearrangement: occurs in children and comprises 20% of MPAL; 48% of MPAL, B/Myeloid cases.

–ALAL with BCL11B rearrangement: comprises 10-15% of MPAL and up to one- third of MPAL, T/myeloid cases.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis: Undefined

•Laboratory findings:

–Blasts may be monotonous or dimorphic. They resemble lymphoblasts, myeloblasts, or megakaryoblasts.

–Immunophenotyping:

○MPAL with ZNF384 rearrangement: B/myeloid.

○ALAL with BCL11B rearrangement: T/myeloid.

–Genetic tests: Detection of ZNF384 and BCL11B rearrangement using RNA sequencing and FISH.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria

○- ≥20% blasts in bone marrow and/or blood expressing mixed-lineage or ambiguous immunophenotype.

○Detection of ZNF386 or BCL11B rearrangement 291

Acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage, immunophenotypically defined

Original page 292

○Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia, B/myeloid

○Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia, T/myeloid

○Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia, rare types

○Acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage, NOS

○Acute undifferentiated leukemia 292

Original page 293

•Definition: It is an acute leukemia that expresses B lineage and myeloid lineage markers but does not meet criteria for MPAL with defined genetic alterations.

•Epidemiology: Rare. Adults and children may be affected.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis: Hematopoietic stem cell/progenitor genetic alterations:

–Rearrangements of ZNF384 are common in children

–Mutations in genes encoding transcriptional regulators, particularly PAX5 and IKZF1.

–NRAS and PTPN11 mutations, resulting in activation of the RAS signaling pathway.

–Mutations in epigenetic regulators as MLLT3, KDM6A, EP300, CREBBP, TET2, EZH2, and ASXL1.

•Laboratory findings:

–Blasts may resemble lymphoblasts, monoblasts, or myeloblasts, or they may consist of dimorphic populations.

–Immunophenotyping: B/myeloid which may be bilineage and/or biphenotypic.

–Most cases have clonal cytogenetic abnormalities, including complex karyotypes, trisomy 4, del(6q), structural abnormalities of chromosome 7, and near-tetraploidy. Exclusion of defining genetic alterations in MPAL is required.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○- ≥20% blasts in bone marrow and/or blood expressing B lineage and myeloid lineage antigens.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria of MPAL with defined genetic alterations.

○No history of exposure to cytotoxic therapy

•Prognosis: It is a high-risk acute leukemia with outcomes that are intermediate between AML and B-ALL despite intensive therapy. 293

Original page 294

•Definition: It is an acute leukemia that expresses T lineage and myeloid lineage markers but does not meet criteria for MPAL with defined genetic alterations.

•Epidemiology: It is the second most common MPAL immunophenotype, representing ~20-30% of cases after excluding MPAL with BCL11B rearrangement.

•Etiology: Unknown.

•Pathogenesis:

–PICALM::MLLT10 rearrangements (10-15% of cases), resulting in a nuclear- localized fusion protein

–Other fusion genes: ETV6, NUP214 and BCL11A.

–WT1 mutations, often co-mutated with ETV6 and RUNX1 in pediatric cases

–DNMT3A and IDH2 mutations in adults.

–PHF6 mutation

•Laboratory findings:

–Blasts may resemble lymphoblasts or myeloblasts, or they may consist of dimorphic populations

–Immunophenotyping: T / myeloid which may be bilineage and/or biphenotypic. Some cases express monocytic markers

–Genetic tests:

○Exclusion of defining genetic abnormalities

○PICALM::MLLT10 rearrangement can be cryptic on conventional karyotyping.

○Mutation of RUNX1, ETV6, WT1, PHF6, and FLT3.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○≥20% blasts in BM and/or blood expressing T lineage and myeloid lineage antigens.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria of MPAL with defined genetic alterations.

○No history of exposure to cytotoxic therapy.

•Prognosis: It is regarded as a high-risk acute leukemia 294

Original page 295

•Definition: They are acute leukemias that express rare combinations of B, T, myeloid and megakaryocytic lineage markers but do not meet criteria for MPAL with defined genetic alterations.

•Subtypes:

–Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia, B/T

–Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia, B/T/Myeloid

–Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia, T/Megakaryocytic (T/Mk)

•Epidemiology:

–MPAL-B/T and MPAL-B/T/M represent ~6% and ~3% of MPAL cases occurring in children, adolescent, and young adults with a median age of ~15 years and a male:female ratio of ~1.5:1.

–MPAL-T/Mk is exceptionally rare; most reported cases are in infants with a male predominance.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis:

–Most patients have cytogenetic abnormalities.

–Mutations of PHF6, JAK3, NOTCH1, RUNX1, EVT6, IL7R, PTPN11, TP53, WT1, and DNMT3A.

–Gene fusions including SET::NUP214, DDX3X::MLLT10, CRBN::GABRB2, and SEM4B:: BCL11A.

–MPAL-T/Mk: Most cases have cytogenetic abnormalities with a non-complex karyotype, including recurrent nonconstitutional trisomy 21. CBFA2T3::GLIS2 and CBFA2T3::GLIS3 fusions have been reported.

•Laboratory findings: 295

Original page 296

–Blasts may resemble lymphoblasts or myeloblasts or megakaryoblasts, and may consist of dimorphic populations

–Immunophenotyping: B/T, B/T/Myeloid or T/Megakaryocytic

–Genetic tests:

○Exclusion of defining genetic abnormalities.

○Mutations (e.g., PHF6 and RUNX1)

○Fusion transcripts (e.g., CBFA2T3::GLIS2).

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○- ≥20% blasts in bone marrow and/or blood expressing combinations of B, T, myeloid and megakaryocytic (Mk) lineage markers.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria of MPAL with defined genetic alterations, MPAL B/Myeloid, or MPAL T/Myeloid.

○No history of exposure to cytotoxic therapy.

○No history of myeloid neoplasms.

•Prognosis: The overall survival is poor. 296

sections.t: Acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage, NOS
sections.html:
Original page 297

•Definition: It is an acute leukemia that expresses combinations of immunophenotypic lineage markers that do not permit definitive lineage assignments.

•Epidemiology: It has been reported in children and adults.

•Etiology: Unknown.

•Pathogenesis: May be mutations in epigenetic regulators, as well as components of the RAS and NOTCH pathways.

•Laboratory findings:

–Immunophenotyping: Blasts do not express lineage-specific markers but rather combinations of markers that do not allow for classification as either acute undifferentiated leukemia (AUL), mixed-phenotype acute leukemia (MPAL), or leukemia of a specific lineage.

–Full cytogenetic and molecular evaluation is generally necessary before a designation of ALAL, NOS is rendered.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○- ≥20% blasts in bone marrow and/or blood expressing combinations of immunophenotypic lineage markers that do not permit definitive lineage assignments.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria of MPAL with defined genetic alterations.

•Prognosis: They are generally considered to have a poor prognosis 297

Original page 298

•Definition: It is an acute leukemia that expresses hematopoietic stem cell markers but no markers permit lineage assignment.

•Epidemiology: It comprises 1-2 % of acute leukemias and occur more common in adults with a male:female ratio of ~1.5 :1.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis:

–About 40% of cases have abnormal karyotype, often as a non-complex karyotype.

–Recurrent gene mutations as PHF6, RUNX1, SRSF2, and ASXL1, and BCOR.

–Gene fusions such as SET::NUP214 are also detected in a subset of cases.

•Laboratory findings:

–Immunophenotyping: Blasts by definition, lack cCD3, MPO, B-cell markers such as cCD22, CD79a or strong CD19, and markers of other unusual lineages, including NK-cells, megakaryocytes, basophils or plasmacytoid dendritic cells.

–Cytochemistry: Blasts are negative for MPO and Sudan Black B by definition. Very rarely blasts may show a positive reaction with non-specific esterase.

–Mutations as PHF6, RUNX1, and SRSF2 and fusion transcripts as SET::NUP214.

•Differential diagnosis:

–AML with minimal differentiation

–Rare MPAL subtypes

–Nonhematopoietic malignancies.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○≥20% blasts in bone marrow and/or blood lacking expression of immunophenotypic lineage markers.

○Not fulfilling diagnostic criteria of MPAL with defined genetic alterations or rare MPAL subtypes. 298

Myeloid Neoplasms, Secondary

Original page 299

•Definition: Myeloid neoplasms that arise secondary to exposure to cytotoxic therapy or germline predisposition.

•They include:

–Myeloid neoplasms post cytotoxic therapy

–Myeloid neoplasms associated with germline predisposition

–Myeloid neoplasms associated with Down syndrome 299

Original page 300

•Definition:Myelodysplastic neoplasms, myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms, and acute myeloid leukemia that arise in a patient with a history of exposure to DNA-damaging cytotoxic chemotherapy and/or large field radiation therapy. N.B.: Progression of myeloproliferative neoplasms and evolution of primary MDS or primary MDS/MPN to AML are excluded from this category.

•Subtypes:

–Myelodysplastic neoplasms post cytotoxic therapy

–Myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms post cytotoxic therapy

–Acute myeloid leukemia post cytotoxic therapy.

•Epidemiology:

–It account for 10- 20% of cases of AML, MDS and MDS/MPN.

–The incidence varies depending on the underlying disease and the treatment strategy:

○Most patients have been treated for either solid tumour malignancy or non- myeloid hematological malignancy.

○Some patients have a history of cytotoxic therapy for a non-neoplastic disorder, commonly an autoimmune condition.

•Etiology: 1-Alkylating agents:Melphalan, cyclophosphamide, nitrogen mustard, chlorambucil, busulfan, carboplatin, cisplatin, dacarbazine, procarbazine, carmustine, mitomycin C, thiotepa, lomustine. 2-Ionizing radiation therapy:Large fields containing active bone marrow. 3-Topoisomerase II inhibitors:Etoposide, teniposide, doxorubicin, daunorubicin, mitoxantrone, amsacrine, actinomycin. 4-Others:

–Antimetabolites: thiopurines, mycophenolate mofetil, fludarabine. 300

Original page 301

–Antitubulin agents (usually in combination with other agents): vincristine, vinblastine, vindesine, paclitaxel, docetaxel.

–PARP1 inhibitors. 5-Adjunctive use of hematopoietic growth factors during chemotherapy. 6-The primary role of therapies such as hydroxyurea, radioisotopes, L- asparaginase, purine analogue, mycophenolate mofetil and limited-field radiation therapy is unclear.

•Pathogenesis: Cytotoxic therapy induces mutations in DNA damage-sensing or repair genes of the hematopoietic stem cells leading to expansion of pre-existing hematopoietic clones especially in individuals with a predisposition as:

○Clonal hematopoiesis in genes TP53, PPM1D, DNMT3A, ASXL1, TET2

○Polymorphisms in genes such as NQO1 that affect drug metabolism.

○Inherited germline mutations

○Polymorphisms in genes involved in DNA damage response and Fanconi anemia pathways.

•Presentation:

301

Original page 302

•Laboratory findings:

–Peripheral blood:

○AML, MDS or MDS/MPN.

○One or more cytopenias with multilineage dysplasia

○Normoblastemia, macrocytosis and poikilocytosis.

○Dysplastic neutrophils including abnormal nuclear segmentation and hypogranular cytoplasm.

○Monocytosis may occur.

–Bone marrow:

○AML, MDS or MDS/MPN.

○Multilineage dysplasia.

–Immunophenotyping: Variable results similar to the de novo counterparts:

○Blasts are CD34 positive.

○The maturing myeloid cells show abnormal patterns of antigen expression and abnormal light-scattering.

○Blasts express panmyeloid antigens such as CD13, CD33, and MPO, with downregulation of MPO in some patients.

○Immunohistochemical staining of bone marrow biopsies demonstrates TP53 mutations which is associated with a poor prognosis.

○Expression of lymphoid markers (CD19, cCD79, cCD3, CD5, CD7, CD25) is common.

–Genetic tests: Variable results similar to the de novo counterparts:

○Abnormal karyotyping in 70-90% of cases.

○Complex karyotypes predominate, with loss of 5q, 7q, and 17p.

○Other frequent abnormalities include loss of 12p, 13q, 18q, and 20q and gains of 1q and 21q.

○IPSS-R high- and very-high-risk cases o MDS are common.

○Mutations in TP53 are frequent with ≥2 mutations, 302

Original page 303

○Other mutations include truncating mutations in PPM1D and DNA damage response genes and mutations in SRSF2, SF3B1, U2AF1, ZRSR2, ASXL1, EZH2, BCOR, STAG2 genes.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○Myeloid neoplasm meeting diagnostic criteria of any myelodysplastic neoplasm, myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm, or acute myeloid leukemia.

○History of prior exposure to cytotoxic therapy and/or large-field radiation therapy for an unrelated disorder.

○Not meeting diagnostic criteria of myeloproliferative neoplasms.

–Desirable criterion: Detection of clonal molecular and/or chromosomal alterations.

•Prognosis:

–Poor prognosis influenced by:

○The associated karyotypic abnormality with the outcome of IPSS-R categories is inferior compared to de novo counterparts: Patients with aberrations of chromosome 5 and/or 7, TP53 mutations, or a complex karyotype have a particularly poor outcome, with a median survival of less than 1 year irrespective of blast count.

○The type of myeloid neoplasm

○The underlying neoplasm.

–Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may improve survival, with outcomes that appear to be influenced by antecedent clonal hematopoiesis. 303

sections.t: Myeloid Neoplasm Associated with Germline Predisposition
sections.html:
Original page 304

•Definition: They include acute myeloid leukemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms, myeloproliferative neoplasms, and MDS/MPN that arise in individuals with genetic conditions associated with increased risk of myeloid malignancies.

•Epidemiology:

–Children and adolescents: Germline (Pathogenic) P/(Likely Pathologenic) LP alleles in SAMD9, SAMD9L, and GATA2 are the most frequent causes of MDS, especially those with monosomy 7.

–Adults 18-40 years: Germline mutations in DNA repair genes and telomere biology disorders cause:

○MDS in 19% of cases

○Aplastic anemia in 15% of cases.

○AML at least 5% of individuals.

○Elderly: Germline DDX41 mutations typically cause MDS.

•Pathogenesis: Patients should acquire additional somatic events to develop myeloid neoplasms but not all events are associated with transformation.

•Laboratory Findings:

–Bone marrow:

○Cases may be presented with severe aplastic anemia, MDS/AML, or normal bone marrow findings

○Bone marrow is hypocellular but may be hypercellular with myeloid hyperplasia.

○Multilineage dysplasia. 304

Original page 305

○Peritrabecular myeloid precursor expansion and promyelocyte arrest with decreased to absent mature neutrophils, and increased eosinophils.

○Reticulin fibrosis.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Altered leukocyte subset frequency in adults.

○Asynchronous maturation of granulocytes in children.

○Aberrant antigen expression.

–Genetic tests:

○Specific functional tests:

▪Telomere length measurement for telomere biology disorders.

▪Chromosomal breakage for Fanconi anaemia.

○DNA Sequencing from cultured skin fibroblasts or capillary bulbs.

○Patients have an increased frequency of clonal hematopoiesis.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–Essential criteria:

○Detection of germline mutation.

○Changes consistent with myeloid neoplasm with features of MDS, or with ≥20% blasts in blood and/or bone marrow.

–Desirable criteria:

○Clonal molecular and/or cytogenetic abnormalities in addition to the germline mutation.

○Positive family history as determined by formal genetic counseling. 305

Original page 306

•Prognosis: It depends both on the specific germline predisposition and the myeloid malignancy itself:

–Myeloid malignancies require stem cell transplantation and some patients require chemotherapy cycles prior to transplantation.

–Patients with bone marrow failure and multi-organ dysfunction have a poor prognosis due to intolerance of intensive chemotherapy cycles prior to transplantation. Other myeloid malignancies are associated with the same prognosis of sporadic myeloid neoplasms.

•Subtypes: 1-Myeloid neoplasms with germline predisposition without a pre-existing disorder or organ dysfunction. 2-Myeloid neoplasms with germline predisposition and pre-existing platelet disorders. 3-Myeloid neoplasms with germ line predisposition and potential organ dysfunction. 306

sections.t: Myeloid neoplasms with germline predisposition without a pre-existing
sections.html:
Original page 307

disorder or organ dysfunction

•They include:

–Germline predisposition due to CEBPA P/LP variants.

–Germline predisposition due to DDX41 P/LP variants.

–Li-Fraumeni Syndrome

Germline predisposition due to CEBPA P/LP variants:

–Autosomal dominant inheritance.

–Germline CEBPA mutation leads to altered transcriptional regulation and second allele mutations are common.

–It has a wide age range.

–AML is an indication for allogeneic stem cell transplantation in first remission because of the development of independent AML clones, because their germline mutation remains. Germline predisposition due to DDX41 P/LP variants:

–Autosomal dominant inheritance.

–Unclear Pathogenesis.

–It is more in adults.

–Male mutation carriers develop myeloid malignancies more often than female.

–Mostly normal karyotype.

Li-Fraumeni Syndrome:

–Autosomal dominant inheritance.

–TP53 mutations which causes disruption of DNA repair and gene expression

–It has a wide age range. 307

disorders

Germline predisposition due to RUNX1 P/LP variants:

–It has a wide age range.

–It is more in adults.

Germline predisposition due to ETV6 P/LP variants:

–Autosomal dominant inheritance.

–It has a wide age range.

Original page 309

Myeloid neoplasms with germ line predisposition and potential organ dysfunction

–Germline predisposition due to GATA2 P/LP variants.

–Severe congenital neutropenia.

–Shwachman Diamond Syndrome.

–Fanconi anaemia.

–Dyskeratosis congenita.

–Noonan syndrome.

–CBL Syndrome.

–Neurofibromatosis type I.

–Down syndrome.

–Germline predisposition due to SAMD9 P/LP variants.

–Germline predisposition due to SAMD9L P/LP variants.

–Bloom Syndrome. Germline predisposition due to GATA2 P/LP variants:

–Autosomal dominant inheritance.

–It causes disruption of transcription factor function

–It is common in adolescents and young adults

–It is associated with immunodeficiencies, lymphedema, and many other disorders. Severe congenital neutropenia:

–Autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance.

–It causes abnormal protein folding and ER stress response

–It occurs in adolescents and young adults

–It is associated with severe opportunistic infections without growth factor support. 309

Original page 310

Shwachman Diamond Syndrome:

–Autosomal recessive inheritance.

–It causes disruption of ribosome biology

–It is more in childhood

–It is associated with exocrine pancreatic dysfunction, variable cytopenias, skeletal dysplasia, and hepatomegaly and may be non-syndromic aplastic anemia or MDS/AML. Fanconi anemia:

–Autosomal recessive inheritance.

–It causes impairment of Fanconi pathway of inter-strand crosslink DNA repair

–It is more in childhood.

–It is associated with congenital malformations, facial dysmorphism , bone marrow failure, squamous cell carcinomas, liver tumors and sensitivity to genotoxic agents. Dyskeratosis congenital:

–Autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and X-linked inheritance.

–It causes disruption of telomere maintenance,

–It is more in adults.

–It is associated with muco-cutaneous triad of nail/hair abnormalities, skin rash, and leukoplakia, bone marrow failure, pulmonary fibrosis, liver cirrhosis, squamous cell carcinoma and vascular anomalies and may present as non-syndromic aplastic anemia or Monosomy 7 MDS. Noonan syndrome:

–It causes over-activation of the RAS pathway signaling

–Autosomal recessive inheritance.

–It is common in Infancy.

–It is associated with JMML and JMML-like MPN and ALL later in life. 310

Original page 311

–It is associated with developmental disorder with characteristic facies, short stature, congenital heart defect, coagulation defects, lymphatic dysplasias, and developmental delay of variable degree. CBL Syndrome:

–Autosomal dominant inheritance.

–It causes over-activation of the RAS pathway signaling

–It occurs in early childhood.

–It is associated with JMML and JMMLlike MPN.

–It is associated with Noonan syndrome-like developmental disorder with highly variable expressivity and vasculopathy. Neurofibromatosis type I:

–Autosomal dominant inheritance.

–It causes over-activation of the RAS pathway signaling

–It is more in childhood.

–It is associated with JMML, AML or ALL and various solid tumors including nervous system tumors.

–It is associated with neurocutaneous genetic disorder with café-au-lait spots, Lisch nodules, axillary freckling, and neurofibromas. Down syndrome:

–It causes disruption of fetal hematopoiesis in cooperation with GATA-1 mutation.

–It occurs in childhood and causes ALL later in life.

–It is associated with low risk of solid tumors.

–It is associated with developmental disorder with characteristic facies, variable intellectual disability, muscular hypotonia, joint laxity, and various anomalies such as cardiac, gastrointestinal, neurosensorial or endocrine defects. 311

Original page 312

Germline predisposition due to SAMD9 P/LP variants:

–Autosomal dominant inheritance.

–It causes alteration of cellular proliferation pathways

–It is more in childhood.

–It is associated with MIRAGE syndrome (MDS with Infections, Renal abnormalities, Adrenal Insufficiency, Genitourinary anomalies, Enteropathy) and may be presented as non-syndromic monosomy 7 MDS or bone marrow failure. Germline predisposition due to SAMD9L P/LP variants:

–Autosomal dominant inheritance.

–It causes alteration of cellular proliferation pathways

–It is more in childhood.

–It is associated with ataxia-pancytopenia Syndrome and may be presented as non-syndromic monosomy 7 MDS or bone marrow failure. Bloom Syndrome:

–Autosomal recessive inheritance.

–It causes abnormal DNA helicase leading to high number of sister chromatid exchanges and quadri-radial configurations

–It is more in adults.

–It is associated with prenatal growth deficiency, mild immunodeficiency, excessive photosensitivity with facial lupus-like skin lesions, type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypogonadism. 312
