sections.t: Myeloid proliferations associated with Down syndrome
toc: Myeloid/lymphoid Neoplasms with Eosinophilia and Defining Gene Rearrangement
sections.html:
Original page 317

•Definition: They are clonal myeloid proliferation arising in children with constitutional trisomy 21: transient abnormal myelopoiesis and myeloid leukemia of Down syndrome.

•Subtypes:

–Transient abnormal myelopoiesis associated with Down syndrome (TAM).

–Myeloid leukemia associated with Down syndrome (ML-DS).

•Epidemiology of TAM:

–TAM is the most common leukemia in neonates.

–AML is 150-fold more in young children with Down syndrome compared with non-Down children.

–25-30% of newborns with Down syndrome have TAM with GATA1 mutation. 10% of them are manifested clinically while 15% are asymptomatic

•Etiology: Unknown.

•Pathogenesis:

–TAM: Somatic mutations in exon 2/3 of GATA1 encode a shorter GATA1 protein (GATA1s) lacking the N-terminal activation domain which is leukemogenic only in trisomy 21 disrupting fetal and early postnatal hematopoiesis causing blast cell accumulation in blood, liver and other tissues.

–ML-DS: Somatic mutations in exon 2/3 of GATA1 with additional acquired mutations, usually in cohesin, epigenetic regulators or tyrosine kinase genes. The exact mechanism of ML-DS development is unknown.

•Clinical picture:

–TAM:

○Most patients present within 7 days of birth.

○It ranges from an asymptomatic disease to life-threatening disorders including hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, vesico-papular skin rash, pleural and/or pericardial effusion and cholestatic jaundice. Mortality is usually from progressive liver failure. 317

Original page 318

–ML-DS:

○Median age is 1.6 years.

○It is preceded by an MDS phase and half of patients have a history of TAM.

•Laboratory findings:

–CBC:

○TAM:

▪Leukocytosis which may be extreme with increased blasts.

▪Anemia.

▪Platelet counts may be normal, reduced or increased.

○Overt ML-DS: It is preceded by an MDS phase with pancytopenia.

–Morphology:

○PB blasts almost always exceed BM blasts.

○Blasts vary from undifferentiated myeloblasts, to typical small megakaryoblasts with cytoplasmic blebbing or large, partially-differentiated megakaryoblasts.

○Normoblastemia and circulating megakaryocytes.

○Fibrosis bwith dry tap.

–Immunophenotyping: TAM blasts usually express CD117 and variable expression of CD34, CD7, CD36, CD41/42b and/or CD235a.

–Genetic tests:

○Cells with mutated GATA1 may be infrequent leading to false-negative results. Analysis should be performed in the first week after birth while PB blasts are present to avoid false negatives.

○Mutation of cohesin complex genes (STAG2, RAD21, SMC1A, CTCF), EZH2, KANSL1 and JAK3.

•Diagnostic criteria:

–TAM:

○Essential criteria: -

▪Confirmation of constitutional trisomy 21. 318

Original page 319

▪Peripheral blood leukocytosis with increased blasts

▪Detection of exon 2/3 GATA1 mutation (GATA1 exon 2/3 sequencing should be performed in all cases with peripheral blood blasts >10%).

–ML-DS:

○Essential criteria:

▪Confirmation of constitutional trisomy 21.

▪Myeloid neoplasm with persistent increased peripheral blood and/or bone marrow blasts (may be < 20%).

▪Detection of exon 2/3 GATA1 mutation.

○Desirable criterion: Mutation profiling and detection of mutations in other genes, e.g. cohesin complex, EZH2, KANSL1 and/or JAK3.

•Prognosis:

–TAM:

○It resolves in 2-3 months without treatment in >90% of patients and 20% of clinical TAM later develop ML-DS.

○Risk factors for early death in severe TAM include:

▪Preterm delivery.

▪Ascites.

▪Leukocyte count >100x10/l. 9

▪Hepatomegaly.

▪Coagulopathy.

–ML-DS: Prognosis is better than AML in children without Down syndrome

–Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is reserved for relapse. 319

Myeloid/lymphoid Neoplasms with Eosinophilia and Defining Gene Rearrangement

Original page 320

•Definition: This is a family of diseases of myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms generated by dysregulated fusion of tyrosine kinase genes commonly associated with eosinophilia but eosinophilia is not invariable.

•Classes:

–Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with PDGFRA rearrangement

–Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with PDGFRB rearrangement

–Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with FGFR1 rearrangement

–Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with JAK2 rearrangement

–Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with FLT3 rearrangement

–Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with ETV6::ABL1 fusion

–Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with other tyrosine kinase fusion genes 320

Original page 321

•Definition: This includes myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms, frequently associated with eosinophilia and characterized by PDGFRA gene rearrangement.

•Epidemiology: Rare.

–Strong male predominance (7:1).

–The median age is the 5th decade of life

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis:

–FIP1L1::PDGFRA activates multiple signaling molecules including phosphatidylinositol- 3-kinase, ERK1/2, and STAT5 inducing malignant transformation.

–Complications result from tissue infiltration by eosinophils and/or cytokine- induced injury.

•Clinical picture:

–Weakness and fatigue, pruritus, cough, dyspnea and other respiratory, cardiac and gastrointestinal symptoms.

–Hepatosplenomegaly.

–Complications: Endomyocardial fibrosis, cardiomyopathy, cardiac valve injury and venous and arterial thromboembolic events, and pulmonary fibrosis.

•Laboratory diagnosis

–The majority of cases manifest as myeloproliferative neoplasms or myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms, typically in chronic and less frequently in blast phase of myeloid or lymphoid lineage.

–CBC:

○Prominent eosinophilia is common but is not invariable.

○Relative and absolute neutrophilia

○Relative basophil and monocyte counts are within normal.

○Anemia and thrombocytopenia. 321

Original page 322

–Bone marrow:

○Hypercellular with increased eosinophils, mast cells and CharcotLeyden crystals. Mast cells are scattered or form loose clusters.

○Reticulin fibrosis is common.

○Necrosis may be seen.

–Biochemistry:

○Serum tryptase: ≥ 12 ng/mL and can replace FIP1L1::PDGFRA fusion in the absence of appropriate molecular methods.

○Serum vitamin B12: Markedly increased.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Eosinophils may show expression of activation markers such as CD23, CD25, and CD69.

○Mast cells are positive for CD117 and tryptase with aberrant expression of CD25, but CD2 expression is negative.

–Genetic tests:

○Cryptic deletion of 4q12 resulting in formation of FIP1L1::PDGFRA fusion

○Other partner genes include KIF5B, CDK5RAP2, STRN, ETV6, BCR, and TNKS2.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: Favorable:

–Imatinib is effective in both the chronic and blast phases.

–Poor prognostics include: Initial presentation with blast phase, complex karyotype, and cardiac involvement. 322

Original page 323

•Definition: This includes myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms, with eosinophilia and PDGFRB gene rearrangement.

•Epidemiology:

–The median age is in the 5th decade of life

–There is male predominance.

•Etiology: Unknown.

•Pathogenesis: Rearrangements involving PDGFRB lead to the formation of an aberrant, constitutively activated tyrosine kinase.

•Clinical picture:

–Splenomegaly

–Hepatomegaly.

–B symptoms.

–Cardiac failure may occur as a result of direct tissue damage.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Most cases manifest with myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm especially chronic myelomonocytic leukemia with eosinophilia and less commonly myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm with neutrophilia with eosinophilia, chronic eosinophilic leukemia or other myeloproliferative neoplasms with eosinophilia.

–Cases with ≥20% blasts are best classified as blast phase of myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with PDGFRB fusion gene.

–Cases of BCR::ABL1-like B-lymphoblastic leukemia having PDGFRB gene rearrangement with evidence of a coexisting myeloid neoplasm are diagnosed as myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with PDGFRB fusion gene in lymphoid transformation. 323

Original page 324

–Cases of BCR::ABL1-like B-lymphoblastic leukemia having PDGFRB gene rearrangement but lacking eosinophilia, monocytosis, dysplasia or myelofibrosis are best classified as BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL.

–Cases which fulfill the diagnostic criteria for systemic mastocytosis, with PDGFRB fusion are classified as as myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with PDGFRB rearrangement.

–CBC:

○Prominent eosinophilia, although eosinophilia is not universal. Eosinophilia have normal morphology

○Leukocytosis

○Variable degrees of neutrophilia and monocytosis

○No basophilia.

○Anemia

○No thrombocytopenia

–Biochemistry: Serum tryptase may be mildly or moderately elevated.

–Bone marrow:

○Hypercellular with increased myeloid:erythroid ratio and variably increased neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes and their precursors.

○Abnormal eosinophils

○Abnormal megakaryocytes with either myelodysplastic-type and/or myeloproliferative-type features,

○Dysgranulopoiesis and dyserythropoiesis are less frequent

○Mast cells may be increased and may include atypical spindled forms.

○Significant fibrosis.

–Genetic tests:

○The most common cytogenetic alteration is t(5;12)(q32;p13.2) resulting in ETV6::PDGFRB.

○Complex chromosomal rearrangements are common. 324

Original page 325

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis:

–Extremely sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib with no relapse or progression to blast-phase.

–Bad prognostics: Complex karyotype and initial presentation with blast-phase. 325

Original page 326

•Definition: This is a heterogenous group of hematological neoplasms with FGFR1 rearrangement, associated with eosinophilia

•Epidemiology:

–Median age is in the 4th decade of life

–Mild male predilection (1.5:1).

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis:

–The FGFR1 fusion genes lead constitutive activation of the FGFR1 tyrosine kinase and associated downstream signaling pathways.

–The fusion partners may impact clinical presentation:

○ZMYM2::FGFR1 is associated with T-lymphoblastic leukemia,

○BCR::FGFR1 and TPR::FGFR1 are associated with myeloproliferative neoplasms with basophilia

○CEP43::FGFR1 and CNTRL::FGFR1 are associated with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia. The former is associated with a polycythemia-vera.

–Lymphadenopathy.

•Clinical picture:

–Lymphadenopathy.

–Mediastinal mass

–Splenomegaly

–Hypermetabolism and B symptoms.

–Eosinophilia is very common, but not invariable.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–It may manifest as precursor B-cell, T-cell, myeloid or mixed-phenotype leukemias or myeloproliferative neoplasms or myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms.

–The phenotype may change throughout the course of disease. 326

Original page 327

–Cases with ≥20% blasts at initial presentation or during the course of the disease are best classified as blast phase of myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with FGFR1 fusion gene.

–CBC:

○Cytopenia

○Eosinophilia is very common, but not invariable.

–Bone marrow: Normocellular or hypercellular with eosinophilia.

–Immunophenotyping:

○It is commonly bi- or multilineal although only one component may predominate.

○Involvement of lymph nodes by lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, most often reported as being of T-cell lineage, but myeloid/T-cell neoplasms and less often myeloid sarcoma may be a manifestation. B lineage is rare

–Genetic tests:

○Rearrangement of FGFR1 at 8p11by karyotyping confirmed by FISH, RT- PCR and RNA-sequencing

○The most common partner gene is ZMYM2/13q12.11 followed by CNTRL, and CEP43, respectively, but at least 14 partner genes have been described.

○Trisomy 21.

○Concurrent mutations of RUNX1 contributing to disease progression.

○Monoclonal TCR rearrangements in some cases.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: Aggressive. 327

Original page 328

•Definition: This includes myeloid and/or lymphoid neoplasms associated with a JAK2 fusion.

•Epidemiology:

–Male (27:5|).

–The median age is in the fifth decade of life.

•Etiology: Unknown.

•Pathogenesis:

–Formation of a JAK2 fusion gene results in constitutive activation of the JAK- STAT pathway leading to dysregulated proliferation of myeloid, erythroid, B- or T-lymphoid lineage cells.

–ETV6::JAK2: BCR::ABL1-like B ALL

–BCR::JAK2: MDS/MPN with neutrophilia or BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL.

•Clinical picture:

–Hepatosplenomegaly

–Lymphadenopathy.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Patients may present as chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms (i.e. chronic eosinophilic leukemia, primary myelofibrosis, etc) or myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms with neutrophilia and/or monocytosis often associated with eosinophilia.

–Some patients initially present with or progress to blast-phase disease of myeloid, B-cell or T-cell lineage.

–Patients of de novo B-ALL with PCM1::JAK2 and no apparent myeloid/myeloproliferative component or eosinophilia may be best classified as BCR::ABL1-like BALL

–Cases presenting as B-ALL with a prior history of a chronic myeloid neoplasm, are diagnosed as myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with JAK2 rearrangement. 328

Original page 329

–Eosinophil morphology: Variable ranging from morphologically unremarkable forms to abnormal/dysplastic forms. Eosinophilic precursors may be increased.

–CBC:

○Cytopenias or cytoses

○Varying degrees of eosinophilia up to hypereosinophilia. Patients with partners other than PCM1 may not be associated with prominent eosinophilia.

○Monocytosis

○Neutrophilia with shift to left.

–Bone marrow:

○Hypercellular with eosinophilia.

○Myelofibrosis is common.

○Erythroid hyperplasia and prominent dyserythropoiesis

○Megakaryocytes may be decreased.

○Mild dysgranulopoiesis and dysmegakaryopoiesis may be present.

○PCM1::JAK2: “Typical triad” of bone marrow hypercellularity with eosinophilia, large aggregates of immature erythroid precursors, and myelofibrosis.

–Genetic tests

○The most common fusion partner for this entity is PCM1. Other partners include but are not limited to ETV6/12p13.2 and BCR/22q11.2.

○It may be visible on routine karyotyping or cryptic detected by FISH, RT- PCR or RNA sequencing

○Concurrent mutations of ASXL1, BCOR, ETV6, RUNX1, SRSF2, TET2, and TP53 genes

•Diagnostic criteria:

329

Original page 330

•Prognosis:

–Variable between chronic phase disease and a more aggressive blast-phase disease.

–Resistant to first and second generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors and may respond to the JAK2 inhibitor, ruxolitinib, but the response is usually short term with relapse within 1 to 2 years.

–Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation should be considered early for eligible patients. 330

Original page 331

•Definition: They are hematological neoplasms associated with gene rearrangements with formation of a fusion gene involving Fms-related receptor tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3).

•Clinical picture:

–Lymphadenopathy

–Splenomegaly

–Lytic bone lesions.

•Epidemiology:

–More common in men (1.4:1.0).

–The median age is in the 5th decade of life.

•Etiology: The etiology remains unknown.

•Pathogenesis: The formation of the FLT3 fusion gene leads to constitutive phosphorylation and growth factor/ligand-independent proliferation.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Most patients are diagnosed in chronic phase as MDS, MPNs including chronic eosinophilic leukemia or juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia; MDS/MPNs including chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, or acute leukemia of myeloid, T- cell or B-cell lineage.

–Cases with ≥20% blasts at initial presentation or during the course of the disease are best classified as blast phase of myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with FLT3 fusion gene.

–Cases fulfilling diagnostic criteria for systemic mastocytosis are best classified as myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with FLT3 fusion gene.

–Cases with secondary acquisition of FLT3 fusion genes are excluded from this category.

–Cases with rearrangements of 13q12 not involving FLT3 are excluded from this diagnosis. 331

Original page 332

–CBC:

○Leukocytosis

○Anemia

○Thrombocytopenia.

○Eosinophilia is common but not invariable.

○There may be monocytosis.

–Genetic tests:

–Chromosomal rearrangements involving 13q12 by karyotyping. Cyptic cases (especially if the partner gene is ZMYM2 at13q12) need FISH, RT-PCR or RNA sequencing.

○The most common partner gene is ETV6/12p131. Additional partners include BCR/22q11, ZMYM2/13q12, TRIP11/14q32, SPTBN1/2p16, GOLGB1/3q13, CCDC88C/14 q32, ZBTB44/11q24 and MYO18A/17q12.

○Complex karyotype.

○Mutations of ASXL1, SETBP1, U2AF1, STAT5B, TP53, SRSF2, TET2, RUNX1, and PTPN11 genes.

•Diagnostic criteris

•Prognosis: Aggressive clinical course. 332

Original page 333

•Definition: It is a hematopoietic stem cell neoplasm associated with fusion of ETV6 and ABL1 genes.

•Clinical picture: Splenomegaly.

•Epidemiology:

–The male-to-female ratio is 1.9:1. Patients presenting with myeloid phenotype are predominantly male.

–Median age of presentation is in the fifth decade of life.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis: ETV6::ABL1 due to t(9;12)(q34;p13) which leads to activation of the non-receptor tyrosine kinase ABL1 with initiation of downstream pathways affecting cellular survival, growth rate and independence as well as transforming capacity.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Diagnosis is typically made in chronic phase and should be separated from B- lymphoblastic ALL with ETV6::ABL1

–CBC:

○Eosinophilia is nearly universal in cases manifesting as myeloid neoplasms and less common in cases presenting as lymphoblastic leukemia.

○Leukocytosis

○Anemia

○Thrombocytosis or thrombocytopenia

○Basophilia

–Bone marrow:

○Hypercellular with increased myeloid:erythroid ratio

○Prominent eosinophilia +/- basophilia.

○Megakaryocytes may show abnormal morphology (either hypo- or hyperlobated) and abnormal clustering 333

Original page 334

–Genetic tests:

○Chromosome banding analysis is insufficient as it results from cytogenetically cryptic inversions, insertions or complex rearrangements

○FISH with a combination of ETV6 and ABL1 probes, RT-PCR, or RNA sequencing are more reliable.

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: Poor with an aggressive course if left untreated. Complete and durable remissions have been reported with ABL1-inhibitors. 334

sections.t: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with other tyrosine kinase fusion genes
sections.html:
Original page 335

•Definition: They are myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms, associated with eosinophilia, resulting from the formation of a tyrosine kinase fusion gene other than those associated with specific myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms

•Clinical picture:

–Constitutional symptoms

–Bone pain

–Lymphadenopathy

–Splenomegaly

•Epidemiology:

–Male predominance is suggested

–Age range is variable (1-82 years old). Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with ALK fusion genes are more commonly reported in children, but have been reported in adults.

•Etiology: Unknown

•Pathogenesis: Formation of a tyrosine fusion gene results in neoplastic transformation of a pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell.

•Laboratory diagnosis:

–Cases with ≥20% blasts at initial presentation or during the course of the disease are best classified as blast phase of myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with a tyrosine kinase fusion gene.

–Cases with tyrosine kinase fusion gene secondary genetic event are excluded from this class.

–CBC:

○Eosinophilia is common.

○Leukocytosis

○Anemia

○Thrombocytopenia

○Monocytosis. 335

Original page 336

–Bone marrow:

○Hypercellular

○Morphologic features overlapping between MDS and MPN

○Eosinophilia, +/- monocytosis.

○Blasts may or may not be increased.

○Mast cell proliferations with abnormal morphology (i.e.spindled)

○There may be fibrosis.

–Immunophenotyping:

○Mast cell proliferations with abnormal immunophenotype (CD25+, CD123)

○T-cell differentiation is more common in the lymphoid component and may manifest both as T-lymphoblastic lymphoma or rarely as peripheral T cell lymphoma.

–Genetic tests:

○Tyrosine kinase fusion genes include ETV6::FGFR2; ETV6::LYN; ETV6::NTRK3; RANBP2::ALK; BCR::RET and FGFR1OP::RET.

○Complex and cryptic rearrangements may occur.

○Karyotyping is typically abnormal and may provide a clue to the specific genes involved

○Diagnosis is made by FISH probes and RNA-sequencing

•Diagnostic criteria:

•Prognosis: Not well defined 336
